On en dirait autant des degrés de saturation. En effet, si les diverses intensités d'une couleur correspondent à autant de nuances différentes comprises entre cette couleur et le noir, les degrés de saturation sont comme des nuances intermédiaires entre cette même couleur et le blanc pur. Toute couleur, dirions-nous, peut être envisagée sous un double aspect, au point de vue du noir et au point de vue du blanc. Le noir serait à l'intensité ce que le blanc est à la saturation. On comprendra maintenant le sens des expériences photométriques. Une bougie, placée à une certaine distance d'une feuille de papier, l'éclaire d'une certaine manière : vous doublez la distance, et vous constatez qu'il faut quatre bougies pour éveiller en vous la même sensation. De là vous concluez que, si vous aviez doublé la distance sans augmenter l'intensité de la source lumineuse, l'effet d'éclairage eût été quatre fois moins considérable. Mais il est trop évident qu'il s'agit ici de l'effet physique, et non pas psychologique. Car on ne peut pas dire que nous ayons comparé deux sensations entre elles : nous avons utilisé une sensation unique, pour comparer entre elles deux sources lumineuses différentes, la seconde quadruple de la première mais deux fois plus éloignée qu'elle. En un mot, le physicien ne fait jamais intervenir des sensations doubles ou triples les unes des autres, mais seulement des sensations identiques, destinées à servir d'intermédiaires entre deux quantités physiques qu'on pourra alors égaler l'une à l'autre. La sensation lumineuse joue ici le rôle de ces inconnues auxiliaires que le mathématicien introduit dans ses calculs, et qui disparaissent du résultat final. Tout autre est l'objet du psychophysicien : c'est la sensation lumineuse elle-même qu'il étudie, et qu'il prétend mesurer. Tantôt il procédera à une intégration de différences infiniment petites, selon la méthode de Fechner ; tantôt il comparera directement une sensation à une autre sensation. Cette dernière méthode, due à Plateau et à Delbœuf, diffère beaucoup moins qu'on ne l'a cru jusqu'ici de celle de Fechner; mais, comme elle porte plus spécialement sur les sensations lumineuses, nous nous en occuperons d'abord. M. Delbœuf place un observateur en présence de trois anneaux concentriques à éclat variable. Un dispositif ingénieux lui permet de faire passer chacun de ces anneaux par toutes les teintes intermédiaires entre le blanc et le noir. Supposons deux de ces teintes grises simultanément produites sur deux anneaux, et maintenues invariables ; nous les appellerons A et B par exemple. M. Delbœuf fait varier l'éclat C du troisième anneau, et demande à l'observateur de lui dire si, à un moment donné, la teinte grise B lui paraît également éloignée des deux autres. Un moment arrive, en effet, où celui-ci déclare le contraste AB égal au contraste BC ; de telle sorte qu'on pourrait construire, selon M. Delbœuf, une échelle d'intensités lumineuses où l'on passerait de chaque sensation à la suivante par contrastes sensibles égaux : nos sensations se mesureraient ainsi les unes par les autres. Nous ne suivrons pas M. Delbœuf dans les conclusions qu'il a tirées de ces remarquables expériences : la question essentielle, la question unique, selon nous, est de savoir si un contraste AB, formé des éléments A et B, est réellement égal à un contraste BC, composé différemment. Le jour où l'on aurait établi que deux sensations peuvent être égales sans être identiques, la psychophysique serait fondée. Mais c'est cette égalité qui nous paraît contestable : il est facile d'expliquer, en effet, comment une sensation d'intensité lumineuse peut être dite à égale distance de deux autres. Supposons un instant que, depuis notre naissance, les variations d'intensité d'une source lumineuse se fussent traduites à notre conscience par la perception successive des diverses couleurs du spectre. Il n'est pas douteux que ces couleurs nous apparaîtraient alors comme autant de notes d'une gamme, comme des degrés plus ou moins élevés dans une échelle, comme des grandeurs en un mot. D'autre part, il nous serait facile d'assigner à chacune d'elles sa place dans la série. En effet, si la cause extensive varie d'une manière continue, la sensation colorée change d'une manière discontinue, passant d'une nuance à une autre nuance. Quelque nombreuses que puissent donc être les nuances intermédiaires entre deux couleurs A et B, on pourra toujours les compter par la pensée, du moins grossièrement, et vérifier si ce nombre est à peu près égal à celui des nuances qui séparent B d'une autre couleur C. Dans ce dernier cas, on dira que B est également distant de A et de C, que le contraste est le même de part et d'autre. Mais ce ne sera toujours là qu'une interprétation commode : car bien que le nombre des nuances intermédiaires soit égal des deux côtés, bien que l'on passe de l'une à l'autre par des sauts brusques, nous ne savons pas si ces sauts sont des grandeurs, ni des grandeurs égales : surtout, il faudrait nous montrer que les intermédiaires qui ont servi à la mesure se retrouvent, en quelque sorte, au sein de l'objet mesuré. Sinon, c'est par métaphore seulement qu'une sensation pourra être dite à égale distance de deux autres. Or, si l'on veut bien nous accorder ce que nous disions plus haut des intensités lumineuses, on reconnaîtra que les diverses teintes grises présentées par M. Delbœuf à notre observation sont tout à fait analogues, pour notre conscience, à des couleurs, et que si nous déclarons une teinte grise équidistante de deux autres teintes grises, c'est dans le même sens où l'on pourrait dire que l'orangé, par exemple, est à égale distance du vert et du rouge. Seulement il y a cette différence que, dans toute notre expérience passée, la succession des teintes grises s'est produite à propos d'une augmentation ou d'une diminution progressive d'éclairage. De là vient que nous faisons pour les différences d'éclat ce que nous ne songeons pas à faire pour les différences de coloration : nous érigeons les changements de qualité en variations de grandeur. La mesure se fait d'ailleurs sans peine, parce que les nuances successives du gris amenées par une diminution continue d'éclairage sont discontinues, étant des qualités, et que nous pouvons compter approximativement les principaux intermédiaires qui séparent deux d'entre elles. Le contraste AB sera donc déclaré égal au contraste BC quand notre imagination, aidée de notre mémoire, interposera de part et d'autre le même nombre de points de repère. Cette appréciation devra d'ailleurs être des plus grossières, et l'on peut prévoir qu'elle variera considérablement avec les personnes. Surtout, il faut s'attendre à ce que les hésitations et les écarts d'appréciation soient d'autant plus marqués qu'on augmentera davantage la différence d'éclat entre les anneaux A et B, car un effort de plus en plus pénible sera requis pour évaluer le nombre des teintes intercalaires. C'est précisément ce qui arrive, comme on s'en convaincra sans peine, en jetant un coup d’œil sur les deux tableaux dressés par M. Delbœuf1. A mesure qu'il fait croître la différence d'éclat entre l'anneau extérieur et l'anneau moyen, l'écart entre les chiffres auxquels s'arrêtent tour à tour un même observateur ou des observateurs différents augmente d'une manière à peu près continue de 3 degrés à 94, de 5 à 73, de 10 à 25, de 7 à 40. Mais laissons de côté ces écarts ; supposons que les observateurs soient toujours d'accord avec eux-mêmes, toujours d'accord entre eux : aura-t-on établi que les contrastes AB et BC soient égaux ? Il faudrait d'abord avoir prouvé que deux contrastes élémentaires successifs sont des quantités égales, et nous savons seulement qu'ils sont successifs. Il faudrait ensuite avoir établi qu'on retrouve dans une teinte grise donnée les teintes inférieures par lesquelles notre imagination a passé pour évaluer l'intensité objective de la source de lumière. En un mot, la psychophysique de M. Delbœuf suppose un postulat théorique de la plus haute importance, qui se dissimule en vain sous des apparences expérimentales, et que nous formulerions ainsi : « Quand on fait croître d'une manière continue la quantité objective de lumière, les différences entre les teintes grises successivement obtenues, différences qui traduisent chacune le plus petit accroissement perçu d'excitation physique, sont des quantités égales entre elles. Et de plus, on peut égaler l'une quelconque des sensations obtenues à la somme des différences qui séparent les unes des autres les sensations antérieures, depuis la sensation nulle. » - Or, c'est là précisément le postulat de la psychophysique de Fechner, que nous allons examiner. Fechner est parti d'une loi découverte par Weber et d'après laquelle, étant donnée une certaine excitation provoquant une certaine sensation, la quantité d'excitation qu'il faut ajouter à la première pour que la conscience s'aperçoive d'un changement sera dans un rapport constant avec elle. Ainsi, en désignant par E l'excitation qui correspond à la sensation S, et par ∆E la quantité d'excitation de même nature qu'il faut ajouter à la première pour qu'une sensation de différence se produise, on aurait ∆E = const. E Cette formule a été profondément modifiée par les disciples de Fechner : nous n'interviendrons pas dans le débat ; il appartient à l'expérience de décider entre la relation établie par Weber et celles qu'on y substitue. Nous ne ferons d'ailleurs aucune difficulté pour admettre l'existence probable d'une loi de ce genre. Il ne s'agit pas ici, en effet, de mesurer la sensation, mais seulement de déterminer le moment précis où un accroissement d'excitation la fait changer. Or, si une quantité déterminée d'excitation produit une nuance déterminée de sensation, il est clair que la quantité minima d’excitation exigée pour provoquer un changement de cette nuance est déterminée aussi; et puisqu'elle n'est pas constante, elle doit être fonction de l'excitation à laquelle elle s'ajoute. - Mais comment passer, d'une relation entre l'excitation et son accroissement minimum, à une équation qui lie la « quantité de la sensation » à l'excitation correspondante ? Toute la psychophysique est dans ce passage, qu'il importe d'étudier attentivement. Nous distinguerons plusieurs artifices différents dans l'opération par laquelle on passe, des expériences de Weber ou de toute autre série d'observations analogues, à une loi psychophysique comme celle de Fechner. On convient d'abord de considérer comme un accroissement de la sensation S la conscience que nous avons d'un accroissement d'excitation; on l'appellera donc ∆S . On pose ensuite en principe que toutes les sensations ∆S correspondant au plus petit accroissement perceptible d'une excitation sont égales entre elles. On les traite alors comme des quantités, et ces quantités étant toujours égales, d'une part, tandis que d'autre part l'expérience a donné entre l'excitation E et son accroissement minimum une certaine relation ∆E = φ(E), on exprime la constance de ∆S en écrivant : ∆S = C ∆E/φ(E), C étant une quantité constante. On convient enfin de remplacer les différences très petites ∆S et ∆E par les différences infiniment petites dS et dE , d'où une équation cette fois différentielle : dS = C dE/φ(E) Il ne restera plus alors qu'à intégrer les deux membres pour obtenir la relation cherchée1 : S = C ∫₀ᴱ dE/φ(E) ; Et l'on passera ainsi d'une loi vérifiée, où l'apparition de la sensation était seule en cause, à une loi invérifiable, qui en donne la mesure. Sans entrer dans une discussion approfondie de cette ingénieuse opération, montrons en quelques mots comment Fechner a saisi la véritable difficulté du problème, comment il a essayé de la surmonter, et où réside, selon nous, le vice de son raisonnement. Fechner a compris qu'on ne saurait introduire la mesure en psychologie sans y définir d'abord l'égalité et l'addition de deux états simples, de deux sensations par exemple. D'autre part, à moins d'être identiques, on ne voit pas d'abord comment deux sensations seraient égales. Sans doute, dans le monde physique, égalité n'est point synonyme d'identité. Mais c'est que tout phénomène, tout objet, s'y présente sous un double aspect, l'un qualitatif, l'autre extensif : rien n'empêche de faire abstraction du premier, et il ne reste plus alors que des termes capables d'être superposés directement ou indirectement l'un à l'autre, et de s'identifier ensemble par conséquent. Or, cet élément qualitatif, que l'on commence par éliminer des choses extérieures pour en rendre la mesure possible, est précisément celui que la psychophysique retient et prétend mesurer. Et c'est en vain qu'elle chercherait à évaluer cette qualité Q par quelque quantité physique Q' située au-dessous d'elle ; car il faudrait préalablement avoir montré que Q est fonction de Q' et ceci ne pourrait se faire que si l'on avait d'abord mesuré la qualité Q avec quelque fraction d'elle-même. Ainsi, rien n'empêcherait de mesurer la sensation de chaleur par le degré de température ; mais ce ne serait là qu'une convention, et la psycho-physique consiste précisément à repousser cette convention et à chercher comment la sensation de chaleur varie quand varie la température. Bref, il semble que deux sensations différentes ne puissent être dites égales que si quelque fond identique demeure après l'élimination de leur différence qualitative ; et, d'autre part, cette différence qualitative étant tout ce que nous sentons, on ne voit pas ce qui pourrait subsister une fois qu'on l'aurait éliminée. L'originalité de Fechner est de n'avoir pas jugé cette difficulté insurmontable. Profitant de ce que la sensation varie par sauts brusques quand l'excitation croît d'une manière continue, il n'a pas hésité à désigner ces différences de sensation par le même nom : ce sont des différences minima, en effet, puisqu'elles correspondent chacune au plus petit accroissement perceptible de l'excitation extérieure. Dès lors, vous pouvez faire abstraction de la nuance ou qualité spécifique de ces différences successives ; un fond ∆S commun demeurera par où elles s'identifieront en quelque sorte ensemble : elles sont minima les unes et les autres. Voilà la définition cherchée de l'égalité. Celle de l'addition suivra naturellement. Car si l'on traite comme une quantité la différence aperçue par la conscience entre deux sensations qui se succèdent le long d'un accroissement continu d'excitation, si l'on appelle la première S et la seconde S + ∆S , on devra considérer toute sensation S comme une somme, obtenue par l'addition des différences minima que l'on traverse avant de l'atteindre. Il ne restera plus alors qu'à utiliser cette double définition pour établir une relation entre les différences ∆S + ∆E d'abord, puis, par l'intermédiaire des différentielles, entre les deux variables. Il est vrai que les mathématiciens pourront protester ici contre le passage de la différence à la différentielle ; les psychologues se demanderont si la quantité ∆S , au lieu d'être constante, ne varierait pas comme la sensation S elle-même1 (1) : enfin l'on discutera sur le sens véritable de la loi psycho-physique, une fois établie. Mais par cela seul que l'on considère ∆S comme une quantité et S comme une somme, on admet le postulat fondamental de l'opération entière. Or, c'est ce postulat qui nous paraît contestable, et même assez peu intelligible. Supposez, en effet, que j'éprouve une sensation S, et que, faisant croître l'excitation d'une manière continue, je m'aperçoive de cet accroissement au bout d'un certain temps. Me voilà averti de l'accroissement de la cause : mais quel rapport établir entre cet avertissement et une différence ? Sans doute l'avertissement consiste ici en ce que l'état primitif S a changé ; il est devenu S' ; mais pour que le passage de S à S' fût comparable à une différence arithmétique, il faudrait que j'eusse conscience, pour ainsi dire, d'un intervalle entre S et S', et que ma sensibilité montât de S à S' par l'addition de quelque chose. En donnant à ce passage un nom, en l'appelant ∆S, vous en faites une réalité d'abord, une quantité ensuite. Or, non seulement vous ne sauriez expliquer en quel sens ce passage est une quantité, mais vous vous apercevrez, en y réfléchissant, que ce n'est même pas une réalité ; il n'y a de réels que les états S et S' par lesquels on passe. Sans doute, si S et S' étaient des nombres, je pourrais affirmer la réalité de la différence S' - S, lors même que S' et S seraient seuls donnés : c'est que le nombre S' - S, qui est une certaine somme d'unités, représentera précisément alors les moments successifs de l'addition par laquelle on passe de S à S'. Mais si S et S' sont des états simples, en quoi consistera l'intervalle qui les sépare ? Et que sera donc le passage du premier état au second, sinon un acte de votre pensée, qui assimile arbitrairement, et pour le besoin de la cause, une succession de deux états à une différenciation de deux grandeurs ? Ou vous vous en tenez à ce que la conscience vous donne, ou vous usez d'un mode de représentation conventionnel. Dans le premier cas, vous trouverez entre S et S' une différence analogue à celle des nuances de l'arc-en-ciel, et point du tout un intervalle de grandeur. Dans le second, vous pourrez introduire le symbole ∆S , si vous voulez, mais c'est par convention que vous parlerez de différence arithmétique, par convention aussi que vous assimilerez une sensation donnée à une somme. Le plus pénétrant des critiques de Fechner, M. Jules Tannery, a mis ce dernier point en pleine lumière : « On dira, par exemple, qu'une sensation de 50 degrés est exprimée par le nombre de sensations différentielles qui se succéderaient depuis l'absence de sensation jusqu'à la sensation de 50 degrés... Je ne vois pas qu'il y ait là autre chose qu'une définition, aussi légitime qu'arbitraire1. » Nous ne croyons pas, quoi qu'on en ait dit, que la méthode des graduations moyennes ait fait entrer la psychophysique dans une voie nouvelle. L'originalité de M. Delbœuf a été de choisir un cas particulier où la conscience parût donner raison à Fechner, et où le sens commun fût lui-même psychophysicien. Il s'est demandé si certaines sensations ne nous apparaissaient pas immédiatement comme égales, quoique différentes, et si l'on ne pourrait pas dresser par leur intermédiaire un tableau de sensations doubles, triples, quadruples les unes des autres. L'erreur de Fechner, disions-nous, était d'avoir cru à un intervalle entre deux sensations successives S et S', alors que de l'une à l'autre il y a simplement passage, et non pas différence au sens arithmétique du mot. Mais si les deux termes entre lesquels le passage s'effectue pouvaient être donnés simultanément, il y aurait cette fois contraste en outre du passage ; et quoique le contraste ne soit pas encore une différence arithmétique, il y ressemble par un certain côté ; les deux termes que l'on compare sont en présence l'un de l'autre comme dans une soustraction de deux nombres. Supposez maintenant que ces sensations soient de même nature, et que constamment, dans notre expérience passée, nous ayons assisté à leur défilé, pour ainsi dire, pendant que l'excitation physique croissait d'une manière continue : il est infiniment probable que nous mettrons la cause dans l'effet, et que l'idée de contraste viendra se fondre dans celle de différence arithmétique. Comme, d'autre part, nous aurons remarqué que la sensation changeait brusquement tandis que le progrès de l'excitation était continu, nous évaluerons sans doute la distance entre deux sensations données par le nombre, grossièrement reconstitué, de ces sauts brusques, ou tout au moins des sensations intermédiaires qui nous servent le plus ordinairement de jalons. En résumé, le contraste nous apparaîtra comme une différence, l'excitation comme une quantité, le saut brusque comme un élément d'égalité, combinant ces trois facteurs ensemble, nous aboutirons à l'idée de différences quantitatives égales. Or, nulle part ces conditions ne sont aussi bien réalisées que lorsque des surfaces de même couleur, plus ou moins éclairées, se présentent à nous simultanément. Non seulement il y a ici contraste entre sensations analogues, mais ces sensations correspondent à une cause dont l'influence nous a toujours paru étroitement liée à sa distance ; et comme cette distance peut varier d'une manière continue, nous avons dû noter, dans notre expérience passée, une innombrable multitude de nuances de sensation se succédant le long d'un accroissement continu de la cause. Nous pourrons donc dire que le contraste d'une première teinte grise avec une seconde, par exemple, nous paraît à peu près égal au contraste de la seconde avec une troisième ; et si l'on définit deux sensations égales en disant que ce sont des sensations qu'un raisonnement plus ou moins confus interprète comme telles, on aboutira, en effet, à une loi comme celle que propose M. Delbœuf. Mais il ne faudra pas oublier que la conscience a passé par les mêmes intermédiaires que le psychophysicien, et que son jugement vaut ici ce que vaut la psycho-physique : c'est une interprétation symbolique de la qualité en quantité, une évaluation plus ou moins grossière du nombre des sensations qui se pourraient intercaler entre deux sensations données. La différence n'est donc pas aussi considérable qu'on le croit entre la méthode des modifications minima et celle des graduations moyennes, entre la psychophysique de Fechner et celle de M. Delbœuf. La première aboutit à une mesure conventionnelle de la sensation ; la seconde en appelle au sens commun dans les cas particuliers où il adopte une convention analogue. Bref, toute psychophysique est condamnée par son origine même a tourner dans un cercle vicieux, car le postulat théorique sur lequel elle repose la condamne à une vérification expérimentale, et elle ne peut être vérifiée expérimentalement que si l'on admet d'abord son postulat. C'est qu'il n'y a pas de point de contact entre l'inétendu et l'étendu, entre la qualité et la quantité. On peut interpréter l'une par l'autre, ériger l'une en équivalent de l'autre ; mais, tôt ou tard, au commencement ou à la fin, il faudra reconnaître le caractère conventionnel de cette assimilation. À vrai dire, la psychophysique n'a fait que formuler avec précision et pousser à ses conséquences extrêmes une conception familière au sens commun. Comme nous parlons plutôt que nous ne pensons, comme aussi les objets extérieurs, qui sont du domaine commun, ont plus d'importance pour nous que les états subjectifs par lesquels nous passons, nous avons tout intérêt à objectiver ces états en y introduisant, dans la plus large mesure possible, la représentation de leur cause extérieure. Et plus nos connaissances s'accroissent, plus nous apercevons l'extensif derrière l'intensif et la quantité derrière la qualité, plus aussi nous tendons à mettre le premier terme dans le second, et à traiter nos sensations comme des grandeurs. La physique, dont le rôle est précisément de soumettre au calcul la cause extérieure de nos états internes, se préoccupe le moins possible de ces états eux-mêmes - sans cesse, et de parti pris, elle les confond avec leur cause. Elle encourage donc et exagère même sur ce point l'illusion du sens commun. Le moment devait fatalement arriver où, familiarisée avec cette confusion de la qualité avec la quantité et de la sensation avec l'excitation, la science chercherait à mesurer l'une comme elle mesure l'autre : tel a été l'objet de la psychophysique. A cette tentative hardie Fechner était encouragé par ses adversaires eux-mêmes, par les philosophes qui parlent de grandeurs intensives tout en déclarant les états psychiques réfractaires à la mesure. Si l'on admet, en effet, qu'une sensation puisse être plus forte qu'une autre sensation, et que cette inégalité réside dans les sensations mêmes, indépendamment de toute association d'idées, de toute considération plus ou moins consciente de nombre et d'espace, il est naturel de chercher de combien la première sensation surpasse la seconde, et d'établir un rapport quantitatif entre leurs intensités. Et il ne sert à rien de répondre, comme font souvent les adversaires de la psychophysique, que toute mesure implique superposition, et qu'il n’y a pas lieu de chercher un rapport numérique entre des intensités, qui ne sont pas choses superposables. Car il faudra alors expliquer pourquoi une sensation est dite plus intense qu'une autre sensation, et comment on peut appeler plus grandes ou plus petites des choses qui - on vient de le reconnaître - n'admettent point entre elles des relations de contenant à contenu. Que si, pour couper court à toute question de ce genre, on distingue deux espèces de quantité, l'une intensive, qui comporte seulement le plus et le moins, l'autre extensive, qui se prête à la mesure, on est bien près de donner raison à Fechner et aux psychophysiciens. Car, dès qu'une chose est reconnue susceptible de grandir et de diminuer, il semble naturel de chercher de combien elle diminue, de combien elle grandit. Et parce qu'une mesure de ce genre ne paraît pas directement possible, il ne s'ensuit pas que la science n'y puisse réussir par quelque procédé indirect, soit par une intégration d'éléments infiniment petits, comme le propose Fechner, soit par tout autre moyen détourné. Ou bien donc la sensation est qualité pure, ou, si c'est une grandeur, on doit chercher à la mesurer. Pour résumer ce qui précède, nous dirons que la notion d'intensité se présente sous un double aspect, selon qu'on étudie les états de conscience représentatifs d'une cause extérieure, ou ceux qui se suffisent à eux-mêmes. Dans le premier cas, la perception de l'intensité consiste dans une certaine évaluation de la grandeur de la cause par une certaine qualité de l'effet : c'est, comme diraient les Écossais, une perception acquise. Dans le second, nous appelons intensité la multiplicité plus ou moins considérable de faits psychiques simples que nous devinons au sein de l'état fondamental : ce n'est plus une perception acquise, mais une perception confuse. D'ailleurs ces deux sens du mot se pénètrent le plus souvent, parce que les faits plus simples qu'une émotion ou qu'un effort enveloppe sont généralement représentatifs, et que la plupart des états représentatifs, étant affectifs en même temps, embrassent eux-mêmes une multiplicité de faits psychiques élémentaires. L'idée d'intensité est donc située au point de jonction de deux courants, dont l'un nous apporte du dehors l'idée de grandeur extensive, et dont l'autre est allé chercher dans les profondeurs de la conscience, pour l'amener à la surface, l'image d'une multiplicité interne. Reste à savoir en quoi cette dernière image consiste, si elle se confond avec celle du nombre, ou si elle en diffère radicalement. Dans le chapitre qui va suivre, nous ne considérerons plus les états de conscience isolément les uns des autres, mais dans leur multiplicité concrète, en tant qu'ils se déroulent dans la pure durée. Et de même que nous nous sommes demandé ce que serait l'intensité d'une sensation représentative si nous n'y introduisions l'idée de sa cause, ainsi nous devrons rechercher maintenant ce que devient la multiplicité de nos états internes, quelle forme affecte la durée, quand on fait abstraction de l'espace où elle se développe. Cette seconde question est autrement importante que la première. Car si la confusion de la qualité avec la quantité se limitait à chacun des faits de conscience pris isolément, elle créerait des obscurités, comme nous venons de le voir, plutôt que des problèmes. Mais en envahissant la série de nos états psychologiques, en introduisant l'espace dans notre conception de la durée, elle corrompt, à leur source même, nos représentations du changement extérieur et du changement interne, du mouvement et de la liberté. De là les sophismes de l'école d'Élée, de là le problème du libre arbitre. Nous insisterons plutôt sur le second point ; mais au lieu de chercher à résoudre la question, nous montrerons l'illusion de ceux qui la posent.  ## Chapitre II. De la multiplicité des états de conscience1. L'idée de durée
e: It is usually admitted that states of consciousness, sensations, feelings, passions, efforts, are capable of increasing and diminishing; some even assert that one sensation can be said to be two, three, four times as intense as another sensation of the same kind. I shall examine this last thesis further on, which is that of the psychophysicists; but even the opponents of psychophysics see no objection to speaking of one sensation as more intense than another sensation, of one effort as greater than another effort, and thus to establishing differences of quantity between purely internal states. Common sense, moreover, pronounces on this point without the least hesitation; people say that they are more or less hot, that they are more or less sad, and this distinction of more and less, even when it is extended into the region of subjective facts and unextended things, surprises nobody. There is here, nevertheless, a very obscure point, and a problem much graver than is generally imagined. When we assert that one number is greater than another number, or one body than another body, we know very well, in fact, what we are talking about. For in both cases it is a question of unequal spaces, as I shall show in detail a little further on, and we call that space the greater which contains the other. But how will a more intense sensation contain a sensation of lesser intensity? Will it be said that the first implies the second, that we reach the sensation of higher intensity only on condition of having passed first through the lower intensities of the same sensation, and that here too, in a certain sense, there is indeed a relation of container to contained? This conception of intensive magnitude appears to be that of common sense, but it cannot be set up as a philosophical explanation without committing a genuine vicious circle. For it is incontestable that one number exceeds another when it comes after it in the natural series of numbers: but if we have been able to arrange the numbers in increasing order, it is precisely because there exist between them relations of container to contained, and because we feel able to explain precisely in what sense one is greater than the other. The question then is how we succeed in forming a series of this kind with intensities, which are not things that can be superposed, and by what sign we recognise that the terms of this series increase, for example, instead of diminishing: which always comes back to asking why an intensity can be assimilated to a magnitude. It is evading the difficulty to distinguish, as is usually done, two kinds of quantity, the first extensive and measurable, the second intensive, which does not admit of measurement, but of which it can nevertheless be said that it is greater or smaller than another intensity. For one thereby recognises that there is something common to these two forms of magnitude, since both are called magnitudes, and both are declared equally capable of increasing and diminishing. But what can there be in common, from the point of view of magnitude, between the extensive and the intensive, between the extended and the unextended? If, in the first case, we call that quantity the greater which contains the other, why go on speaking of quantity and magnitude when there is no longer either container or contained? If a quantity can increase and diminish, if we perceive in it, so to speak, the less within the more, is it not by that very fact divisible, by that very fact extended? and is there not then a contradiction in speaking of an inextensive quantity? Yet common sense agrees with the philosophers in setting up a pure intensity as a magnitude, just like an extension. And not only do we use the same word, but whether we are thinking of a greater intensity or of a greater extension, we experience an analogous impression in both cases; the terms "greater" and "smaller" do indeed call up the same idea in both cases. If we now ask ourselves what this idea consists in, it is again the image of a container and a contained that consciousness offers us. We picture a greater intensity of effort, for example, as a greater length of wound-up thread, as a spring which, in uncoiling, will occupy a greater space. In the idea of intensity, and even in the word which expresses it, we shall find the image of a present contraction and consequently of a future expansion, the image of a virtual extension and, if one may so speak, of a compressed space. We must therefore believe that we translate the intensive into the extensive, and that the comparison of two intensities is made, or at least expressed, through the confused intuition of a relation between two extensions. But it is the nature of this operation which seems hard to determine. The solution which immediately presents itself to the mind, once we have set out along this road, would consist in defining the intensity of a sensation or of any state of the self by the number and the magnitude of the objective, and consequently measurable, causes which gave rise to it. It is incontestable that a more intense sensation of light is the one which has been obtained, or would be obtained, by means of a greater number of light sources, assumed to be at the same distance and identical with one another. But in the immense majority of cases we pronounce on the intensity of the effect without even knowing the nature of the cause, still less its magnitude: indeed, it is often the intensity of the effect which leads us to hazard a hypothesis about the number and nature of the causes, and thus to revise the judgement of our senses, which at first sight showed them to us as insignificant. It will be urged in vain that we then compare the present state of the self with some earlier state in which the cause was perceived in its entirety at the same time as its effect was felt. We no doubt proceed in this way in a fairly large number of cases; but this does not explain the differences of intensity which we establish between deep psychological facts, which emanate from us and no longer from an external cause. On the other hand, we never pronounce so boldly on the intensity of a psychic state as when the subjective aspect of the phenomenon alone strikes us, or when the external cause to which we relate it hardly admits of measurement. Thus it seems evident to us that one feels a more intense pain in having a tooth pulled out than a hair; the artist knows beyond doubt that a master's painting gives him a more intense pleasure than a shop sign; and there is no need ever to have heard of the forces of cohesion to assert that less effort is spent in bending a steel blade than in trying to bend an iron bar. Thus the comparison of two intensities is most often made without the slightest estimate of the number of the causes, of their mode of action or of their extension. There would still be room, it is true, for a hypothesis of the same kind, but subtler. We know that mechanical, and above all kinetic, theories tend to explain the apparent and sensible properties of bodies by well-defined movements of their elementary parts, and that some foresee the moment when the intensive differences of qualities, that is to say of our sensations, will be reduced to extensive differences between the changes which take place behind them. May it not be maintained that, without knowing these theories, we have a vague presentiment of them, that beneath the more intense sound we divine a wider vibration propagating itself within the disturbed medium, and that we are alluding to this very precise, though confusedly perceived, mathematical relation when we assert of a sound that it has a higher intensity? Without even going so far, might it not be laid down as a principle that every state of consciousness corresponds to a certain disturbance of the molecules and atoms of the cerebral substance, and that the intensity of a sensation measures the amplitude, the complication or the extension of these molecular movements? This last hypothesis is at least as plausible as the other, but it does not solve the problem any better. For it is possible that the intensity of a sensation bears witness to a greater or lesser amount of work done in our organism; but it is the sensation that is given to us by consciousness, and not this mechanical work. Indeed, it is by the intensity of the sensation that we judge of the greater or lesser quantity of work done: intensity therefore remains, in appearance at least, a property of the sensation. And always the same question arises: why do we say of a higher intensity that it is greater? Why do we think of a greater quantity or of a greater space? Perhaps the difficulty of the problem lies chiefly in the fact that we call by the same name and picture in the same way intensities of very different nature, the intensity of a feeling, for example, and that of a sensation or of an effort. Effort is accompanied by a muscular sensation, and sensations themselves are bound up with certain physical conditions which probably count for something in the estimate of their intensity; these are phenomena which take place at the surface of consciousness, and which are always associated, as we shall see further on, with the perception of a movement or of an external object. But certain states of the soul appear to us, rightly or wrongly, to be self-sufficient: such are deep joys and sorrows, reflective passions, aesthetic emotions. Pure intensity ought to be more easily defined in these simple cases, where no extensive element seems to intervene. We shall see, in fact, that it is reduced here to a certain quality or shade with which a more or less considerable mass of psychic states is coloured, or, if one prefers, to the greater or lesser number of simple states which permeate the fundamental emotion. For example, an obscure desire has gradually become a deep passion. You will see that the feeble intensity of this desire consisted at first in its seeming to you isolated and as it were foreign to all the rest of your inner life. But little by little it has permeated a greater number of psychic elements, tingeing them, so to speak, with its own colour; and now your point of view on things as a whole seems to you to have changed. Is it not true that you become aware of a deep passion, once it has taken hold, by the fact that the same objects no longer make the same impression on you? All your sensations, all your ideas seem to you refreshed by it; it is like a new childhood. We experience something analogous in certain dreams, in which we imagine nothing but what is quite ordinary, and through which there nevertheless resounds some indefinable original note. The reason is that the further we descend into the depths of consciousness, the less right we have to treat psychological facts as things which are juxtaposed. When it is said that an object occupies a large place in the soul, or even that it fills the whole of it, we must simply understand by this that its image has altered the shade of a thousand perceptions or recollections, and that in this sense it permeates them, without however making itself seen in them. But this wholly dynamic representation is repugnant to reflective consciousness, because it loves sharp distinctions, which are easily expressed in words, and things with well-defined outlines, like those which we perceive in space. It will therefore suppose that, all the rest remaining identical, a certain desire has passed through successive magnitudes: as if one could still speak of magnitude where there is neither multiplicity nor space! And just as we shall see it concentrate at a given point of the organism, so as to make of them an effort of increasing intensity, the more and more numerous muscular contractions which take place over the surface of the body, so it will crystallise apart, in the form of a desire which grows, the progressive modifications that have come about in the confused mass of coexisting psychic facts. But this is a change of quality rather than of magnitude. What makes hope so intense a pleasure is that the future, which we dispose of as we please, appears to us at the same time under a multitude of forms, equally smiling, equally possible. Even if the most desired among them comes about, the others will have to be sacrificed, and we shall have lost a great deal. The idea of the future, pregnant with an infinity of possibilities, is therefore more fruitful than the future itself, and that is why we find more charm in hope than in possession, in the dream than in reality. Let us try to make out what an increasing intensity of joy or of sorrow consists in, in the exceptional cases where no physical symptom intervenes. Inner joy is no more than passion an isolated psychological fact which would at first occupy a corner of the soul and gradually gain ground. At its lowest degree, it rather resembles an orientation of our states of consciousness in the direction of the future. Then, as if this attraction lessened their weight, our ideas and our sensations succeed one another more rapidly; our movements no longer cost us the same effort. Finally, in extreme joy, our perceptions and our recollections acquire an indefinable quality, comparable to a warmth or a light, and so new that at certain moments, turning back upon ourselves, we experience something like an astonishment at being. Thus there are several characteristic forms of purely inner joy, so many successive stages corresponding to qualitative modifications of the mass of our psychological states. But the number of states which each of these modifications reaches is more or less considerable, and although we do not count them explicitly, we know well enough whether our joy permeates all our impressions of the day, for example, or whether some escape it. We thus establish points of division in the interval which separates two successive forms of joy, and this gradual progression from one to the other makes them appear to us in their turn as the intensities of one and the same feeling, which would be changing in magnitude. It could easily be shown that the different degrees of sorrow also correspond to qualitative changes. It begins by being no more than an orientation towards the past, an impoverishment of our sensations and our ideas, as if each of them were now wholly contained in the little it gives, as if the future were in some sort closed to us. And it ends in an impression of being crushed, which makes us long for nothingness, and makes each new misfortune, by making us understand better the uselessness of the struggle, cause us a bitter pleasure. Aesthetic feelings offer us still more striking examples of this progressive intervention of new elements, visible in the fundamental emotion, which seem to increase its magnitude although they merely alter its nature. Let us consider the simplest of them, the feeling of grace. At first it is only the perception of a certain ease, a certain facility in outward movements. And as easy movements are those which prepare the way for one another, we end by finding a superior ease in the movements which could be foreseen, in the present attitudes in which the attitudes to come are indicated and as it were preformed. If jerky movements lack grace, it is because each of them is self-sufficient and does not announce those which are to follow it. If grace prefers curves to broken lines, it is because the curved line changes its direction at every moment, but each new direction was indicated in the one which preceded it. The perception of an ease in moving thus comes to melt here into the pleasure of in some sort arresting the march of time, and of holding the future in the present. A third element intervenes when the graceful movements obey a rhythm, and music accompanies them. For rhythm and measure, by allowing us to foresee the artist's movements still better, make us believe this time that we are their masters. As we almost divine the attitude he is going to take, he seems to obey us when he does in fact take it; the regularity of the rhythm establishes a kind of communication between him and us, and the periodic returns of the measure are like so many invisible threads by means of which we work this imaginary puppet. Indeed, if it stops for an instant, our impatient hand cannot help moving as if to push it, as if to put it back into the midst of this movement whose rhythm has become the whole of our thought and the whole of our will. There will therefore enter into the feeling of the graceful a kind of physical sympathy, and in analysing the charm of this sympathy you will see that it pleases you itself through its affinity with moral sympathy, the idea of which it subtly suggests to you. This last element, into which the others come to melt after having in some sort announced it, explains the irresistible attraction of grace: we should not understand the pleasure it gives us if it were reduced to an economy of effort, as Spencer maintains1. But the truth is that in everything that is very graceful we believe we make out, besides the lightness which is a sign of mobility, the indication of a possible movement towards us, of a virtual or even nascent sympathy. It is this mobile sympathy, always on the point of giving itself, which is the very essence of the higher grace. Thus the increasing intensities of aesthetic feeling resolve themselves here into so many different feelings, each of which, already announced by the preceding one, becomes visible in it and then definitively eclipses it. It is this qualitative progress which we interpret in the sense of a change of magnitude, because we like simple things, and because our language is ill made to render the subtleties of psychological analysis. To understand how the feeling of the beautiful itself admits of degrees, we should have to subject it to a minute analysis. Perhaps the difficulty one has in defining it lies chiefly in the fact that the beauties of nature are regarded as prior to those of art: the processes of art are then no more than means by which the artist expresses the beautiful, and the essence of the beautiful remains mysterious. But one might ask whether nature is beautiful otherwise than through the happy meeting with certain processes of our art, and whether, in a certain sense, art does not precede nature. Without even going so far, it seems more in keeping with the rules of a sound method to study the beautiful first in the works where it has been produced by a conscious effort, and then to descend by imperceptible transitions from art to nature, which is an artist in its own way. Placing ourselves at this point of view, we shall perceive, I believe, that the object of art is to put to sleep the active or rather resistant powers of our personality, and thus to bring us to a state of perfect docility in which we realise the idea that is suggested to us, in which we sympathise with the feeling expressed. In the processes of art we shall find again, in an attenuated form, refined and in some sort spiritualised, the processes by which the state of hypnosis is ordinarily obtained. - Thus, in music, rhythm and measure suspend the normal circulation of our sensations and ideas by making our attention oscillate between fixed points, and take hold of us with such force that the imitation, even infinitely discreet, of a moaning voice will suffice to fill us with extreme sadness. If musical sounds act more powerfully upon us than those of nature, it is because nature confines itself to expressing feelings, whereas music suggests them to us. Whence comes the charm of poetry? The poet is one in whom feelings develop into images, and the images themselves into words, obedient to rhythm, to translate them. In seeing these images pass again before our eyes, we in our turn shall experience the feeling which was, so to speak, their emotional equivalent; but these images would not be realised so strongly for us without the regular movements of the rhythm, by which our soul, lulled and put to sleep, forgets itself as in a dream in order to think and to see with the poet. The plastic arts obtain an effect of the same kind through the fixity which they suddenly impose on life, and which a physical contagion communicates to the attention of the spectator. If the works of ancient statuary express slight emotions, which barely touch them like a breath, the pale immobility of the stone on the other hand gives to the feeling expressed, to the movement begun, an indefinable something final and eternal, in which our thought is absorbed and our will is lost. We should find in architecture, in the very midst of this striking immobility, certain effects analogous to those of rhythm. The symmetry of the forms, the indefinite repetition of the same architectural motif, make our faculty of perceiving oscillate from the same to the same, and break it of the habit of those incessant changes which, in daily life, constantly bring us back to the consciousness of our personality: the indication, however slight, of an idea will then suffice to fill our whole soul with that idea. Thus art aims at impressing feelings on us rather than at expressing them; it suggests them to us, and readily dispenses with the imitation of nature when it finds more effective means. Nature proceeds by suggestion as art does, but it does not have rhythm at its disposal. It makes up for it by that long fellowship which the community of influences undergone has created between it and us, and which makes us sympathise with it at the slightest indication of a feeling, as a practised subject obeys the gesture of the mesmerist. And this sympathy arises in particular when nature presents to us beings of normal proportions, such that our attention is divided equally among all the parts of the figure without fixing on any one of them: our faculty of perceiving then finding itself lulled by this kind of harmony, nothing any longer checks the free flight of sensibility, which only ever waits for the obstacle to fall in order to be moved sympathetically. - It follows from this analysis that the feeling of the beautiful is not a special feeling, but that every feeling we experience will take on an aesthetic character, provided that it has been suggested and not caused. We then understand why aesthetic emotion appears to us to admit of degrees of intensity, and also of degrees of elevation. Sometimes, in fact, the suggested feeling barely interrupts the close-woven fabric of psychological facts which make up our history; sometimes it draws our attention away from them without, however, making us lose sight of them; sometimes, finally, it takes their place, absorbs us, and monopolises our whole soul. There are therefore distinct phases in the progress of an aesthetic feeling, as in the state of hypnosis; and these phases correspond less to variations of degree than to differences of state or of nature. But the merit of a work of art is measured not so much by the power with which the suggested feeling takes hold of us as by the richness of this feeling itself: in other words, alongside degrees of intensity, we instinctively distinguish degrees of depth or of elevation. On analysing this last concept, we shall see that the feelings and thoughts which the artist suggests to us express and sum up a more or less considerable part of his history. If an art which gives only sensations is an inferior art, it is because analysis does not often make out in a sensation anything other than that sensation itself. But most emotions are pregnant with a thousand sensations, feelings or ideas which permeate them: each of them is therefore a state unique of its kind, indefinable, and it seems that one would have to live again the life of the one who experiences it in order to grasp it in its complex originality. Yet the artist aims at bringing us into this emotion so rich, so personal, so new, and at making us experience what he could not make us understand. He will therefore fix, among the outward manifestations of his feeling, those which our body will imitate mechanically, though slightly, on perceiving them, so as to put us back all at once into the indefinable psychological state which provoked them. Thus will fall the barrier which time and space interposed between his consciousness and ours; and the richer in ideas, the fuller of sensations and emotions the feeling within whose frame he has made us enter, the more depth or elevation the beauty expressed will have. The successive intensities of aesthetic feeling thus correspond to changes of state that have come about in us, and the degrees of depth to the greater or lesser number of elementary psychic facts which we confusedly make out in the fundamental emotion. Moral feelings could be subjected to a study of the same kind. Let us consider pity, for example. It consists first in putting oneself in thought in the place of others, in suffering from their suffering. But if it were nothing more, as some have maintained, it would inspire us with the idea of fleeing from the wretched rather than of bringing them help, for suffering naturally horrifies us. It is possible that this feeling of horror is found at the origin of pity; but a new element soon joins it, a need to help our fellow men and to relieve their suffering. Shall we say, with La Rochefoucauld, that this so-called sympathy is a calculation, "a shrewd foresight of evils to come"? Perhaps fear does in fact still count for something in the compassion which the ills of others inspire in us; but these are still only lower forms of pity. True pity consists less in fearing suffering than in desiring it. A slight desire, which one would hardly wish to see realised, and which one forms nevertheless in spite of oneself, as if nature were committing some great injustice, and it were necessary to set aside all suspicion of complicity with it. The essence of pity is thus a need to humble oneself, an aspiration to descend. This painful aspiration has, moreover, its charm, because it raises us in our own esteem, and makes us feel superior to those sensible goods from which our thought momentarily detaches itself. The increasing intensity of pity thus consists in a qualitative progress, in a passage from disgust to fear, from fear to sympathy, and from sympathy itself to humility. I shall not push this analysis further. The psychic states whose intensity I have just defined are deep states, which do not appear bound up with their external cause, and which do not seem either to involve the perception of a muscular contraction. But these states are rare. There is hardly a passion or desire, a joy or sorrow, which is not accompanied by physical symptoms; and, where these symptoms present themselves, they probably serve us in some way in the estimate of intensities. As for sensations properly so called, they are manifestly bound up with their external cause, and, although the intensity of the sensation cannot be defined by the magnitude of its cause, there no doubt exists some relation between these two terms. Indeed, in some of its manifestations consciousness seems to expand outwards, as if intensity were developing into extension: such is muscular effort. Let us place ourselves at once before this last phenomenon: we shall thus transport ourselves at a single bound to the opposite end of the series of psychological facts. If there is one phenomenon which seems to present itself immediately to consciousness in the form of quantity, or at least of magnitude, it is without question muscular effort. It seems to us that psychic force, imprisoned in the soul like the winds in the cave of Aeolus, merely waits there for an opportunity to rush out; the will would watch over this force and, from time to time, open an outlet for it, proportioning the outflow to the effect desired. Indeed, on careful reflection we shall see that this rather crude conception of effort plays a large part in our belief in intensive magnitudes. As muscular force, which unfolds in space and manifests itself in measurable phenomena, strikes us as having pre-existed its manifestations, but in a smaller volume and in a compressed state, so to speak, we do not hesitate to contract this volume more and more, and finally we believe we understand that a purely psychic state, no longer occupying space, should nevertheless have a magnitude. Science, moreover, tends to strengthen the illusion of common sense on this point. Mr Bain tells us, for example, that the sensibility accompanying muscular movement coincides with the centrifugal current of nervous force: it would thus be the very emission of nervous force that consciousness perceives. M. Wundt likewise speaks of a sensation of central origin accompanying the voluntary innervation of the muscles, and cites the example of the paralytic who has a very distinct sensation of the force he puts forth in trying to lift his leg, although it remains inert1. Most authors side with this opinion, which would be law in positive science if, some years ago, Mr William James had not drawn the attention of physiologists to certain phenomena which had been rather little noticed, and are yet very noteworthy. When a paralytic makes an effort to lift the inert limb, he does not perform this movement, no doubt, but, willy-nilly, he performs another. Some movement takes place somewhere: otherwise there is no sensation of effort2. Vulpian had already pointed out that if a hemiplegic is asked to close his paralysed fist, he unconsciously performs this action with the fist which is not affected. Ferrier noted a still more curious phenomenon3. Stretch out your arm, crooking your forefinger slightly, as if you were about to press the trigger of a pistol: you may not move the finger, not contract any muscle of the hand, not produce any apparent movement, and yet feel that you are expending energy. However, on looking more closely, you will notice that this sensation of effort coincides with the fixing of the muscles of your chest, that you are holding your glottis closed, and that you are actively contracting your respiratory muscles. As soon as breathing resumes its normal course, the consciousness of effort vanishes, unless the finger is really moved. These facts already seemed to indicate that we are conscious not of an emission of force but of the movement of the muscles which is its result. Mr William James's originality has been to verify the hypothesis on examples which seemed absolutely refractory to it. Thus, when the external rectus muscle of the right eye is paralysed, the patient tries in vain to turn the eye to the right; yet objects seem to him to move away to the right, and since the act of will has produced no effect, it must indeed be, said Helmholtz1, that the very effort of the will has manifested itself to consciousness. - But no account has been taken, replies Mr James, of what goes on in the other eye: this eye remains covered during the experiments; it moves nevertheless, as can easily be ascertained. It is this movement of the left eye, perceived by consciousness, which gives us the sensation of effort, at the same time as it makes us believe in the movement of the objects seen by the right eye. These observations, and others like them, lead Mr James to assert that the feeling of effort is centripetal and not centrifugal. We do not become conscious of a force which we would send out into the organism: our feeling of the muscular energy put forth "is a complex afferent sensation, which comes from the contracted muscles, the stretched ligaments, the squeezed joints, the fixed chest, the closed glottis, the knitted brow, the clenched jaws", in short, from all the points of the periphery where the effort brings about a modification. It is not for me to take sides in the debate. Besides, the question that concerns me is not whether the feeling of effort comes from the centre or from the periphery, but in what exactly our perception of its intensity consists. Now, one need only observe oneself attentively to arrive, on this last point, at a conclusion which Mr James has not formulated, but which seems to me entirely in keeping with the spirit of his doctrine. I maintain that the more a given effort strikes us as increasing, the more the number of muscles contracting sympathetically increases, and that the apparent consciousness of a greater intensity of effort at a given point of the organism reduces, in reality, to the perception of a larger surface of the body taking part in the operation. Try, for example, to clench your fist "more and more". It will seem to you that the sensation of effort, wholly localised in your hand, passes successively through increasing magnitudes. In reality your hand always feels the same thing. Only, the sensation which was at first localised there has invaded your arm, risen up to the shoulder; finally, the other arm stiffens, both legs follow suit, breathing stops; it is the whole body that is giving. But you become distinctly aware of these concomitant movements only on condition of being told of them; until then, you thought you were dealing with a single state of consciousness which was changing in magnitude. When you press your lips more and more tightly together, you believe you feel at that spot one and the same sensation growing stronger and stronger: here again you will notice, on further reflection, that this sensation remains identical, but that certain muscles of the face and head, then of all the rest of the body, have taken part in the operation. You have felt this gradual invasion, this increase of surface which is quite really a change of quantity; but as you were thinking chiefly of your pressed lips, you localised the increase at that spot, and you made of the psychic force expended there a magnitude, although it had no extension. Examine carefully a person who is lifting heavier and heavier weights: the muscular contraction gradually spreads over his whole body. As for the more particular sensation he feels in the arm that is working, it remains constant for a very long time, and changes hardly at all except in quality, the heaviness becoming at a certain moment fatigue, and the fatigue pain. Yet the subject will imagine he is conscious of a continuous increase of the psychic force flowing into his arm. He will recognise his error only on condition of being told of it, so prone is he to measure a given psychological state by the conscious movements which accompany it! From these facts and many others of the same kind we shall draw, I believe, the following conclusion: our consciousness of an increase of muscular effort reduces to the twofold perception of a greater number of peripheral sensations and of a qualitative change that has come about in some of them. We are thus led to define the intensity of a superficial effort in the same way as that of a deep feeling of the soul. In both cases there is qualitative progress and increasing complexity, confusedly perceived. But consciousness, accustomed to think in space and to tell itself what it thinks, will designate the feeling by a single word and will localise the effort at the precise point where it yields a useful result: it will then perceive an effort, always like itself, which grows on the spot it has assigned to it, and a feeling which, not changing its name, swells without changing its nature. It is probable that we shall find this illusion of consciousness again in the states intermediate between superficial efforts and deep feelings. A great number of psychological states are accompanied, in fact, by muscular contractions and peripheral sensations. Sometimes these superficial elements are coordinated with one another by a purely speculative idea, sometimes by a representation of a practical order. In the first case there is intellectual effort or attention; in the second there arise emotions which might be called violent or acute: anger, fright, and certain varieties of joy, of pain, of passion and of desire. Let us show briefly that the same definition of intensity fits these intermediate states. Attention is not a purely physiological phenomenon; but it cannot be denied that movements accompany it. These movements are neither the cause nor the result of the phenomenon; they form part of it, they express it in extension, as M. Ribot has so remarkably shown1. Fechner had already reduced the feeling of the effort of attention, in a sense organ, to the muscular feeling "produced by setting in motion, by a sort of reflex action, the muscles which are connected with the different sense organs". He had noticed that very distinct sensation of tension and contraction of the scalp, that pressure from without inwards over the whole skull, which one feels when making a great effort to remember something. M. Ribot has studied more closely the movements characteristic of voluntary attention. "Attention," he says, "contracts the frontal muscle: this muscle... draws the eyebrow towards it, raises it, and produces transverse wrinkles on the forehead... In extreme cases the mouth opens wide. In children and in many adults, keen attention produces a protrusion of the lips, a kind of pout." Certainly, a purely psychic factor will always enter into voluntary attention, were it only the exclusion, by the will, of all ideas foreign to the one with which we wish to occupy ourselves. But, once this exclusion has been made, we still believe we are conscious of an increasing tension of the soul, of an immaterial effort which grows. Analyse this impression, and you will find in it nothing other than the feeling of a muscular contraction which gains in surface or changes its nature, the tension becoming pressure, fatigue, pain. Now, I see no essential difference between the effort of attention and what might be called the effort of tension of the soul: acute desire, unbridled anger, passionate love, violent hatred. Each of these states would reduce, I believe, to a system of muscular contractions coordinated by an idea: but in attention it is the more or less reflective idea of knowing; in emotion, the unreflective idea of acting. The intensity of these violent emotions must therefore be nothing other than the muscular tension which accompanies them. Darwin has remarkably described the physiological symptoms of rage. "The beating of the heart is quickened; the face reddens or takes on a deathly pallor; breathing is laboured; the chest heaves; the quivering nostrils dilate. Often the whole body trembles. The voice is altered; the teeth are clenched or ground against one another, and the muscular system is generally excited to some violent, almost frantic act... The gestures represent more or less perfectly the act of striking or of fighting with an enemy."1 I shall not go so far as to maintain, with Mr William James2, that the emotion of rage reduces to the sum of these organic sensations - there will always enter into anger an irreducible psychic element, were it only that idea of striking or fighting of which Darwin speaks, an idea which gives a common direction to so many diverse movements. But if this idea determines the direction of the emotional state and the orientation of the concomitant movements, the increasing intensity of the state itself is nothing other, I believe, than the deeper and deeper disturbance of the organism, a disturbance which consciousness easily measures by the number and extension of the surfaces concerned. It will be urged in vain that there are restrained rages, and all the more intense for it. The reason is that where emotion is given free rein, consciousness does not dwell on the detail of the concomitant movements: it does dwell on them, on the contrary, it concentrates on them, when it aims at concealing them. Eliminate, finally, every trace of organic disturbance, every slightest impulse to muscular contraction: nothing will remain of anger but an idea, or, if you still insist on making it an emotion, you will be unable to assign it any intensity. "Fear, when strong," says Herbert Spencer1, "expresses itself in cries, in efforts to hide or escape, in palpitations and tremblings." I go further, and maintain that these movements form part of the fear itself: through them fear becomes an emotion, capable of passing through different degrees of intensity. Suppress them entirely, and the more or less intense fear will be succeeded by an idea of fear, the wholly intellectual representation of a danger which it is important to avoid. There is also an acuteness of joy and of pain, of desire, of aversion and even of shame, whose reason for being would be found in the movements of automatic reaction which the organism begins and which consciousness perceives. "Love," says Darwin, "makes the heart beat, quickens the breathing, flushes the face2." Aversion is marked by movements of disgust which one repeats, without noticing it, when one thinks of the detested object. One blushes, one involuntarily clenches one's fingers when one feels shame, even retrospective shame. The acuteness of these emotions is estimated by the number and nature of the peripheral sensations which accompany them. Little by little, and in proportion as the emotional state loses in violence to gain in depth, the peripheral sensations will give way to internal elements: it will no longer be our outward movements, but our ideas, our recollections, our states of consciousness in general, which will be oriented, in greater or lesser number, in a determinate direction. There is thus no essential difference, from the point of view of intensity, between the deep feelings of which I spoke at the beginning of this study and the acute or violent emotions which we have just passed in review. To say that love, hatred, desire gain in violence is to express that they project themselves outwards, that they radiate to the surface, that peripheral sensations take the place of internal elements: but superficial or deep, violent or reflective, the intensity of these feelings always consists in the multiplicity of simple states which consciousness confusedly makes out in them. I have so far confined myself to feelings and efforts, complex states whose intensity does not depend absolutely on an external cause. But sensations appear to us as simple states: in what will their magnitude consist? The intensity of these sensations varies as the external cause of which they are held to be the conscious equivalent: how are we to explain the invasion of quantity into an effect which is inextensive, and this time indivisible? To answer this question we must first distinguish between so-called affective sensations and representative sensations. No doubt we pass gradually from the one to the other; no doubt an affective element enters into most of our simple representations. But nothing prevents us from isolating it, and from inquiring separately in what the intensity of an affective sensation, pleasure or pain, consists. Perhaps the difficulty of this last problem lies chiefly in our unwillingness to see in the affective state anything other than the conscious expression of an organic disturbance, or the inner echo of an external cause. We notice that a greater nervous disturbance generally corresponds to a more intense sensation; but as these disturbances are unconscious as movements, since for consciousness they take on the aspect of a sensation which hardly resembles them, we do not see how they could transmit to the sensation something of their own magnitude. For there is nothing in common, I repeat, between superposable magnitudes such as amplitudes of vibration, for example, and sensations which occupy no space. If the more intense sensation seems to us to contain the sensation of lesser intensity, if it takes on for us, like the organic disturbance itself, the form of a magnitude, it is probably because it retains something of the physical disturbance to which it corresponds. And it will retain nothing of it if it is merely the conscious translation of a movement of molecules; for precisely because this movement is translated into a sensation of pleasure or pain, it remains unconscious as a molecular movement. But one might ask whether pleasure and pain, instead of expressing only what has just taken place or what is taking place in the organism, as is usually believed, do not also indicate what is about to happen there, what tends to take place there. It seems in fact rather improbable that nature, so profoundly utilitarian, should here have assigned to consciousness the wholly scientific task of informing us about the past or the present, which no longer depend on us. It must be noted, moreover, that we rise by imperceptible degrees from automatic movements to free movements, and that the latter differ from the former chiefly in presenting to us, between the external action which is their occasion and the willed reaction which follows, an intercalated affective sensation. One could even conceive that all our actions were automatic, and we know, moreover, of an infinite variety of organised beings in whom an external stimulus gives rise to a determinate reaction without passing through the intermediary of consciousness. If pleasure and pain arise in a privileged few, it is probably in order to allow on their part a resistance to the automatic reaction which would take place; either sensation has no reason for being, or it is a beginning of freedom. But how would it enable us to resist the reaction which is in preparation if it did not make its nature known to us by some precise sign? and what can this sign be, if not the sketch and as it were the preformation of the future automatic movements within the very sensation experienced? The affective state must therefore correspond not only to the disturbances, movements or physical phenomena which have been, but also and above all to those which are in preparation, to those which would like to be. It is true that we do not at first see how this hypothesis simplifies the problem. For we are seeking what there can be in common between a physical phenomenon and a state of consciousness from the point of view of magnitude, and it seems that we merely turn the difficulty round when we make the present state of consciousness an indication of the reaction to come, rather than a psychic translation of the past stimulus. The difference between the two hypotheses is nevertheless considerable. For the molecular disturbances of which we spoke a moment ago were necessarily unconscious, since nothing of these movements themselves could subsist in the sensation which translated them. But the automatic movements which tend to follow the stimulus undergone, and which would constitute its natural prolongation, are probably conscious as movements: or else the sensation itself, whose role is to invite us to a choice between this automatic reaction and other possible movements, would have no reason for being. The intensity of affective sensations would thus be nothing but the consciousness we take of the involuntary movements which are beginning, which are in some sort being sketched out in these states, and which would have followed their free course if nature had made us automata and not conscious beings. If this reasoning is sound, we must not compare a pain of increasing intensity to a note of the scale which would grow more and more sonorous, but rather to a symphony in which an increasing number of instruments make themselves heard. Within the characteristic sensation, which gives the tone to all the others, consciousness will make out a more or less considerable multiplicity of sensations emanating from the different points of the periphery, muscular contractions, organic movements of every kind: the concert of these elementary psychic states expresses the new demands of the organism in the presence of the new situation in which it is placed. In other words, we estimate the intensity of a pain by the interest which a greater or smaller part of the organism is willing to take in it. M. Richet1 has observed that one refers one's hurt to a spot all the more precise the weaker the pain is: if it becomes more intense, one refers it to the whole affected limb. And he concludes by saying that "pain radiates the more, the more intense it is2". I believe that this proposition must be reversed, and that the intensity of pain should be defined precisely by the number and extension of the parts of the body which sympathise with it and react, in full view of consciousness. To be convinced of this, it will suffice to read the remarkable description which the same author has given of disgust: "If the stimulus is weak, there may be neither nausea nor vomiting... If the stimulus is stronger, instead of being confined to the pneumogastric nerve, it radiates and affects almost the whole system of organic life. The face grows pale, the smooth muscles of the skin contract, the skin is covered with a cold sweat, the heart suspends its beats: in a word, there is a general organic disturbance consequent on the stimulation of the medulla oblongata, and this disturbance is the supreme expression of disgust3." - But is it only its expression? In what, then, will the general sensation of disgust consist, if not in the sum of these elementary sensations? And what can we understand here by increasing intensity, if not the ever-increasing number of sensations which come to be added to the sensations already perceived? Darwin has drawn a striking picture of the reactions consequent on a more and more acute pain: "It urges the animal to make the most violent and diversified efforts to escape from the cause which produces it... In intense suffering the mouth is strongly contracted, the lips are drawn tight, the teeth are clenched. Sometimes the eyes open wide, sometimes the eyebrows are strongly contracted; the body is bathed in sweat; the circulation is altered, as is the respiration4." - Is it not precisely by this contraction of the muscles concerned that we measure the intensity of a pain? Analyse the idea you form of a suffering which you declare extreme: do you not mean by this that it is unbearable, that is to say that it incites the organism to a thousand diverse actions in order to escape from it? It is conceivable that a nerve should transmit a pain independent of any automatic reaction; it is conceivable too that stronger or weaker stimuli should affect this nerve differently. But these differences of sensation would not be interpreted by your consciousness as differences of quantity if you did not connect with them the more or less extensive, more or less serious reactions which usually accompany them. Without these consequent reactions, the intensity of pain would be a quality, and not a magnitude. We have hardly any other means of comparing several pleasures with one another. What is a greater pleasure, if not a preferred pleasure? And what can our preference be, if not a certain disposition of our organs, which makes our body incline towards one of two pleasures when they present themselves simultaneously to our mind? Analyse this inclination itself, and you will find in it a thousand little movements which are beginning, which are being sketched out in the organs concerned and even in the rest of the body, as if the organism were going out to meet the pleasure represented. When inclination is defined as a movement, no metaphor is being used.
