In the presence of several pleasures conceived by the intellect, our body turns towards one of them spontaneously, as if by a reflex action. It is in our power to check it, but the attraction of pleasure is nothing other than this movement begun, and the very acuteness of pleasure, while we are enjoying it, is nothing but the inertia of the organism which is immersed in it, refusing every other sensation. Without this force of inertia, of which we become conscious through the resistance we offer to whatever might distract us, pleasure would still be a state, but no longer a magnitude. In the moral world, as in the physical world, attraction serves to explain movement rather than to produce it. I have studied affective sensations separately. Let us now note that many representative sensations have an affective character, and thus provoke on our part a reaction which we take into account in estimating their intensity. A considerable increase of light is translated for us into a characteristic sensation, which is not yet pain but which presents analogies with dazzling. As the amplitude of the sound vibration increases, our head, and then our body, seem to us to vibrate or to receive a shock. Certain representative sensations, those of taste, smell and temperature, even have a constantly agreeable or disagreeable character. Between more or less bitter tastes you would hardly make out anything but differences of quality; they are like the shades of one and the same colour. But these differences of quality are at once interpreted as differences of quantity, because of their affective character and of the more or less pronounced movements of reaction, pleasure or disgust, which they suggest to us. Moreover, even when the sensation remains purely representative, its external cause cannot go beyond a certain degree of strength or weakness without provoking on our part movements which serve us to measure it. Sometimes, in fact, we have to make an effort to perceive this sensation, as if it were slipping away; sometimes, on the contrary, it invades us, imposes itself on us, and absorbs us in such a way that we use all our effort to free ourselves from it and to remain ourselves. The sensation is said to be of little intensity in the first case, and very intense in the other. Thus, to perceive a distant sound, to distinguish what we call a faint smell and a weak light, we strain all the springs of our activity, we "pay attention". And it is precisely because the smell and the light then require to be reinforced by our effort that they appear weak to us. Conversely, we recognise the sensation of extreme intensity by the irresistible movements of automatic reaction which it provokes on our part, or by the powerlessness with which it strikes us. A cannon shot fired close to our ears, a dazzling light suddenly flaring up, deprive us for an instant of the consciousness of our personality; this state may even be prolonged in a predisposed subject. It must be added that, even in the region of so-called medium intensities, when we treat on equal terms with the representative sensation, we often estimate its importance by comparing it with another which it supplants, or by taking into account the persistence with which it recurs. Thus the ticking of a watch seems louder at night, because it easily absorbs a consciousness almost empty of sensations and ideas. Foreigners conversing among themselves in a language we do not understand strike us as speaking very loudly, because their words, no longer calling up ideas in our mind, burst out in the midst of a kind of intellectual silence, and monopolise our attention like the ticking of a watch at night. With these so-called medium sensations, however, we come to a series of psychic states whose intensity must have a new meaning. For most of the time the organism hardly reacts, at least not in any apparent way; and yet we still set up as a magnitude a pitch of sound, an intensity of light, a saturation of colour. No doubt the minute observation of what goes on in the organism as a whole when we hear this or that note, when we perceive this or that colour, holds more than one surprise in store for us: has not M. Ch. Féré shown that every sensation is accompanied by an increase of muscular force, measurable with the dynamometer1? This increase, however, hardly strikes consciousness, and if we reflect on the precision with which we distinguish sounds and colours, and even weights and temperatures, we shall easily guess that a new element of estimation must come into play here. The nature of this element is, moreover, easy to determine. For in proportion as a sensation loses its affective character to pass into the state of representation, the movements of reaction which it provoked on our part tend to fade away; but at the same time we perceive the external object which is its cause, or, if we do not perceive it, we have perceived it, and we think of it. Now, this cause is extensive and consequently measurable: an experience of every moment, which began with the first glimmers of consciousness and continues throughout our whole existence, shows us a determinate shade of the sensation answering to a determinate value of the stimulus. We then associate with a certain quality of the effect the idea of a certain quantity of the cause; and finally, as happens with every acquired perception, we put the idea into the sensation, the quantity of the cause into the quality of the effect. At this precise moment intensity, which was only a certain shade or quality of the sensation, becomes a magnitude. This process can easily be grasped by holding a pin in the right hand, for example, and pricking the left hand more and more deeply. You will feel first something like a tickling, then a contact which is followed by a prick, then a pain localised at one point, and finally a radiation of this pain into the surrounding area. And the more you reflect on it, the more you will see that these are so many qualitatively distinct sensations, so many varieties of one and the same species. Yet you spoke at first of one and the same sensation, more and more invasive, of a more and more intense prick. The reason is that, without noticing it, you were localising in the sensation of the left hand, which is pricked, the progressive effort of the right hand, which pricks it. You were thus introducing the cause into the effect, and unconsciously interpreting quality as quantity, intensity as magnitude. It is easy to see that the intensity of every representative sensation must be understood in the same way. Sensations of sound present us with very marked degrees of intensity. I have already said that we must take into account the affective character of these sensations, the shock received by the organism as a whole. I have shown that a very intense sound is one which absorbs our attention, which supplants all the others. But abstract from the shock, from the well-marked vibration which you sometimes feel in the head or even in the whole body; abstract from the competition between simultaneous sounds: what will remain, if not an indefinable quality of the sound heard? Only, this quality is at once interpreted as quantity, because you have obtained it yourself a thousand times, by striking an object, for example, and thereby supplying a determinate quantity of effort. You know too how far you would have to raise your voice to produce a similar sound, and the idea of this effort instantly presents itself to your mind when you set up the intensity of the sound as a magnitude. Wundt1 has drawn attention to the quite special connections between vocal and auditory nerve fibres which are effected in the human brain. Has it not been said that to hear is to speak to oneself? Certain neuropaths cannot be present at a conversation without moving their lips; this is only an exaggeration of what takes place in each of us. Could we understand the expressive, or rather suggestive, power of music if we did not admit that we inwardly repeat the sounds we hear, so as to put ourselves back into the psychological state from which they issued, an original state, which cannot be expressed, but which the movements adopted by our body as a whole suggest to us? When we speak of the intensity of a sound of medium strength as a magnitude, we are therefore alluding chiefly to the greater or lesser effort we should have to supply in order to procure the same auditory sensation for ourselves again. But alongside intensity we distinguish another characteristic property of sound, pitch. Are differences of pitch, as our ear perceives them, quantitative differences? I grant that a greater acuteness of sound calls up the image of a more elevated position in space. But does it follow from this that the notes of the scale, as auditory sensations, differ otherwise than in quality? Forget what physics has taught you, examine carefully the idea you have of a higher or lower note, and say whether you are not simply thinking of the greater or lesser effort which the tensor muscle of your vocal cords would have to supply in order to produce the note in its turn? As the effort by which your voice passes from one note to the next is discontinuous, you picture these successive notes as points in space which would be reached one after the other by abrupt leaps, each time crossing an empty interval which separates them: and that is why you establish intervals between the notes of the scale. It remains to be seen, it is true, why the line on which we range them is vertical rather than horizontal, and why we say that the sound rises in some cases and falls in others. It is incontestable that high notes seem to us to produce effects of resonance in the head, and low notes in the chest cavity; this perception, real or illusory, has no doubt helped to make us count the intervals vertically. But it must also be noted that the greater the effort of tension of the vocal cords in the chest voice, the larger the surface of the body which takes part in it in the inexperienced singer; that is indeed why he feels the effort as more intense. And as he breathes out the air from below upwards, he will attribute the same direction to the sound which the current of air produces; it is therefore by a movement from below upwards that the sympathy of a greater part of the body with the muscles of the voice will be expressed. We shall then say that the note is higher, because the body makes an effort as if to reach an object higher up in space. The habit has thus been formed of assigning a height to each note of the scale, and on the day when the physicist was able to define it by the number of vibrations to which it corresponds in a given time, we no longer hesitated to say that our ear directly perceived differences of quantity. But sound would remain pure quality if we did not introduce into it the muscular effort which would produce it, or the vibration which explains it. The recent experiments of Blix, Goldscheider and Donaldson1 have shown that it is not the same points of the surface of the body that feel cold and heat. Physiology is therefore already inclined to establish between the sensations of hot and cold a distinction of nature, and no longer of degree. But psychological observation goes further, for an attentive consciousness would easily find specific differences between the various sensations of heat, as also between the sensations of cold. A more intense heat is really a different heat. We call it more intense because we have a thousand times experienced this same change when we drew nearer to a source of heat, or when a larger surface of our body was affected by it. Moreover, the sensations of heat and cold very quickly become affective, and then provoke on our part more or less marked reactions which measure their external cause: how should we not establish analogous quantitative differences between the sensations which correspond to intermediate strengths of this cause? I shall not insist further; it is for each person to question himself scrupulously on this point, making a clean sweep of everything his past experience has taught him about the cause of his sensation, and placing himself face to face with this sensation itself. The result of this examination does not seem to me doubtful: one will very soon notice that the magnitude of the representative sensation arises from one's putting the cause into the effect, and the intensity of the affective element from one's introducing into the sensation the more or less important movements of reaction which continue the external stimulus. I shall request the same examination for the sensations of pressure and even of weight. When you say that a pressure exerted on your hand becomes stronger and stronger, see whether you do not represent to yourself by this that contact has become pressure, then pain, and that this pain itself, after passing through several phases, has radiated into the surrounding region. See further, see above all, whether you do not bring in the more and more intense, that is to say more and more extended, antagonistic effort which you oppose to the external pressure. When the psychophysicist lifts a heavier weight, he experiences, he says, an increase of sensation. Consider whether this increase of sensation ought not rather to be called a sensation of increase. The whole question lies there, for in the first case the sensation would be a quantity, like its external cause, and in the second a quality, which has become representative of the magnitude of its cause. The distinction between the heavy and the light may seem as backward, as naive, as that between hot and cold. But the very naivety of this distinction makes it a psychological reality. And not only do the heavy and the light constitute different genera for our consciousness, but the degrees of lightness and of heaviness are so many species of these two genera. It must be added that the difference of quality is spontaneously translated here into a difference of quantity, because of the more or less extended effort which our body supplies in order to lift a given weight. You will easily convince yourself of this if you are invited to lift a basket which you have been told is full of scrap iron, when it is in reality empty. You will think you are losing your balance as you take hold of it, as if extraneous muscles had taken part in the operation in advance and were suffering a sudden disappointment. It is above all by the number and nature of these sympathetic efforts, carried out at various points of the organism, that you measure the sensation of weight at a given point; and this sensation would be only a quality if you did not thus introduce into it the idea of a magnitude. What strengthens your illusion on this point, moreover, is the habit you have formed of believing in the immediate perception of a homogeneous movement in a homogeneous space. When I lift a light weight with my arm, all the rest of my body remaining motionless, I experience a series of muscular sensations each of which has its "local sign", its own shade: it is this series which my consciousness interprets in the sense of a continuous movement in space. If I then lift a heavier weight to the same height and with the same speed, I pass through a new series of muscular sensations, each of which differs from the corresponding term of the preceding series: of this I shall easily convince myself by examining them closely. But as I interpret this new series too in the sense of a continuous movement, as this movement has the same direction, the same duration and the same speed as the preceding one, my consciousness must needs localise the difference between the second series of sensations and the first somewhere other than in the movement itself. It then materialises this difference at the end of the arm which is moving; it persuades itself that the sensation of the movement was identical in the two cases, while the sensation of weight differed in magnitude. But movement and weight are distinctions of reflective consciousness: immediate consciousness has the sensation of a heavy movement, so to speak, and this sensation itself resolves on analysis into a series of muscular sensations, each of which represents by its shade the place where it occurs, and by its colouring the magnitude of the weight being lifted. Shall we call the intensity of light a quantity, or shall we treat it as a quality? Perhaps not enough notice has been taken of the multitude of very different elements which combine, in daily life, to inform us about the nature of the source of light. We have long known that this light is distant, or about to go out, when we have difficulty in making out the outlines and details of objects. Experience has taught us that we must ascribe to a greater strength of the cause that affective sensation, prelude to dazzling, which we experience in certain cases. According as the number of light sources is increased or diminished, the edges of bodies do not stand out in the same way, nor do the shadows they cast. But a still larger share must be given, I believe, to the changes of hue which coloured surfaces undergo - even the pure colours of the spectrum - under the influence of a fainter or a more brilliant light. As the light source draws nearer, violet takes on a bluish hue, green tends towards whitish yellow and red towards bright yellow. Conversely, when this light moves away, ultramarine blue passes into violet, yellow into green; finally red, green and violet approach whitish yellow. These changes of hue have been noticed for some time by physicists1; but what is far more remarkable, in my view, is that most people hardly notice them, unless they pay attention to them or are told of them. Determined to interpret changes of quality as changes of quantity, we begin by laying down as a principle that every object has its own colour, determinate and invariable. And when the hue of objects approaches yellow or blue, instead of saying that we see their colour change under the influence of an increase or decrease of illumination, we shall assert that this colour remains the same, but that our sensation of luminous intensity increases or diminishes. Here again, then, we substitute for the qualitative impression which our consciousness receives the quantitative interpretation which our understanding gives of it. Helmholtz has pointed out a phenomenon of interpretation of the same kind, but still more complicated: "If white is compounded," he says, "from two spectral colours, and the intensities of the two coloured lights are increased or diminished in the same ratio, so that the proportions of the mixture remain the same, the resulting colour remains the same, although the ratio of intensity of the sensations changes noticeably... This is because sunlight, which we regard as normal white during the day, itself undergoes analogous modifications of its hue when the luminous intensity varies2." However, if we often judge of the variations of the light source by the relative changes of hue of the objects around us, this is no longer so in the simple cases where a single object, a white surface for example, passes successively through different degrees of luminosity. I must insist quite particularly on this last point. Physics, in fact, speaks to us of degrees of luminous intensity as of true quantities: does it not measure them with the photometer? The psychophysicist goes further still: he claims that our eye itself estimates the intensities of light. Experiments have been attempted, first by M. Delboeuf3, then by MM. Lehmann and Neiglick4, to establish a psychophysical formula on the direct measurement of our sensations of light. I shall not dispute the results of these experiments, nor the value of photometric procedures; but everything depends on the interpretation given of them. Consider attentively a sheet of paper lit by four candles, for example, and have one, two, three of them put out in succession. You say that the surface remains white and that its brightness diminishes. You know, in fact, that a candle has just been put out; or, if you do not know it, you have many times noted a similar change in the appearance of a white surface when the lighting was reduced. But abstract from your recollections and your habits of speech: what you really perceived was not a diminution of the illumination of the white surface, it was a layer of shadow passing over this surface at the moment when the candle went out. This shadow is a reality for your consciousness, like the light itself. If you called the original surface in all its brightness white, you will have to give another name to what you see, for it is something else: it would be, if one could so speak, a new shade of white. Must I now say everything? We have been accustomed by our past experience, and also by physical theories, to regard black as an absence, or at least as a minimum, of luminous sensation, and the successive shades of grey as decreasing intensities of white light. Well, black has as much reality for our consciousness as white, and the decreasing intensities of the white light illuminating a given surface would be, for an unprejudiced consciousness, so many different shades, rather like the various colours of the spectrum. What proves this clearly is that the change is not continuous in the sensation as it is in its external cause, that the light can increase or diminish for a certain time without the illumination of our white surface seeming to us to change: it will seem to change, in fact, only when the increase or diminution of the external light is enough to create a new quality. The variations in brightness of a given colour - leaving aside the affective sensations spoken of above - would thus reduce to qualitative changes, if we had not formed the habit of putting the cause into the effect, and of substituting for our naive impression what experience and science teach us. The same could be said of the degrees of saturation. In fact, if the various intensities of a colour correspond to so many different shades lying between this colour and black, the degrees of saturation are like intermediate shades between this same colour and pure white. Every colour, I should say, can be regarded under a twofold aspect, from the point of view of black and from the point of view of white. Black would be to intensity what white is to saturation. We shall now understand the meaning of photometric experiments. A candle, placed at a certain distance from a sheet of paper, lights it in a certain way: you double the distance, and you find that four candles are needed to awaken the same sensation in you. From this you conclude that, if you had doubled the distance without increasing the intensity of the light source, the effect of illumination would have been four times less. But it is only too evident that we are dealing here with the physical effect, and not the psychological one. For it cannot be said that we have compared two sensations with each other: we have used a single sensation in order to compare with each other two different light sources, the second four times the first but twice as far away. In a word, the physicist never brings in sensations which are double or triple one another, but only identical sensations, meant to serve as intermediaries between two physical quantities which can then be equated with each other. The luminous sensation plays here the part of those auxiliary unknowns which the mathematician introduces into his calculations, and which disappear from the final result. Quite different is the object of the psychophysicist: it is the sensation of light itself that he studies, and that he claims to measure. Sometimes he will proceed by an integration of infinitely small differences, according to Fechner's method; sometimes he will compare one sensation directly with another sensation. This latter method, due to Plateau and to Delbœuf, differs much less than has hitherto been believed from Fechner's; but, as it bears more especially on sensations of light, I shall deal with it first. M. Delbœuf places an observer in front of three concentric rings of variable brightness. An ingenious device enables him to make each of these rings pass through all the intermediate shades between white and black. Let us suppose two of these grey shades produced simultaneously on two rings, and kept unvarying; we shall call them A and B, for example. M. Delbœuf varies the brightness C of the third ring, and asks the observer to tell him whether, at a given moment, the grey shade B appears to him equally distant from the other two. A moment does in fact arrive when the latter declares the contrast AB equal to the contrast BC; so that one could construct, according to M. Delbœuf, a scale of luminous intensities in which one would pass from each sensation to the next by equal sensible contrasts: our sensations would thus be measured by one another. I shall not follow M. Delbœuf into the conclusions he has drawn from these remarkable experiments: the essential question, the only question, in my view, is whether a contrast AB, formed of the elements A and B, is really equal to a contrast BC, differently composed. On the day it was established that two sensations can be equal without being identical, psychophysics would be founded. But it is just this equality that seems to me open to question: it is easy to explain, in fact, how a sensation of luminous intensity can be said to be at an equal distance from two others. Let us suppose for a moment that, since our birth, the variations in intensity of a source of light had been conveyed to our consciousness by the successive perception of the various colours of the spectrum. There is no doubt that these colours would then appear to us like so many notes of a scale, like higher or lower degrees on a ladder, like magnitudes, in a word. On the other hand, it would be easy for us to assign to each of them its place in the series. For if the extensive cause varies continuously, the sensation of colour changes discontinuously, passing from one shade to another shade. However numerous, then, the intermediate shades between two colours A and B may be, we shall always be able to count them in thought, at least roughly, and to ascertain whether this number is approximately equal to that of the shades separating B from another colour C. In the latter case we shall say that B is equally distant from A and from C, that the contrast is the same on either side. But this will never be more than a convenient interpretation: for although the number of intermediate shades is equal on both sides, although we pass from one to the other by sudden leaps, we do not know whether these leaps are magnitudes, nor whether they are equal magnitudes: above all, it would have to be shown us that the intermediates which have served for the measurement are found again, in some sort, within the object measured. Otherwise it is only by metaphor that a sensation can be said to be at an equal distance from two others. Now, if what I said above about luminous intensities is granted me, it will be recognised that the various grey shades presented by M. Delbœuf to our observation are quite analogous, for our consciousness, to colours, and that if we declare one grey shade equidistant from two other grey shades, it is in the same sense in which one might say that orange, for example, is at an equal distance from green and from red. Only there is this difference, that in all our past experience the succession of grey shades has occurred in connection with a progressive increase or decrease of illumination. Hence it is that we do for differences of brightness what we do not think of doing for differences of colouring: we set up changes of quality as variations of magnitude. The measurement, moreover, is made without difficulty, because the successive shades of grey brought about by a continuous decrease of illumination are discontinuous, being qualities, and because we can count approximately the principal intermediates that separate two of them. The contrast AB will therefore be declared equal to the contrast BC when our imagination, aided by our memory, interposes the same number of landmarks on either side. This estimate is bound, moreover, to be of the roughest, and one may foresee that it will vary considerably from person to person. Above all, we must expect the hesitations and the discrepancies of estimate to be the more marked the more the difference of brightness between the rings A and B is increased, for an ever more laborious effort will be required to assess the number of intervening shades. This is precisely what happens, as one will readily be convinced by glancing at the two tables drawn up by M. Delbœuf1. As he increases the difference of brightness between the outer ring and the middle ring, the gap between the figures at which one and the same observer, or different observers, successively stop increases in an almost continuous way from 3 degrees to 94, from 5 to 73, from 10 to 25, from 7 to 40. But let us leave these discrepancies aside; let us suppose that the observers are always in agreement with themselves, always in agreement with one another: will it have been established that the contrasts AB and BC are equal? It would first have to be proved that two successive elementary contrasts are equal quantities, and we know only that they are successive. It would next have to be established that in a given grey shade we find again the lower shades through which our imagination passed in order to estimate the objective intensity of the source of light. In a word, M. Delbœuf's psychophysics presupposes a theoretical postulate of the highest importance, which vainly hides beneath an experimental appearance, and which I should formulate thus: "When the objective quantity of light is increased continuously, the differences between the grey shades successively obtained, differences each of which expresses the smallest perceived increase of physical stimulus, are quantities equal to one another. And further, any one of the sensations obtained can be equated to the sum of the differences that separate the preceding sensations from one another, starting from zero sensation." Now this is precisely the postulate of Fechner's psychophysics, which we are about to examine. Fechner started from a law discovered by Weber, according to which, given a certain stimulus provoking a certain sensation, the quantity of stimulus that has to be added to the first for consciousness to notice a change will stand in a constant ratio to it. Thus, denoting by E the stimulus corresponding to the sensation S, and by ∆E the quantity of stimulus of the same kind that has to be added to the first for a sensation of difference to arise, we should have ∆E = const. E This formula has been profoundly modified by Fechner's disciples: I shall not intervene in the debate; it is for experience to decide between the relation established by Weber and those put in its place. Nor shall I make any difficulty, moreover, about admitting the probable existence of a law of this kind. For it is not a question here of measuring the sensation, but only of determining the precise moment at which an increase of stimulus makes it change. Now, if a determinate quantity of stimulus produces a determinate shade of sensation, it is clear that the minimum quantity of stimulus required to provoke a change in this shade is determinate too; and since it is not constant, it must be a function of the stimulus to which it is added. But how are we to pass from a relation between the stimulus and its minimum increase to an equation connecting the "quantity of the sensation" with the corresponding stimulus? The whole of psychophysics lies in this passage, which it is important to study attentively. I shall distinguish several different artifices in the operation by which one passes from Weber's experiments, or from any other series of analogous observations, to a psychophysical law like Fechner's. It is first agreed to regard as an increase of the sensation S the consciousness we have of an increase of stimulus; it will accordingly be called ∆S. It is next laid down as a principle that all the sensations ∆S corresponding to the smallest perceptible increase of a stimulus are equal to one another. They are then treated as quantities, and since these quantities are always equal, on the one hand, while on the other hand experience has given a certain relation ∆E = φ(E) between the stimulus E and its minimum increase, the constancy of ∆S is expressed by writing: ∆S = C ∆E/φ(E), C being a constant quantity. Finally it is agreed to replace the very small differences ∆S and ∆E by the infinitely small differences dS and dE, whence an equation which is this time differential: dS = C dE/φ(E) It will then only remain to integrate both sides to obtain the relation sought1: S = C ∫₀ᴱ dE/φ(E); and in this way one will pass from a verified law, in which only the appearance of the sensation was in question, to an unverifiable law, which gives its measure. Without entering into a thorough discussion of this ingenious operation, let me show in a few words how Fechner grasped the real difficulty of the problem, how he tried to overcome it, and where, in my view, the flaw in his reasoning lies. Fechner understood that measurement cannot be introduced into psychology without first defining there the equality and the addition of two simple states, of two sensations for example. On the other hand, unless they are identical, one does not see at first how two sensations could be equal. No doubt, in the physical world, equality is by no means synonymous with identity. But that is because every phenomenon, every object, presents itself there under a twofold aspect, the one qualitative, the other extensive: nothing prevents us from abstracting from the first, and there then remain only terms capable of being superposed directly or indirectly on one another, and consequently of being identified with one another. Now this qualitative element, which we begin by eliminating from external things in order to make their measurement possible, is precisely the one that psychophysics retains and claims to measure. And it would be in vain for it to seek to assess this quality Q by some physical quantity Q' lying beneath it; for it would first have to be shown that Q is a function of Q', and this could be done only if the quality Q had first been measured with some fraction of itself. Thus nothing would prevent us from measuring the sensation of heat by the degree of temperature; but that would be no more than a convention, and psychophysics consists precisely in rejecting this convention and seeking how the sensation of heat varies when the temperature varies. In short, it seems that two different sensations can be said to be equal only if some identical ground remains after the elimination of their qualitative difference; and, on the other hand, since this qualitative difference is all that we feel, one does not see what could subsist once it had been eliminated. Fechner's originality lies in not having judged this difficulty insurmountable. Taking advantage of the fact that the sensation varies by sudden leaps when the stimulus increases continuously, he did not hesitate to designate these differences of sensation by the same name: they are minimum differences, in fact, since each of them corresponds to the smallest perceptible increase of the external stimulus. From then on you can abstract from the specific shade or quality of these successive differences; a ground common to them will remain, by which they will in some sort be identified with one another: they are, the one and the other, minima. There is the definition of equality that was sought. That of addition will follow naturally. For if we treat as a quantity the difference perceived by consciousness between two sensations that succeed one another along a continuous increase of stimulus, if we call the first S and the second S + ∆S, we shall have to regard every sensation S as a sum, obtained by the addition of the minimum differences that are passed through before it is reached. It will then only remain to use this twofold definition to establish a relation first between the differences ∆S and ∆E, and then, by means of the differentials, between the two variables. It is true that mathematicians may protest here against the passage from the difference to the differential; psychologists will ask whether the quantity ∆S, instead of being constant, might not vary like the sensation S itself1: finally there will be debate about the true meaning of the psychophysical law, once established. But by the mere fact that ∆S is regarded as a quantity and S as a sum, the fundamental postulate of the whole operation is admitted. Now it is this postulate that seems to me open to question, and even rather unintelligible. Suppose, in fact, that I experience a sensation S, and that, the stimulus being increased continuously, I become aware of this increase after a certain time. Here I am, notified of the increase of the cause: but what relation is to be established between this notification and a difference? No doubt the notification consists here in the fact that the original state S has changed; it has become S'; but for the passage from S to S' to be comparable to an arithmetical difference, I should have to be conscious, so to speak, of an interval between S and S', and my sensibility would have to rise from S to S' by the addition of something. By giving this passage a name, by calling it ∆S, you make it first a reality, then a quantity. Now not only are you unable to explain in what sense this passage is a quantity, but you will notice, on reflection, that it is not even a reality; the only real things are the states S and S' through which one passes. No doubt, if S and S' were numbers, I could affirm the reality of the difference S' - S even if S' and S alone were given: this is because the number S' - S, which is a certain sum of units, will then represent precisely the successive moments of the addition by which one passes from S to S'. But if S and S' are simple states, in what will the interval separating them consist? And what, then, will the passage from the first state to the second be, if not an act of your thought, which arbitrarily, and to suit the case, assimilates a succession of two states to a differentiation of two magnitudes? Either you keep to what consciousness gives you, or you use a conventional mode of representation. In the first case you will find between S and S' a difference analogous to that between the shades of the rainbow, and not at all an interval of magnitude. In the second, you may introduce the symbol ∆S if you like, but it is by convention that you will speak of an arithmetical difference, by convention too that you will assimilate a given sensation to a sum. The most penetrating of Fechner's critics, M. Jules Tannery, has brought this last point fully to light: "One will say, for example, that a sensation of 50 degrees is expressed by the number of differential sensations that would succeed one another from the absence of sensation up to the sensation of 50 degrees... I do not see that there is anything there but a definition, as legitimate as it is arbitrary1." I do not believe, whatever may have been said, that the method of mean gradations has set psychophysics on a new path. M. Delbœuf's originality was to choose a particular case in which consciousness seemed to bear Fechner out, and in which common sense was itself a psychophysicist. He asked himself whether certain sensations did not appear to us immediately as equal, though different, and whether one could not draw up by their means a table of sensations that are double, triple, quadruple one another. Fechner's error, I was saying, was to have believed in an interval between two successive sensations S and S', whereas from the one to the other there is simply passage, and not difference in the arithmetical sense of the word. But if the two terms between which the passage takes place could be given simultaneously, there would this time be contrast in addition to passage; and although contrast is not yet an arithmetical difference, it resembles one in a certain respect; the two terms being compared stand in each other's presence as in a subtraction of two numbers. Suppose now that these sensations are of the same kind, and that constantly, in our past experience, we have witnessed their procession, so to speak, while the physical stimulus increased continuously: it is infinitely probable that we shall put the cause into the effect, and that the idea of contrast will melt into that of arithmetical difference. As, on the other hand, we shall have noticed that the sensation changed suddenly while the progress of the stimulus was continuous, we shall no doubt assess the distance between two given sensations by the number, roughly reconstituted, of these sudden leaps, or at least of the intermediate sensations that most usually serve us as markers. In short, the contrast will appear to us as a difference, the stimulus as a quantity, the sudden leap as an element of equality; combining these three factors together, we shall arrive at the idea of equal quantitative differences. Now nowhere are these conditions so well realised as when surfaces of the same colour, more or less illuminated, present themselves to us simultaneously. Not only is there contrast here between analogous sensations, but these sensations correspond to a cause whose influence has always seemed to us closely bound up with its distance; and as this distance can vary continuously, we must have noted, in our past experience, an innumerable multitude of shades of sensation succeeding one another along a continuous increase of the cause. We shall therefore be able to say that the contrast of a first grey shade with a second, for example, seems to us roughly equal to the contrast of the second with a third; and if two sensations are defined as equal by saying that they are sensations which a more or less confused reasoning interprets as such, we shall indeed arrive at a law like the one M. Delbœuf proposes. But it must not be forgotten that consciousness has passed through the same intermediates as the psychophysicist, and that its judgement is worth here what psychophysics is worth: it is a symbolic interpretation of quality as quantity, a more or less rough estimate of the number of sensations that could be intercalated between two given sensations. The difference, then, is not as considerable as is believed between the method of minimum changes and that of mean gradations, between the psychophysics of Fechner and that of M. Delbœuf. The first arrives at a conventional measurement of sensation; the second appeals to common sense in the particular cases in which it adopts an analogous convention. In short, all psychophysics is condemned by its very origin to move in a vicious circle, for the theoretical postulate on which it rests condemns it to an experimental verification, and it can be verified experimentally only if its postulate is first admitted. The reason is that there is no point of contact between the unextended and the extended, between quality and quantity. We can interpret the one by the other, set up the one as the equivalent of the other; but sooner or later, at the beginning or at the end, we shall have to acknowledge the conventional character of this assimilation. In truth, psychophysics has only formulated with precision, and pushed to its extreme consequences, a conception familiar to common sense. Since we speak rather than think, since also external objects, which belong to the common domain, are of more importance to us than the subjective states through which we pass, it is wholly in our interest to objectify these states by introducing into them, as far as possible, the representation of their external cause. And the more our knowledge grows, the more we perceive the extensive behind the intensive and quantity behind quality, the more too we tend to put the first term into the second, and to treat our sensations as magnitudes. Physics, whose role is precisely to submit the external cause of our internal states to calculation, concerns itself as little as possible with these states themselves - unceasingly, and deliberately, it confuses them with their cause. It therefore encourages, and even exaggerates, the illusion of common sense on this point. The moment was bound to come when science, grown familiar with this confusion of quality with quantity and of sensation with stimulus, would seek to measure the one as it measures the other: such was the object of psychophysics. In this bold attempt Fechner was encouraged by his very adversaries, by the philosophers who speak of intensive magnitudes while declaring psychic states refractory to measurement. For if it is admitted that one sensation can be stronger than another sensation, and that this inequality resides in the sensations themselves, independently of any association of ideas, of any more or less conscious consideration of number and space, it is natural to seek by how much the first sensation exceeds the second, and to establish a quantitative ratio between their intensities. And it is no use replying, as the adversaries of psychophysics often do, that all measurement implies superposition, and that there is no ground for seeking a numerical ratio between intensities, which are not superposable things. For it will then have to be explained why one sensation is said to be more intense than another sensation, and how things can be called greater or smaller which - as has just been acknowledged - admit of no relations of container to contained among themselves. If, to cut short any question of this kind, two species of quantity are distinguished, the one intensive, which admits only of more and less, the other extensive, which lends itself to measurement, one comes very close to bearing out Fechner and the psychophysicists. For as soon as a thing is recognised as capable of increasing and diminishing, it seems natural to seek by how much it diminishes, by how much it increases. And because a measurement of this kind does not seem directly possible, it does not follow that science cannot succeed in it by some indirect procedure, whether by an integration of infinitely small elements, as Fechner proposes, or by any other roundabout means. Either, then, sensation is pure quality, or, if it is a magnitude, we must seek to measure it. To sum up the foregoing, I shall say that the notion of intensity presents itself under a twofold aspect, according as we study the states of consciousness that represent an external cause, or those that are self-sufficient. In the first case, the perception of intensity consists in a certain estimate of the magnitude of the cause by a certain quality of the effect: it is, as the Scots would say, an acquired perception. In the second, we call intensity the more or less considerable multiplicity of simple psychic facts that we divine within the fundamental state: it is no longer an acquired perception, but a confused perception. Moreover, these two senses of the word most often permeate one another, because the simpler facts that an emotion or an effort involves are generally representative, and because most representative states, being affective at the same time, themselves embrace a multiplicity of elementary psychic facts. The idea of intensity is thus situated at the point of junction of two currents, one of which brings us from outside the idea of extensive magnitude, while the other has gone to seek in the depths of consciousness, to bring it up to the surface, the image of an inner multiplicity. It remains to be seen in what this latter image consists, whether it is one with that of number, or whether it differs from it radically. In the chapter that follows I shall no longer consider states of consciousness in isolation from one another, but in their concrete multiplicity, inasmuch as they unfold in pure duration. And just as I asked what the intensity of a representative sensation would be if we did not introduce into it the idea of its cause, so I shall now have to inquire what becomes of the multiplicity of our inner states, what form duration takes, when we abstract from the space in which it unfolds. This second question is far more important than the first. For if the confusion of quality with quantity were confined to each of the facts of consciousness taken in isolation, it would create obscurities, as we have just seen, rather than problems. But by invading the series of our psychological states, by introducing space into our conception of duration, it corrupts at their very source our representations of external change and of inner change, of movement and of freedom. Hence the sophisms of the Eleatic school, hence the problem of free will. I shall dwell rather on the second point; but instead of seeking to solve the question, I shall show the illusion of those who raise it.

o: On définit généralement le nombre une collection d'unités ou, pour parler avec plus de précision, la synthèse de l'un et du multiple. Tout nombre est un, en effet, puisqu'on se le représente par une intuition simple de l'esprit et qu'on lui donne un nom ; mais cette unité est celle d'une somme ; elle embrasse une multiplicité de parties qu'on peut considérer isolément. Sans approfondir pour le moment ces notions d'unité et de multiplicité, demandons-nous si l'idée de nombre n'impliquerait pas la représentation de quelque autre chose encore. Il ne suffit pas de dire que le nombre est une collection d'unités ; il faut ajouter que ces unités sont identiques entre elles, ou du moins qu’on les suppose identiques dès qu'on les compte. Sans doute on comptera les moutons d'un troupeau et l'on dira qu'il y en a cinquante, bien qu'ils se distinguent les uns des autres et que le berger les reconnaisse sans peine ; mais c'est que l'on convient alors de négliger leurs différences individuelles pour ne tenir compte que de leur fonction commune. Au contraire, dès qu'on fixe son attention sur les traits particuliers des objets ou des individus, on peut bien en faire l'énumération, mais non plus la somme. C'est à ces deux points de vue bien différents qu'on se place quand on compte les soldats d'un bataillon, et quand on en fait l'appel. Nous dirons donc que l'idée de nombre implique l'intuition simple d'une multiplicité de parties ou d'unités, absolument semblables les unes aux autres. Et pourtant il faut bien qu'elles se distinguent par quelque endroit, puisqu'elles ne se confondent pas en une seule. Supposons tous les moutons du troupeau identiques entre eux ; ils diffèrent au moins par la place qu'ils occupent dans l'espace ; sinon, ils ne formeraient point un troupeau. Mais laissons de côté les cinquante moutons eux-mêmes pour n'en retenir que l'idée. Ou nous les comprenons tous dans la même image, et il faut bien par conséquent que nous les juxtaposions dans un espace idéal ; ou nous répétons cinquante fois de suite l'image d'un seul d'entre eux, et il semble alors que la série prenne place dans la durée plutôt que dans l'espace. Il n'en est rien cependant. Car si je me figure tour à tour, et isolément, chacun des moutons du troupeau, je n'aurai jamais affaire qu'à un seul mouton. Pour que le nombre en aille croissant à mesure que j'avance, il faut bien que je retienne les images successives et que je les juxtapose à chacune des unités nouvelles dont j'évoque l'idée : or c'est dans l'espace qu'une pareille juxtaposition s'opère, et non dans la durée pure. On nous accordera d'ailleurs sans peine que toute opération par laquelle on compte des objets matériels implique la représentation simultanée de ces objets, et que, par là même, on les laisse dans l'espace. Mais cette intuition de l'espace accompagne-t-elle toute idée de nombre, même celle d'un nombre abstrait ? Pour répondre à cette question, il suffira à chacun de passer en revue les diverses formes que l'idée de nombre a prises pour lui depuis son enfance. On verra que nous avons commencé par imaginer une rangée de boules, par exemple, puis que ces boules sont devenues des points, puis enfin que cette image elle-même s'est évanouie pour ne plus laisser derrière elle, disons-nous, que le nombre abstrait. Mais à ce moment aussi le nombre a cessé d'être imaginé et même d'être pensé ; nous n'avons conservé de lui que le signe, nécessaire au calcul, par lequel on est convenu de l'exprimer. Car on peut fort bien affirmer que 12 est la moitié de 24 sans penser ni le nombre 12 ni le nombre 24 : même, pour la rapidité des opérations, on a tout intérêt à n'en rien faire. Mais, dès qu'on désire se représenter le nombre, et non plus seulement des chiffres ou des mots, force est bien de revenir à une image étendue. Ce qui fait illusion sur ce point, c'est l'habitude contractée de compter dans le temps, semble-t-il, plutôt que dans l'espace. Pour imaginer le nombre cinquante, par exemple, on répétera tous les nombres à partir de l'unité; et quand on sera arrivé au cinquantième, on croira bien avoir construit ce nombre dans la durée, et dans la durée seulement. Et il est incontestable qu'on aura compté ainsi des moments de la durée, plutôt que des points de l'espace; mais la question est de savoir si ce n'est pas avec des points de l'espace qu'on aura compté les moments de la durée. Certes, il est possible d'apercevoir dans le temps, et dans le temps seulement, une succession pure et simple, mais non pas une addition, c'est-à-dire une succession qui aboutisse à une somme. Car si une somme s'obtient par la considération successive de différents termes, encore faut-il que chacun de ces termes demeure lorsqu'on passe au suivant, et attende, pour ainsi dire, qu'on l'ajoute aux autres : comment attendrait-il, s'il n'était qu'un instant de la durée ? et où attendrait-il, si nous ne le localisions dans l'espace ? Involontairement, nous fixons en un point de l'espace chacun des moments que nous comptons, et c'est à cette condition seulement que les unités abstraites forment une somme. Sans doute il est possible, comme nous le montrerons plus loin, de concevoir les moments successifs du temps indépendamment de l'espace ; mais lorsqu'on ajoute à l'instant actuel ceux qui le précédaient, comme il arrive quand on additionne des unités, ce n'est pas sur ces instants eux-mêmes qu'on opère, puisqu'ils sont à jamais évanouis, mais bien sur la trace durable qu'ils nous paraissent avoir laissée dans l'espace en le traversant. Il est vrai que nous nous dispensons le plus souvent de recourir à cette image, et qu'après en avoir usé pour les deux ou trois premiers nombres, il nous suffit de savoir qu'elle servirait aussi bien à la représentation des autres, si nous en avions besoin. Mais toute idée claire du nombre implique une vision dans l'espace ; et l'étude directe des unités qui entrent dans la composition d'une multiplicité distincte va nous conduire, sur ce point, à la même conclusion que l'examen du nombre lui-même. Tout nombre est une collection d'unités, avons-nous dit, et d'autre part tout nombre est une unité lui-même, en tant que synthèse des 'unités qui le composent. Mais le mot unité est-il pris dans les deux cas avec le même sens ? Quand nous affirmons que le nombre est un, nous entendons par là que nous nous le représentons dans sa totalité par une intuition simple et indivisible de l'esprit : cette unité renferme donc une multiplicité, puisque c'est l'unité d'un tout. Mais lorsque nous parlons des unités qui composent le nombre, ces dernières unités ne sont plus des sommes, pensons-nous, mais bien des unités pures et simples, irréductibles, et destinées à donner la série des nombres en se composant indéfiniment entre elles. Il semble donc qu'il y ait deux espèces d'unités, l'une définitive, qui formera un nombre en s'ajoutant à elle-même, l'autre provisoire, celle de ce nombre qui, multiple en lui-même, emprunte son unité à l'acte simple par lequel l'intelligence l'aperçoit. Et il est incontestable que, lorsque nous nous figurons les unités composantes du nombre, nous croyons penser à des indivisibles : cette croyance entre pour une forte part dans l'idée qu'on pourrait concevoir le nombre indépendamment de l'espace. Toutefois, en y regardant de plus près, on verra que toute unité est celle d'un acte simple de l'esprit, et que, cet acte consistant à unir, il faut bien que quelque multiplicité lui serve de matière. Sans doute, au moment où je pense chacune de ces unités isolément, je la considère comme indivisible, puisqu'il est entendu que je ne pense qu'à elle. Mais dès que je la laisse de côté pour passer à la suivante, je l'objective, et par là même j'en fais une chose, c'est-à-dire une multiplicité. Il suffira, pour s'en convaincre, de remarquer que les unités avec lesquelles l'arithmétique forme des nombres sont des unités provisoires, susceptibles de se morceler indéfiniment, et que chacune d'elles constitue une somme de quantités fractionnaires, aussi petites et aussi nombreuses qu'on voudra l'imaginer. Comment diviserait-on l'unité, s'il s'agissait ici de cette unité définitive qui caractérise un acte simple de l'esprit ? Comment la fractionnerait-on tout en la déclarant une, si on ne la considérait implicitement comme un objet étendu, un dans l'intuition, multiple dans l'espace ? Vous ne tirerez jamais d'une idée par vous construite ce que vous n'y aurez point mis, et si l'unité avec laquelle vous composez votre nombre est l'unité d'un acte, et non d'un objet, aucun effort d'analyse n'en fera sortir autre chose, que l'unité pure ou simple. Sans doute, quand vous égalez le nombre 3 à la somme 1 + 1 + 1, rien ne vous empêche de tenir pour indivisibles les unités qui le composent : mais c'est que vous n'utilisez point la multiplicité dont chacune de ces unités est grosse. Il est d'ailleurs probable que le nombre 3 se présente d'abord sous cette forme simple à notre esprit, parce que nous songerons plutôt à la manière dont nous l'avons obtenu qu'à l'usage que nous en pourrions faire. Mais nous ne tardons pas à nous apercevoir que, si toute multiplication implique la possibilité de traiter un nombre quelconque comme une unité provisoire qui s'ajoutera à elle-même, inversement les unités à leur tour sont de véritables nombres, aussi grands qu'on voudra, mais que l'on considère comme provisoirement indécomposables pour les composer entre eux. Or, par cela même que l'on admet la possibilité de diviser l'unité en autant de parties que l'on voudra, on la tient pour étendue. Il ne faudrait pas se faire illusion, en effet, sur la discontinuité du nombre. On ne saurait contester que la formation ou construction d'un nombre implique la discontinuité. En d'autres termes, ainsi que nous le disions plus haut, chacune des unités avec lesquelles je forme le nombre trois paraît constituer un indivisible pendant que j'opère sur elle, et je passe sans transition de celle qui précède à celle qui suit. Que si maintenant je construis le même nombre avec des demis, des quarts, des unités quelconques, ces unités constitueront encore, en tant qu'elles serviront à former ce nombre, des éléments provisoirement indivisibles, et c'est toujours par saccades, par sauts brusques pour ainsi dire, que nous irons de l'une à l'autre. Et la raison en est que, pour obtenir un nombre, force est bien de fixer son attention, tour à tour, sur chacune des unités qui le composent. L'indivisibilité de l'acte par lequel on conçoit l'une quelconque d'entre elles se traduit alors sous forme d'un point mathématique, qu'un intervalle vide d'espace sépare du point suivant. Mais, si une série de points mathématiques échelonnés dans l'espace vide exprime assez bien le processus par lequel nous formons l'idée de nombre, ces points mathématiques ont une tendance à se développer en lignes à mesure que notre attention se détache d'eux, comme s'ils cherchaient à se rejoindre les uns les autres. Et quand nous considérons le nombre à l'état d'achèvement, cette jonction est un fait accompli : les points sont devenus des lignes, les divisions se sont effacées, l'ensemble présente tous les caractères de la continuité. C'est pourquoi le nombre, composé selon une loi déterminée, est décomposable selon une loi quelconque. En un mot, il faut distinguer entre l'unité à laquelle on pense et l'unité qu'on érige en chose après y avoir pensé, comme aussi entre le nombre en voie de formation et le nombre une fois formé. L'unité est irréductible pendant qu'on la pense, et le nombre est discontinu pendant qu'on le construit : mais dès que l'on considère le nombre à l'état d'achèvement, on l'objective : et c'est précisément pourquoi il apparaît alors indéfiniment divisible. Remarquons, en effet, que nous appelons subjectif ce qui paraît entièrement et adéquatement connu, objectif ce qui est connu de telle manière qu'une multitude toujours croissante d'impressions nouvelles pourrait être substituée à l'idée que nous en avons actuellement. Ainsi un sentiment complexe contiendra un assez grand nombre d'éléments plus simples ; mais, tant que ces éléments ne se dégageront pas avec une netteté parfaite, on ne pourra pas dire qu'ils étaient entièrement réalisés, et, dès que la conscience en aura la perception distincte, l'état psychique qui résulte de leur synthèse aura par là même changé. Mais rien ne change à l'aspect total d'un corps, de quelque manière que la pensée le décompose, parce que ces diverses décompositions, ainsi qu'une infinité d'autres, sont déjà visibles dans l'image, quoique non réalisées : cette aperception actuelle, et non pas seulement virtuelle, de subdivisions dans l’indivisé est précisément ce que nous appelons objectivité. Dès lors, il devient aisé de faire la part exacte du subjectif et de l'objectif dans l'idée de nombre. Ce qui appartient en propre à l'esprit, c'est le processus indivisible par lequel il fixe son attention successivement sur les diverses parties d'un espace donné ; mais les parties ainsi isolées se conservent pour s'ajouter à d'autres, et une fois additionnées entre elles se prêtent à une décomposition quelconque : ce sont donc bien des parties d'espace, et l'espace est la matière avec laquelle l'esprit construit le nombre, le milieu où l'esprit le place. A vrai dire, c'est l'arithmétique qui nous apprend à morceler indéfiniment les unités dont le nombre est fait. Le sens commun est assez porté à construire le nombre avec des indivisibles. Et cela se conçoit sans peine, puisque la simplicité provisoire des unités composantes est précisément ce qui leur vient de l'esprit, et que celui-ci prête plus d'attention à ses actes qu'à la matière sur laquelle il agit. La science se borne à attirer notre regard sur cette matière : si nous ne localisions déjà le nombre dans l'espace, elle ne réussirait certes pas à nous l'y faire transporter. Il faut donc bien que, dès l'origine nous nous soyons représenté le nombre par une juxtaposition dans l'espace. C'est la conclusion à laquelle nous avions abouti d'abord, en nous fondant sur ce que toute addition implique une multiplicité de parties, perçues simultanément. Or, si l'on admet cette conception du nombre, on verra que toutes choses ne se comptent pas de la même manière, et qu'il y a deux espèces bien différentes de multiplicité. Quand nous parlons d'objets matériels, nous faisons allusion à la possibilité de les voir et de les toucher ; nous les localisons dans l'espace. Dès lors, aucun effort d'invention ou de représentation symbolique ne nous est nécessaire pour les compter ; nous n'avons qu'à les penser séparément d'abord, simultanément ensuite, dans le milieu même où ils se présentent à notre observation. Il n'en est plus de même si nous considérons des états purement affectifs de l'âme, ou même des représentations autres que celles de la vue et du toucher. Ici, les termes n'étant plus donnés dans l'espace, on ne pourra guère les compter, semble-t-il, a priori, que par quelque processus de figuration symbolique. Il est vrai que ce mode de représentation paraît tout indiqué lorsqu'il s'agit de sensations dont la cause est évidemment située dans l'espace. Ainsi, quand j'entends un bruit de pas dans la rue, je vois confusément la personne qui marche ; chacun des sons successifs se localise alors en un point de l'espace où le marcheur pourrait poser le pied ; je compte mes sensations dans l'espace même où leurs causes tangibles s'alignent. Peut-être quelques-uns comptent-ils d'une manière analogue les coups successifs d'une cloche lointaine leur imagination se figure la cloche qui va et qui vient cette représentation de nature spatiale leur suffit pour les deux premières unités ; les autres unités suivent naturellement. Mais la plupart des esprits ne procèdent pas ainsi : ils alignent les sons successifs dans un espace idéal, et s'imaginent compter alors les sons dans la pure durée. Il faut pourtant s'entendre sur ce point. Certes, les sons de la cloche m'arrivent successivement ; mais de deux choses l'une. Ou je retiens chacune de ces sensations successives pour l'organiser avec les autres et former un groupe qui me rappelle un air ou un rythme connu : alors je ne compte pas les sons, je me borne à recueillir l'impression pour ainsi dire qualitative que leur nombre fait sur moi. Ou bien je me propose explicitement de les compter, et il faudra bien alors que je les dissocie, et que cette dissociation s'opère dans quelque milieu homogène où les sons, dépouillés de leurs qualités, vidés en quelque sorte, laissent des traces identiques de leur passage. Reste à savoir, il est vrai, si ce milieu est du temps ou de l'espace. Mais un moment du temps, nous le répétons, ne saurait se conserver pour s'ajouter à d'autres. Si les sons se dissocient, c'est qu'ils laissent entre eux des intervalles vides. Si on les compte, c'est que les intervalles demeurent entre les sons qui passent : comment ces intervalles demeureraient-ils, s'ils étaient durée pure, et non pas espace ? C'est donc bien dans l'espace que s'effectue l'opération. Elle devient d'ailleurs de plus en plus difficile à mesure que nous pénétrons plus avant dans les profondeurs de la conscience. Ici nous nous trouvons en présence d'une multiplicité confuse de sensations et de sentiments que l'analyse seule distingue. Leur nombre se confond avec le nombre même des moments qu'ils remplissent quand nous les comptons ; mais ces moments susceptibles de s'additionner entre eux sont encore des points de l'espace. D'où résulte enfin qu'il y a deux espèces de multiplicité : celle des objets matériels, qui forme un nombre immédiatement, et celle des faits de conscience, qui ne saurait prendre l'aspect d'un nombre sans l'intermédiaire de quelque représentation symbolique, où intervient nécessairement l'espace. À vrai dire, chacun de nous établit une distinction entre ces deux espèces de multiplicité quand il parle de l'impénétrabilité de la matière. On érige parfois l'impénétrabilité en propriété fondamentale des corps, connue de la même manière et admise au même titre que la pesanteur ou la résistance par exemple. Cependant une propriété de ce genre, purement négative, ne saurait nous être révélée par les sens ; même, certaines expériences de mélange et de combinaison nous amèneraient à la révoquer en doute, si notre conviction n'était faite sur ce point. Imaginez qu'un corps pénètre un autre corps : vous supposerez aussitôt dans celui-ci des vides où les particules du premier viendront se loger ; ces particules à leur tour ne pourront se pénétrer que si l'une d'elles se divise pour remplir les interstices de l'autre ; et notre pensée continuera cette opération indéfiniment plutôt que de se représenter deux corps à la même place. Or, si l'impénétrabilité était réellement une qualité de la matière, connue par les sens, on ne voit pas pourquoi nous éprouverions plus de difficulté à concevoir deux corps se fondant l'un dans l'autre qu'une surface sans résistance ou un fluide impondérable. De fait, ce n'est pas une nécessité d'ordre physique, c'est une nécessité logique qui s'attache à la proposition suivante : deux corps ne sauraient occuper en même temps le même lieu. L'affirmation contraire renferme une absurdité qu'aucune expérience concevable ne réussirait à dissiper : bref, elle implique contradiction. Mais cela ne revient-il pas à reconnaître que l'idée même du nombre deux, ou plus généralement d'un nombre quelconque, renferme celle d'une juxtaposition dans l'espace ? Si l'impénétrabilité passe le plus souvent pour une qualité de la matière, c'est parce que l'on considère l'idée du nombre comme indépendante de l'idée d'espace. On croit alors ajouter quelque chose à la représentation de deux ou plusieurs objets en disant qu'ils ne sauraient occuper le même lieu : comme si la représentation du nombre deux, même abstrait, n'était pas déjà, comme nous l'avons montré, celle de deux positions différentes dans l'espace ! Poser l'impénétrabilité de la matière, c'est donc simplement reconnaître la solidarité des notions de nombre et d'espace, c'est énoncer une propriété du nombre, plutôt que de la matière. - Pourtant on compte des sentiments, des sensations, des idées, toutes choses qui se pénètrent les unes les autres et qui, chacune de son côté, occupent l'âme tout entière ? - Oui, sans doute, mais précisément parce qu'elles se pénètrent, on ne les compte qu'à la condition de les représenter par des unités homogènes, occupant des places distinctes dans l'espace, des unités qui ne se pénètrent plus par conséquent. L'impénétrabilité fait donc son apparition en même temps que le nombre ; et lorsqu'on attribue cette qualité à la matière pour la distinguer de tout ce qui n'est point elle, on se borne à énoncer sous une autre forme la distinction que nous établissions plus haut entre les choses étendues, qui se peuvent traduire immédiatement en nombre, et les faits de conscience, qui impliquent d'abord une représentation symbolique dans l'espace. Il convient de s'arrêter sur ce dernier point. Si, pour compter les faits de conscience, nous devons les représenter symboliquement dans l'espace, n'est-il pas vraisemblable que cette représentation symbolique modifiera les conditions normales de la perception interne ? Rappelons-nous ce que nous disions un peu plus haut de l'intensité de certains états psychiques. La sensation représentative, envisagée en elle-même, est qualité pure ; mais vue à travers l'étendue, cette qualité devient quantité en un certain sens ; on l'appelle intensité. Ainsi la projection que nous faisons de nos états psychiques dans l'espace pour en former une multiplicité distincte doit influer sur ces états eux-mêmes, et leur donner dans la conscience réfléchie une forme nouvelle, que l'aperception immédiate ne leur attribuait pas. Or remarquons que, lorsque nous parlons du temps, nous pensons le plus souvent à un milieu homogène où nos faits de conscience s'alignent, se juxtaposent comme dans l'espace, et réussissent à former une multiplicité distincte. Le temps ainsi compris ne serait-il pas à la multiplicité de nos états psychiques ce que l'intensité est à certains d'entre eux, un signe, un symbole, absolument distinct de la vraie durée ? Nous allons donc demander à la conscience de s'isoler du monde extérieur, et, par un vigoureux effort d'abstraction, de redevenir elle-même. Nous lui poserons alors cette question : la multiplicité de nos états de conscience a-t-elle la moindre analogie avec la multiplicité des unités d'un nombre ? La vraie durée a-t-elle le moindre rapport avec l'espace ? Certes, notre analyse de l'idée de nombre devrait nous faire douter de celle analogie, pour ne pas dire davantage. Car si le temps, tel que se le représente la conscience réfléchie, est un milieu où nos états de conscience se succèdent distinctement de manière à pouvoir se compter, et si, d'autre part, notre conception du nombre aboutit à éparpiller dans l'espace tout ce qui se compte directement, il est à présumer que le temps, entendu au sens d'un milieu où l'on distingue et où l'on compte, n'est que de l'espace. Ce qui confirmerait d'abord cette opinion, c'est qu'on emprunte nécessairement à l'espace, les images par lesquelles on décrit le sentiment que la conscience réfléchie a du temps et même de la succession : il faut donc que la pure durée soit autre chose. Mais ces questions, que nous sommes amenés à nous poser par l'analyse même de la notion de multiplicité distincte, nous ne pourrons les élucider que par une étude directe des idées d'espace et de temps, dans les rapports qu'elles soutiennent entre elles. On aurait tort d'attribuer une trop grande importance à la question de la réalité absolue de l'espace : autant vaudrait peut-être se demander si l'espace est ou n'est pas dans l'espace. En somme, nos sens perçoivent les qualités des corps, et l'espace avec elles : la grosse difficulté paraît avoir été de démêler si l'étendue est un aspect de ces qualités physiques - une qualité de la qualité - ou si ces qualités sont inétendues par essence, l'espace venant s'y ajouter, mais se suffisant à lui-même, et subsistant sans elles. Dans la première hypothèse, l'espace se réduirait à une abstraction, ou pour mieux dire à un extrait, il exprimerait ce que certaines sensations, dites représentatives, ont de commun entre elles. Dans la seconde, ce serait une réalité aussi solide que ces sensations mêmes, quoique d'un autre ordre. On doit à Kant la formule précise de cette dernière conception : la théorie qu'il développe dans l'Esthétique transcendantale consiste à doter l'espace d'une existence indépendante de son contenu, à déclarer isolable en droit ce que chacun de nous sépare en fait, et à ne pas voir dans l'étendue une abstraction comme les autres. En ce sens, la conception kantienne de l'espace diffère moins qu'on ne se l'imagine de la croyance populaire. Bien loin d'ébranler notre foi à la réalité de l'espace, Kant en a déterminé le sens précis et en a même apporté la justification. Il ne semble pas, d'ailleurs, que la solution donnée par Kant ait été sérieusement contestée depuis ce philosophe ; même, elle s'est imposée - parfois à leur insu - à la plupart de ceux qui ont de nouveau abordé le problème, nativistes ou empiristes. Les psychologues sont d'accord pour attribuer une origine kantienne à l'explication nativistique de Jean Muller ; mais l'hypothèse des signes locaux de Lotze, la théorie de Bain, et l'explication plus compréhensive proposée par Wundt paraîtront, au premier abord, tout à fait indépendantes de l'Esthétique transcendantale. Les auteurs de ces théories semblent, en effet, avoir laissé de côté le problème de la nature de l'espace pour rechercher seulement par quel processus nos sensations viennent y prendre place et se juxtaposer, pour ainsi dire, les unes aux autres : mais, par là même, ils considèrent les sensations comme inextensives, et établissent, à la manière de Kant, une distinction radicale entre la matière de la représentation et sa forme. Ce qui ressort des idées de Lotze, de Bain et de la conciliation que Wundt paraît en avoir tentée, c'est que les sensations par lesquelles nous arrivons à former la notion d'espace sont inétendues elles-mêmes et simplement qualitatives : l'étendue résulterait de leur synthèse, comme l'eau de la combinaison de deux gaz. Les explications empiristiques ou génétiques ont donc bien repris le problème de l'espace au point précis où Kant l'avait laissé : Kant a détaché l'espace de son contenu ; les empiristes cherchent comment ce contenu, isolé de l'espace par notre pensée, arriverait à y reprendre place. Il est vrai qu'ils paraissent avoir méconnu ensuite l'activité de l'intelligence, et qu'ils inclinent visiblement à engendrer la forme extensive de notre représentation par une espèce d'alliance des sensations entre elles : l'espace, sans être extrait des sensations, résulterait de leur coexistence. Mais comment expliquer une pareille genèse sans une intervention active de l'esprit ? L'extensif diffère par hypothèse de l'inextensif ; et à supposer que l'extension ne soit qu'un rapport entre des termes inextensifs, encore faut-il que ce rapport soit établi par un esprit capable d'associer ainsi plusieurs termes. En vain on alléguera l'exemple des combinaisons chimiques, où le tout paraît revêtir, de lui-même, une forme et des qualités qui n'appartenaient à aucun des atomes élémentaires. Cette forme, ces qualités naissent précisément de ce que nous embrassons la multiplicité des atomes dans une aperception unique : supprimez l'esprit qui opère cette synthèse, et vous anéantirez aussitôt les qualités, c'est-à-dire l'aspect sous lequel se présente à notre conscience la synthèse des parties élémentaires. Ainsi, des sensations inextensives resteront ce qu'elles sont, sensations inextensives, si rien ne s'y ajoute. Pour que l'espace naisse de leur coexistence, il faut un acte de l'esprit qui les embrasse toutes à la fois et les juxtapose ; cet acte sui generis ressemble assez à ce que Kant appelait une forme a priori de la sensibilité. Que si maintenant on cherchait à caractériser cet acte, on verrait qu'il consiste essentiellement dans l'intuition ou plutôt dans la conception d'un milieu vide homogène. Car il n'y a guère d'autre définition possible de l'espace : c'est ce qui nous permet de distinguer l'une de l'autre plusieurs sensations identiques et simultanées : c'est donc un principe de différenciation autre que celui de la différenciation qualitative, et, par suite, une réalité sans qualité. Dira-t-on, avec les partisans de la théorie des signes locaux, que des sensations simultanées ne sont jamais identiques, et que, par suite de la diversité des éléments organiques qu'ils influencent, il n'y a pas deux points d'une surface homogène qui produisent sur la vue ou sur le toucher la même impression ? Nous l'accorderons sans peine, car si ces deux points nous affectaient de la même manière, il n'y aurait aucune raison pour placer l'un d'eux à droite plutôt qu'à gauche. Mais précisément parce que nous interprétons ensuite cette différence de qualité dans le sens d'une différence de situation, il faut bien que nous ayons l'idée claire d'un milieu homogène, c'est-à-dire d'une simultanéité de termes qui, identiques en qualité, se distinguent néanmoins les uns des autres. Plus on insistera sur la différence des impressions faites sur notre rétine par deux points d'une surface homogène, plus seulement on fera de place à l'activité de l'esprit, qui aperçoit sous forme d'homogénéité étendue ce qui lui est donné comme hétérogénéité qualitative. Nous estimons d'ailleurs que si la représentation d'un espace homogène est due à un effort de l'intelligence, inversement il doit y avoir dans les qualités mêmes qui différencient deux sensations une raison en vertu de laquelle elles occupent dans l'espace telle ou telle place déterminée. Il faudrait donc distinguer entre la perception de l'étendue et la conception de l'espace : elles sont sans doute impliquées l'une dans l'autre, mais, plus on s'élèvera dans la série des êtres intelligents, plus se dégagera avec netteté l'idée indépendante d'un espace homogène. En ce sens, il est douteux que l'animal perçoive le monde extérieur absolument comme nous, et surtout qu'il s'en représente tout à fait comme nous l'extériorité.
