We must, however, be clear on this point. Certainly the sounds of the bell reach me successively; but one of two things must be the case. Either I retain each of these successive sensations in order to organise it with the others and form a group that reminds me of a known tune or rhythm: then I do not count the sounds, I confine myself to gathering the impression, qualitative so to speak, that their number makes on me. Or else I explicitly set out to count them, and then I shall have to dissociate them, and this dissociation will have to take place in some homogeneous medium in which the sounds, stripped of their qualities, emptied in some sort, leave identical traces of their passage. It remains to be seen, it is true, whether this medium is time or space. But a moment of time, I repeat, cannot be preserved in order to be added to others. If the sounds are dissociated, it is because they leave empty intervals between them. If they are counted, it is because the intervals remain between the sounds that pass: how could these intervals remain, if they were pure duration and not space? It is indeed in space, then, that the operation is carried out. It becomes, moreover, more and more difficult as we penetrate further into the depths of consciousness. Here we find ourselves in the presence of a confused multiplicity of sensations and feelings which analysis alone distinguishes. Their number is one with the very number of the moments they fill when we count them; but these moments, capable of being added together, are still points of space. Whence it follows, finally, that there are two species of multiplicity: that of material objects, which forms a number immediately, and that of facts of consciousness, which cannot take on the aspect of a number without the intermediary of some symbolic representation, in which space necessarily intervenes. In truth, each of us draws a distinction between these two species of multiplicity when he speaks of the impenetrability of matter. Impenetrability is sometimes set up as a fundamental property of bodies, known in the same way and admitted on the same footing as weight or resistance, for example. Yet a property of this kind, purely negative, cannot be revealed to us by the senses; indeed, certain experiments in mixture and combination would lead us to call it in question, if our conviction were not already settled on this point. Imagine one body penetrating another body: you will at once suppose in the latter empty spaces in which the particles of the former come to lodge; these particles in their turn will be able to penetrate one another only if one of them divides in order to fill the interstices of the other; and our thought will continue this operation indefinitely rather than represent two bodies in the same place. Now, if impenetrability were really a quality of matter, known by the senses, one does not see why we should find it more difficult to conceive two bodies melting into one another than a surface without resistance or an imponderable fluid. In fact, it is not a necessity of a physical order, it is a logical necessity, that attaches to the following proposition: two bodies cannot occupy the same place at the same time. The contrary assertion contains an absurdity that no conceivable experience would succeed in dispelling: in short, it implies contradiction. But does this not amount to acknowledging that the very idea of the number two, or more generally of any number whatever, contains that of a juxtaposition in space? If impenetrability most often passes for a quality of matter, it is because the idea of number is regarded as independent of the idea of space. One then believes one is adding something to the representation of two or more objects by saying that they cannot occupy the same place: as if the representation of the number two, even abstract, were not already, as I have shown, that of two different positions in space! To posit the impenetrability of matter is therefore simply to acknowledge the solidarity of the notions of number and space; it is to state a property of number rather than of matter. - Yet we count feelings, sensations, ideas, all of them things that permeate one another and each of which, for its part, occupies the whole soul? - Yes, no doubt, but precisely because they permeate one another, we count them only on condition of representing them by homogeneous units occupying distinct places in space, units, consequently, that no longer permeate one another. Impenetrability thus makes its appearance at the same time as number; and when this quality is attributed to matter in order to distinguish it from all that is not matter, one is merely stating in another form the distinction I drew above between extended things, which can be translated immediately into number, and facts of consciousness, which first imply a symbolic representation in space. It is worth dwelling on this last point. If, in order to count facts of consciousness, we have to represent them symbolically in space, is it not likely that this symbolic representation will modify the normal conditions of inner perception? Let us recall what I said a little above about the intensity of certain psychic states. Representative sensation, considered in itself, is pure quality; but seen through extension, this quality becomes quantity in a certain sense; it is called intensity. Thus the projection we make of our psychic states into space in order to form a distinct multiplicity of them must influence these states themselves, and give them in reflective consciousness a new form, which immediate apperception did not attribute to them. Now let us note that, when we speak of time, we most often think of a homogeneous medium in which our facts of consciousness are ranged, juxtaposed as in space, and succeed in forming a distinct multiplicity. Might not time thus understood be to the multiplicity of our psychic states what intensity is to some of them, a sign, a symbol, absolutely distinct from true duration? I shall therefore ask consciousness to isolate itself from the external world and, by a vigorous effort of abstraction, to become itself again. I shall then put this question to it: has the multiplicity of our states of consciousness the slightest analogy with the multiplicity of the units of a number? Has true duration the slightest relation to space? Certainly, our analysis of the idea of number ought to make us doubt this analogy, to say no more. For if time, as reflective consciousness represents it, is a medium in which our states of consciousness succeed one another distinctly so as to be capable of being counted, and if, on the other hand, our conception of number ends by scattering in space everything that is counted directly, it is to be presumed that time, understood in the sense of a medium in which we distinguish and count, is nothing but space. What would confirm this opinion in the first place is that we necessarily borrow from space the images by which we describe the feeling that reflective consciousness has of time and even of succession: pure duration, then, must be something else. But these questions, which we are led to ask ourselves by the very analysis of the notion of distinct multiplicity, can be elucidated only by a direct study of the ideas of space and time, in the relations they bear to one another. It would be a mistake to attach too great an importance to the question of the absolute reality of space: one might perhaps as well ask whether space is or is not in space. In short, our senses perceive the qualities of bodies, and space along with them: the great difficulty seems to have been to make out whether extension is an aspect of these physical qualities - a quality of quality - or whether these qualities are unextended by essence, space being added to them, but sufficient unto itself and subsisting without them. On the first hypothesis, space would be reduced to an abstraction, or, better, to an extract; it would express what certain sensations, called representative, have in common. On the second, it would be a reality as solid as these sensations themselves, though of another order. We owe to Kant the precise formulation of this latter conception: the theory he develops in the Transcendental Aesthetic consists in endowing space with an existence independent of its content, in declaring isolable in principle what each of us separates in fact, and in not seeing in extension an abstraction like the others. In this sense the Kantian conception of space differs less than is imagined from popular belief. Far from shaking our faith in the reality of space, Kant determined its precise meaning and even supplied its justification. It does not seem, moreover, that the solution given by Kant has been seriously contested since that philosopher's time; indeed, it has imposed itself - sometimes without their knowing it - on most of those who have approached the problem afresh, nativists or empiricists. Psychologists agree in attributing a Kantian origin to the nativistic explanation of Johannes Müller; but Lotze's hypothesis of local signs, Bain's theory, and the more comprehensive explanation proposed by Wundt will seem at first sight wholly independent of the Transcendental Aesthetic. The authors of these theories seem, in fact, to have left aside the problem of the nature of space in order to inquire only by what process our sensations come to take their place in it and to be juxtaposed, so to speak, with one another: but by that very fact they regard sensations as unextended, and establish, after the manner of Kant, a radical distinction between the matter of representation and its form. What emerges from the ideas of Lotze, of Bain, and from the reconciliation of them that Wundt seems to have attempted, is that the sensations by which we come to form the notion of space are themselves unextended and simply qualitative: extension would result from their synthesis, as water from the combination of two gases. The empiricist or genetic explanations have thus indeed taken up the problem of space at the precise point where Kant had left it: Kant detached space from its content; the empiricists inquire how this content, isolated from space by our thought, could come to take its place in it again. It is true that they seem afterwards to have overlooked the activity of the intellect, and that they visibly incline to engender the extensive form of our representation by a kind of alliance of sensations with one another: space, without being extracted from the sensations, would result from their coexistence. But how is such a genesis to be explained without an active intervention of the mind? The extensive differs by hypothesis from the unextended; and supposing that extension is only a relation between unextended terms, still this relation must be established by a mind capable of thus associating several terms. It would be vain to adduce the example of chemical combinations, in which the whole seems to put on, of itself, a form and qualities that belonged to none of the elementary atoms. This form and these qualities arise precisely from the fact that we embrace the multiplicity of atoms in a single apperception: suppress the mind that effects this synthesis, and you will at once annihilate the qualities, that is to say the aspect under which the synthesis of the elementary parts presents itself to our consciousness. Thus unextended sensations will remain what they are, unextended sensations, if nothing is added to them. For space to arise from their coexistence, there must be an act of the mind that embraces them all at once and juxtaposes them; this act sui generis rather resembles what Kant called an a priori form of sensibility. If now we sought to characterise this act, we should see that it consists essentially in the intuition, or rather the conception, of an empty homogeneous medium. For there is hardly any other possible definition of space: it is what enables us to distinguish from one another several identical and simultaneous sensations: it is therefore a principle of differentiation other than that of qualitative differentiation, and consequently a reality without quality. Will it be said, with the supporters of the theory of local signs, that simultaneous sensations are never identical, and that, owing to the diversity of the organic elements they affect, there are no two points of a homogeneous surface that produce the same impression on sight or on touch? I shall readily grant it, for if these two points affected us in the same way, there would be no reason for placing one of them to the right rather than to the left. But precisely because we afterwards interpret this difference of quality in the sense of a difference of situation, we must have the clear idea of a homogeneous medium, that is to say of a simultaneity of terms which, identical in quality, are nevertheless distinguished from one another. The more one insists on the difference between the impressions made on our retina by two points of a homogeneous surface, the more room one merely makes for the activity of the mind, which perceives in the form of extended homogeneity what is given to it as qualitative heterogeneity. I consider, moreover, that if the representation of a homogeneous space is due to an effort of the intellect, conversely there must be in the very qualities that differentiate two sensations a reason by virtue of which they occupy this or that determinate place in space. We should therefore have to distinguish between the perception of extension and the conception of space: they are no doubt implied in one another, but the higher we rise in the series of intelligent beings, the more clearly will the independent idea of a homogeneous space stand out. In this sense it is doubtful whether the animal perceives the external world exactly as we do, and above all whether it represents externality to itself quite as we do. Naturalists have pointed out, as a fact worthy of remark, the astonishing ease with which many vertebrates and even some insects manage to find their way in space. Animals have been seen to return almost in a straight line to their former home, covering, over a distance that may reach several hundred kilometres, a route they did not yet know. Attempts have been made to explain this sense of direction by sight or smell, and more recently by a perception of magnetic currents, which would enable the animal to orient itself like a compass. This amounts to saying that space is not as homogeneous for the animal as for us, and that the determinations of space, or directions, by no means take on for it a purely geometrical form. Each of them would appear to it with its own shade, its own quality. The possibility of a perception of this kind will be understood if we consider that we ourselves distinguish our right from our left by a natural feeling, and that these two determinations of our own extension do then present us with a difference of quality; that is even why we fail to define them. In truth, qualitative differences are everywhere in nature; and one does not see why two concrete directions should not be as marked in immediate apperception as two colours. But the conception of an empty homogeneous medium is a far more extraordinary thing, and seems to demand a kind of reaction against the heterogeneity that constitutes the very ground of our experience. We should therefore say not only that certain animals have a special sense of direction, but also, and above all, that we have the special faculty of perceiving or conceiving a space without quality. This faculty is not that of abstraction: indeed, if one notes that abstraction presupposes sharply drawn distinctions and a kind of externality of concepts or of their symbols with respect to one another, one will find that the faculty of abstraction already implies the intuition of a homogeneous medium. What we must say is that we know two realities of different orders, the one heterogeneous, that of sensible qualities, the other homogeneous, which is space. The latter, clearly conceived by the human intellect, enables us to make sharp distinctions, to count, to abstract, and perhaps also to speak. Now, if space is to be defined as the homogeneous, it seems that conversely every homogeneous and unbounded medium will be space. For since homogeneity here consists in the absence of all quality, one does not see how two forms of the homogeneous could be distinguished from one another. Nevertheless it is generally agreed to regard time as an unbounded medium, different from space but homogeneous like it: the homogeneous would thus take on a twofold form, according as a coexistence or a succession fills it. It is true that when we make time a homogeneous medium in which states of consciousness seem to unfold, we thereby give it to ourselves all at once, which amounts to saying that we withdraw it from duration. This simple reflection ought to warn us that we are then unconsciously falling back on space. On the other hand, it is understandable that material things, external to one another and external to us, should derive this twofold character from the homogeneity of a medium that sets intervals between them and fixes their outlines: but facts of consciousness, even successive ones, permeate one another, and in the simplest of them the whole soul may be reflected. There would therefore be ground for asking whether time, conceived in the form of a homogeneous medium, is not a bastard concept, due to the intrusion of the idea of space into the domain of pure consciousness. In any case, we cannot definitively admit two forms of the homogeneous, time and space, without first inquiring whether one of them might not be reducible to the other. Now externality is the distinctive character of things that occupy space, whereas facts of consciousness are not essentially external to one another, and become so only by an unfolding in time, regarded as a homogeneous medium. If, then, one of these two supposed forms of the homogeneous, time and space, derives from the other, we may affirm a priori that the idea of space is the fundamental datum. But, misled by the apparent simplicity of the idea of time, the philosophers who have attempted a reduction of these two ideas have believed they could construct the representation of space out of that of duration. By showing the flaw in this theory, I shall make it plain how time, conceived in the form of an unbounded and homogeneous medium, is nothing but the ghost of space haunting reflective consciousness. The English school endeavours, in fact, to reduce relations of extension to more or less complex relations of succession in duration. When, with our eyes closed, we pass our hand along a surface, the rubbing of our fingers against this surface, and above all the varied play of our joints, give us a series of sensations which are distinguished only by their qualities, and which present a certain order in time. On the other hand, experience tells us that this series is reversible, that we could, by an effort of a different kind (or, as I shall say later, in the opposite direction), give ourselves the same sensations again in an inverse order: relations of situation in space would then be defined, if one may so put it, as reversible relations of succession in duration. But such a definition contains a vicious circle, or at least a very superficial idea of duration. There are in fact, as I shall show in detail a little further on, two possible conceptions of duration, the one pure of all admixture, the other in which the idea of space surreptitiously intervenes. Wholly pure duration is the form that the succession of our states of consciousness takes when our self lets itself live, when it refrains from establishing a separation between the present state and the earlier states. It need not, for this, be wholly absorbed in the passing sensation or idea, for then, on the contrary, it would cease to endure. Nor need it forget the earlier states: it is enough that, in recalling these states, it does not juxtapose them with the present state as one point with another point, but organises them with it, as happens when we recall the notes of a melody, melted, so to speak, into one another. Might it not be said that, although these notes succeed one another, we nevertheless perceive them in one another, and that their whole is comparable to a living being, whose parts, though distinct, permeate one another by the very effect of their solidarity? The proof is that if we break the time by dwelling longer than is right on one note of the melody, it is not its exaggerated length, as length, that will warn us of our fault, but the qualitative change thereby brought to the whole of the musical phrase. One can thus conceive succession without distinction, and as a mutual penetration, a solidarity, an intimate organisation of elements, each of which, representative of the whole, is distinguished and isolated from it only for a thought capable of abstraction. Such is without any doubt the representation of duration that would be formed by a being at once identical and changing, who had no idea of space. But being familiar with this latter idea, indeed obsessed by it, we introduce it unawares into our representation of pure succession; we juxtapose our states of consciousness so as to perceive them simultaneously, no longer one in the other, but one beside the other; in short, we project time into space, we express duration in terms of extension, and succession takes for us the form of a continuous line or a chain, whose parts touch without permeating one another. Let us note that this last image implies the perception, no longer successive but simultaneous, of the before and the after, and that it would be a contradiction to suppose a succession which was only succession and yet was contained in one and the same instant. Now, when one speaks of an order of succession in duration, and of the reversibility of this order, is the succession in question pure succession, as I defined it above, without admixture of extension, or succession developing in space, in such a way that several separate and juxtaposed terms of it can be embraced at once? The answer is not in doubt: one cannot establish an order among terms without first distinguishing them, without then comparing the places they occupy; one therefore perceives them as multiple, simultaneous and distinct; in a word, one juxtaposes them, and if one establishes an order in the successive, it is because succession becomes simultaneity and is projected into space. In short, when the movement of my finger along a surface or a line gives me a series of sensations of diverse qualities, one of two things will happen: either I shall picture these sensations in duration only, but then they will succeed one another in such a way that I cannot, at a given moment, represent several of them to myself as simultaneous and yet distinct; - or else I shall discern an order of succession, but then it is because I have the faculty not only of perceiving a succession of terms, but also of ranging them together after having distinguished them; in a word, I already have the idea of space. The idea of a reversible series in duration, or even simply of a certain order of succession in time, thus itself implies the representation of space, and cannot be used to define it. To put this argument in a more rigorous form, let us imagine a straight line, unbounded, and on this line a material point A which moves. If this point became conscious of itself, it would feel itself change, since it moves: it would perceive a succession; but would this succession take on for it the form of a line? Yes, no doubt, provided it could rise in some sort above the line it is traversing and perceive simultaneously several juxtaposed points of it: but by that very fact it would form the idea of space, and it is in space that it would see the changes it undergoes unfold, not in pure duration. Here we put our finger on the error of those who regard pure duration as something analogous to space, but of a simpler nature. They like to juxtapose psychological states, to form a chain or a line out of them, and do not imagine that they are bringing into this operation the idea of space properly so called, the idea of space in its totality, because space is a medium of three dimensions. But who does not see that, in order to perceive a line in the form of a line, one must place oneself outside it, take account of the void that surrounds it, and consequently think a space of three dimensions? If our conscious point A does not yet have the idea of space - and it is indeed on this hypothesis that we must place ourselves - the succession of states through which it passes cannot take on for it the form of a line; but its sensations will be added dynamically to one another, and will organise themselves among themselves as do the successive notes of a melody by which we let ourselves be lulled. In short, pure duration might well be nothing but a succession of qualitative changes that melt into one another, that permeate one another, without precise outlines, without any tendency to externalise themselves in relation to one another, without any kinship with number: it would be pure heterogeneity. But I shall not dwell on this point for the moment: let it suffice to have shown that, from the instant one attributes the least homogeneity to duration, one surreptitiously introduces space. It is true that we count the successive moments of duration, and that, through its relations with number, time appears to us at first as a measurable magnitude, quite analogous to space. But there is an important distinction to be made here. I say, for example, that a minute has just elapsed, and I mean by this that a pendulum beating seconds has performed sixty oscillations. If I represent these sixty oscillations to myself all at once and by a single apperception of the mind, I exclude by hypothesis the idea of a succession: I think, not of sixty beats that succeed one another, but of sixty points on a fixed line, each of which symbolises, so to speak, an oscillation of the pendulum. - If, on the other hand, I wish to represent these sixty oscillations to myself successively, but without changing anything in their mode of production in space, I shall have to think of each oscillation while excluding the recollection of the preceding one, for space has preserved no trace of it: but by that very fact I shall condemn myself to remain forever in the present; I shall give up thinking a succession or a duration. If finally I preserve, joined to the image of the present oscillation, the recollection of the oscillation that preceded it, one of two things will happen: either I shall juxtapose the two images, and we then fall back on our first hypothesis; or I shall perceive them in one another, permeating one another and organising themselves among themselves like the notes of a melody, so as to form what I shall call an indistinct or qualitative multiplicity, without any resemblance to number: I shall thus obtain the image of pure duration, but I shall also have entirely freed myself from the idea of a homogeneous medium or of a measurable quantity. By carefully questioning consciousness, one will recognise that it proceeds in this way every time it refrains from representing duration symbolically. When the regular oscillations of the pendulum invite us to sleep, is it the last sound heard, the last movement perceived, that produces this effect? No, no doubt, for one would not understand why the first had not acted in the same way. Is it the recollection of those that precede, juxtaposed with the last sound or the last movement? But this same recollection, juxtaposed later with a single sound or movement, will remain ineffective. We must therefore admit that the sounds combined with one another, and acted, not by their quantity as quantity, but by the quality that their quantity presented, that is to say by the rhythmic organisation of their whole. Could the effect of a weak and continuous stimulus be understood otherwise? If the sensation remained identical with itself, it would remain indefinitely weak, indefinitely bearable. But the truth is that each addition of stimulus is organised with the preceding stimuli, and that the whole affects us like a musical phrase that was always on the point of ending and was ceaselessly modified in its totality by the addition of some new note. If we assert that it is always the same sensation, it is because we are thinking not of the sensation itself but of its objective cause, situated in space. We then in turn spread it out in space, and instead of an organism that develops, instead of modifications that permeate one another, we perceive one and the same sensation stretching out lengthwise, so to speak, and indefinitely juxtaposed with itself. True duration, the duration that consciousness perceives, ought thus to be ranked among the so-called intensive magnitudes, if indeed intensities could be called magnitudes; in truth, it is not a quantity, and as soon as one tries to measure it, one unconsciously substitutes space for it. But we experience an incredible difficulty in representing duration to ourselves in its original purity; and this is due, no doubt, to the fact that we do not endure alone: external things, it seems, endure as we do, and time, regarded from this latter point of view, has every appearance of a homogeneous medium. Not only do the moments of this duration seem external to one another, as bodies in space would be, but the movement perceived by our senses is the in some sort palpable sign of a homogeneous and measurable duration. What is more, time enters into the formulas of mechanics, into the calculations of the astronomer and even of the physicist, in the form of a quantity. We measure the velocity of a movement, which implies that time too is a magnitude. The very analysis I have just attempted needs to be completed, for if duration properly so called is not measured, what is it, then, that the oscillations of the pendulum measure? At a pinch, it will be admitted that inner duration, perceived by consciousness, is one with the fitting of the facts of consciousness into one another, with the gradual enrichment of the self; but the time that the astronomer introduces into his formulas, the time that our clocks divide into equal portions, that time, it will be said, is something else; it is a measurable magnitude, and consequently homogeneous. - Yet this is not so, and attentive examination will dispel this last illusion. When I follow with my eyes, on the dial of a clock, the movement of the hand that corresponds to the oscillations of the pendulum, I am not measuring duration, as seems to be believed; I am merely counting simultaneities, which is quite different. Outside me, in space, there is never more than a single position of the hand and of the pendulum, for of the past positions nothing remains. Within me, a process of organisation or mutual penetration of facts of consciousness is going on, which constitutes true duration. It is because I endure in this way that I represent to myself what I call the past oscillations of the pendulum, at the same time as I perceive the present oscillation. Now let us suppress for an instant the self that thinks these oscillations of the pendulum, a single position even of this pendulum, and consequently no duration. Let us suppress, on the other hand, the pendulum and its oscillations; there will be nothing left but the heterogeneous duration of the self, without moments external to one another, without relation to number. Thus within our self there is succession without mutual externality; outside the self, mutual externality without succession: mutual externality, since the present oscillation is radically distinct from the previous oscillation, which is no more; but absence of succession, since succession exists only for a conscious spectator who recalls the past and juxtaposes the two oscillations, or their symbols, in an auxiliary space. - Now between this succession without externality and this externality without succession a kind of exchange takes place, rather like what physicists call a phenomenon of endosmosis. As the successive phases of our conscious life, which nevertheless permeate one another, each correspond to an oscillation of the pendulum simultaneous with it, and as, on the other hand, these oscillations are sharply distinct, since the one is no more when the other occurs, we contract the habit of establishing the same distinction between the successive moments of our conscious life: the oscillations of the pendulum break it up, so to speak, into parts external to one another. Hence the mistaken idea of a homogeneous inner duration, analogous to space, whose identical moments would follow one another without permeating one another. But, on the other hand, the pendulum's oscillations, which are distinct only because one has vanished when the other appears, profit in some sort from the influence they have thus exerted on our conscious life. Thanks to the recollection of their whole that our consciousness has organised, they are preserved, then they are ranged in line: in short, we create for them a fourth dimension of space, which we call homogeneous time, and which enables the movement of the pendulum, although it takes place on the spot, to be juxtaposed indefinitely with itself. - If now we try, in this very complex process, to assign exactly their shares to the real and the imaginary, here is what we find. There is a real space, without duration, but in which phenomena appear and disappear simultaneously with our states of consciousness. There is a real duration, whose heterogeneous moments permeate one another, but each moment of which can be brought into relation with a state of the external world that is contemporaneous with it, and can be separated from the other moments by the effect of this very bringing together. From the comparison of these two realities there arises a symbolic representation of duration, drawn from space. Duration thus takes the illusory form of a homogeneous medium, and the link between these two terms, space and duration, is simultaneity, which might be defined as the intersection of time with space. By submitting the concept of movement, the living symbol of an apparently homogeneous duration, to the same analysis, we shall be led to carry out a dissociation of the same kind. It is most often said that a movement takes place in space, and when movement is declared homogeneous and divisible, it is the space traversed that one has in mind, as if it could be confused with the movement itself. Now, on further reflection, it will be seen that the successive positions of the moving body do indeed occupy space, but that the operation by which it passes from one position to the other, an operation which occupies duration and which has reality only for a conscious spectator, eludes space. We are dealing here not with a thing but with a progress: movement, in so far as it is the passage from one point to another, is a mental synthesis, a psychic and therefore unextended process. In space there are only parts of space, and at whatever point of space the moving body is considered, one will obtain only a position. If consciousness perceives something other than positions, it is because it recollects the successive positions and makes a synthesis of them. But how does it carry out a synthesis of this kind? It cannot be by a fresh unfolding of these same positions in a homogeneous medium, for a fresh synthesis would become necessary to connect the positions with one another, and so on indefinitely. We are therefore compelled to admit that there is here a synthesis which is, so to speak, qualitative, a gradual organisation of our successive sensations with one another, a unity analogous to that of a melodic phrase. Such is precisely the idea we form of movement when we think of it alone, when we extract from this movement, in a manner of speaking, its mobility. To be convinced of this, it will suffice to think of what one experiences on suddenly catching sight of a shooting star: in this extremely rapid movement, the dissociation takes place of itself between the space traversed, which appears to us in the form of a line of fire, and the absolutely indivisible sensation of movement or of mobility. A rapid gesture performed with the eyes closed will present itself to consciousness in the form of a purely qualitative sensation, as long as one has not thought of the space traversed. In short, there are two elements to be distinguished in movement: the space traversed and the act by which it is traversed, the successive positions and the synthesis of these positions. The first of these elements is a homogeneous quantity; the second has reality only in our consciousness; it is, as one pleases, a quality or an intensity. But here again a phenomenon of endosmosis occurs, an intermingling of the purely intensive sensation of mobility with the extensive representation of the space traversed. On the one hand, in fact, we attribute to movement the very divisibility of the space it traverses, forgetting that a thing can indeed be divided, but not an act; - and on the other hand we grow accustomed to projecting this act itself into space, to laying it along the line the moving body traverses, to solidifying it, in a word: as if this localisation of a progress in space did not amount to asserting that, even outside consciousness, the past coexists with the present! - From this confusion between movement and the space traversed by the moving body arose, in my view, the sophisms of the Eleatic school; for the interval separating two points is infinitely divisible, and if movement were composed of parts like those of the interval itself, the interval would never be crossed. But the truth is that each of Achilles' steps is a simple, indivisible act, and that after a given number of these acts Achilles will have passed the tortoise. The illusion of the Eleatics comes from their identifying this series of indivisible and sui generis acts with the homogeneous space which underlies them. As this space can be divided and recomposed according to any law whatever, they think themselves entitled to reconstitute the total movement of Achilles, no longer with Achilles' steps, but with tortoise steps: for Achilles pursuing the tortoise they in reality substitute two tortoises regulated on each other, two tortoises condemned to take the same kind of steps or simultaneous acts, so as never to reach each other. Why does Achilles pass the tortoise? Because each of Achilles' steps and each of the tortoise's steps are indivisibles in so far as they are movements, and different magnitudes in so far as they are space: so that the addition will soon give, for the space traversed by Achilles, a length greater than the sum of the space traversed by the tortoise and of the lead it had over him. This is what Zeno takes no account of when he recomposes the movement of Achilles according to the same law as the movement of the tortoise, forgetting that space alone lends itself to an arbitrary mode of decomposition and recomposition, and thus confusing space and movement. - I therefore do not think it necessary to admit, even after the subtle and profound analysis of a thinker of our time1, that the meeting of the two moving bodies implies a discrepancy between real movement and imagined movement, between space in itself and indefinitely divisible space, between concrete time and abstract time. Why resort to a metaphysical hypothesis, however ingenious, about the nature of space, time and movement, when immediate intuition shows us movement in duration, and duration outside space? There is no need to suppose a limit to the divisibility of concrete space; it may be left infinitely divisible, provided a distinction is drawn between the simultaneous positions of the two moving bodies, which are indeed in space, and their movements, which cannot occupy space, being duration rather than extension, quality and not quantity. To measure the velocity of a movement, as we shall see, is simply to note a simultaneity; to introduce this velocity into calculations is to use a convenient means of foreseeing a simultaneity. Thus mathematics remains within its role so long as it is concerned with determining the simultaneous positions of Achilles and the tortoise at a given moment, or when it admits a priori the meeting of the two moving bodies at a point X, a meeting which is itself a simultaneity. But it goes beyond this role when it claims to reconstitute what takes place in the interval between two simultaneities; or at least it is inevitably led, even then, to consider simultaneities again, fresh simultaneities, whose indefinitely increasing number ought to warn it that movement is not made out of immobilities, nor time out of space. In short, just as in duration nothing is homogeneous but what does not endure, that is to say space, in which the simultaneities are set out in a line, so the homogeneous element of movement is what belongs to it least, the space traversed, that is to say immobility. Now, precisely for this reason, science operates on time and movement only on condition of first eliminating from them their essential and qualitative element - from time, duration, and from movement, mobility. One would easily be convinced of this by examining the role played by considerations of time, movement and velocity in astronomy and mechanics. Treatises on mechanics take care to announce that they will define not duration itself, but the equality of two durations: "Two intervals of time are equal," they say, "when two identical bodies, placed in identical circumstances at the beginning of each of these intervals, and subjected to the same actions and influences of every kind, have traversed the same space at the end of these intervals." In other words, we shall note the precise instant at which the movement begins, that is to say the simultaneity of an external change with one of our psychic states; we shall note the moment at which the movement ends, that is to say a simultaneity again; finally we shall measure the space traversed, the only thing that is in fact measurable. There is therefore no question here of duration, but only of space and of simultaneities. To announce that a phenomenon will occur at the end of a time t is to say that consciousness will note between now and then a number t of simultaneities of a certain kind. And we must not let the words "between now and then" deceive us, for the interval of duration exists only for us, and on account of the mutual penetration of our states of consciousness. Outside us, one would find only space, and consequently simultaneities, of which one cannot even say that they are objectively successive, since all succession is thought through the comparison of the present with the past. – What clearly proves that the interval of duration itself does not count from the point of view of science is that, if all the movements of the universe took place two or three times faster, there would be nothing to alter either in our formulae or in the numbers we put into them. Consciousness would have an indefinable and, in a manner of speaking, qualitative impression of this change, but nothing of it would appear outside consciousness, since the same number of simultaneities would still occur in space. We shall see further on that when the astronomer predicts an eclipse, for example, he performs precisely an operation of this kind: he reduces the intervals of duration infinitely, which do not count for science, and thus perceives in a very short time - a few seconds at most - a succession of simultaneities which will take up several centuries for concrete consciousness, obliged as it is to live through their intervals. We shall arrive at the same conclusion by analysing the notion of velocity directly. Mechanics obtains this notion by way of a series of ideas whose filiation can easily be traced. It first constructs the idea of uniform movement by representing to itself, on the one hand, the trajectory AB of a certain moving body, and on the other a physical phenomenon which repeats itself indefinitely under identical conditions, for example the fall of a stone always dropping from the same height on to the same spot. If we mark on the trajectory AB the points M, N, P, ..., reached by the moving body at each of the moments at which the stone touches the ground, and the intervals AM, MN, NP, ..., are found to be equal to one another, the movement will be said to be uniform: and any one of these intervals will be called the velocity of the moving body, provided it is agreed to adopt as unit of duration the physical phenomenon chosen as term of comparison. The velocity of a uniform movement is thus defined without appeal to any notions other than those of space and simultaneity. - There remains variable movement, that whose elements AM, MN, NP, ..., have been found unequal to one another. To define the velocity of the moving body A at the point M, it will suffice to imagine an indefinite number of moving bodies A1, A2, A3, ..., all animated by uniform movements, and whose velocities v1, v2, v3, ..., arranged in increasing order for example, correspond to all possible magnitudes. Let us then consider, on the trajectory of the moving body A, two points M' and M" situated on either side of the point M, but very close to it. At the same time as this moving body reaches the points M', M, M", the other moving bodies arrive on their respective trajectories at points M'1, M1, M"1, M'2, M2, M"2, ..., etc.; and there necessarily exist two moving bodies Ah, Ap such that we have on the one hand M'M = M'hMh and on the other MM" = MpM"p. It will then be agreed to say that the velocity of the moving body A at the point M lies between vh and vp. But nothing prevents us from supposing the points M' and M" still closer to the point M, and it is conceivable that v h and v p must then be replaced by two new velocities vj and vn, the one greater than vh, the other less than vp. And as the two intervals M'M and MM" are made to decrease, so too will the difference between the two velocities of the corresponding uniform movements diminish. Now, since the two intervals can decrease down to zero, there evidently exists between vj and vn a certain velocity vm such that the difference between this velocity and vh, vj, ..., on the one hand, vp, vn, ..., on the other, can become smaller than any given quantity. It is this common limit vm that will be called the velocity of the moving body A at the point M. - Now, in this analysis of variable movement, as in that of uniform movement, there is question only of spaces once traversed and of simultaneous positions once reached. I was therefore justified in saying that if mechanics retains of time only simultaneity, it retains of movement itself only immobility. This result might have been foreseen by observing that mechanics necessarily operates on equations, and that an algebraic equation always expresses an accomplished fact. Now it is of the very essence of duration and of movement, as they appear to our consciousness, to be ceaselessly in the process of formation: thus algebra will be able to translate the results acquired at a certain moment of duration and the positions taken by a certain moving body in space, but not duration and movement themselves. In vain will one increase the number of simultaneities and positions under consideration by the hypothesis of very small intervals; in vain even, in order to mark the possibility of increasing the number of these intervals of duration indefinitely, will one replace the notion of difference by that of the differential: it is always at one extremity of the interval that mathematics places itself, however small it conceives it to be. As for the interval itself, as for duration and movement, in a word, they necessarily remain outside the equation. The reason is that duration and movement are mental syntheses, and not things; that, if the moving body occupies in turn the points of a line, movement has nothing in common with this line itself; and finally that, if the positions occupied by the moving body vary with the different moments of duration, if it even creates distinct moments by the mere fact of occupying different positions, duration properly so called has no moments that are identical or external to one another, being essentially heterogeneous to itself, indistinct, and without analogy with number. It follows from this analysis that space alone is homogeneous, that the things situated in space constitute a distinct multiplicity, and that every distinct multiplicity is obtained by an unrolling in space. It follows likewise that in space there is neither duration nor even succession, in the sense in which consciousness takes these words: each of the so-called successive states of the external world exists alone, and their multiplicity has reality only for a consciousness capable first of retaining them, then of juxtaposing them by externalising them in relation to one another. If it retains them, it is because these various states of the external world give rise to facts of consciousness which permeate one another, organise themselves imperceptibly together, and bind the past to the present by the effect of this very solidarity. If it externalises them in relation to one another, it is because, thinking afterwards of their radical distinctness (the one having ceased to be when the other appears), it perceives them in the form of a distinct multiplicity; which amounts to setting them out together in a line in the space in which each of them existed separately. The space employed for this purpose is precisely what is called homogeneous time. But another conclusion emerges from this analysis: it is that the multiplicity of states of consciousness, considered in its original purity, bears no resemblance to the distinct multiplicity which forms a number. There would be here, I said, a qualitative multiplicity. In short, we should have to admit two kinds of multiplicity, two possible senses of the word distinguish, two conceptions, the one qualitative and the other quantitative, of the difference between the same and the other. Sometimes this multiplicity, this distinctness, this heterogeneity contain number only potentially, as Aristotle would say; this is because consciousness carries out a qualitative discrimination without any ulterior thought of counting the qualities or even of making several of them; there is then indeed multiplicity without quantity. Sometimes, on the contrary, it is a matter of a multiplicity of terms which are counted or which are conceived as capable of being counted; but one then thinks of the possibility of externalising them in relation to one another; one develops them in space. Unfortunately, we are so accustomed to elucidating these two senses of the same word by each other, even to perceiving the one in the other, that we experience an incredible difficulty in distinguishing them, or at the very least in expressing this distinction in language. Thus I said that several states of consciousness organise themselves with one another, permeate one another, grow richer and richer, and might thus give a self ignorant of space the feeling of pure duration; but already, in order to use the word "several", I had isolated these states from one another, I had externalised them in relation to one another, I had juxtaposed them, in a word; and I thus betrayed, by the very expression to which I was obliged to resort, the deeply rooted habit of developing time in space. It is from the image of this development once effected that we necessarily borrow the terms intended to render the state of a soul which had not yet effected it: these terms are therefore tainted with an original vice, and the representation of a multiplicity having no relation to number or space, though clear to a thought which withdraws into itself and abstracts, cannot be translated into the language of common sense. And yet we cannot form the very idea of distinct multiplicity without considering alongside it what I have called a qualitative multiplicity. When we explicitly count units by setting them out in a line in space, is it not true that, alongside this addition whose identical terms stand out against a homogeneous background, there goes on, in the depths of the soul, an organisation of these units with one another, a wholly dynamic process, rather analogous to the purely qualitative representation that a sentient anvil would have of the increasing number of the hammer's blows? In this sense, one might almost say that the numbers in daily use each have their emotional equivalent. Shopkeepers know this well, and instead of indicating the price of an object by a round number of francs, they will mark the figure immediately below, at the cost of inserting afterwards a sufficient number of centimes. In short, the process by which we count units and form a distinct multiplicity of them presents a double aspect: on the one side we suppose them identical, which can be conceived only on condition that these units are set out in a line in a homogeneous medium; but on the other the third unit, for example, in being added to the other two, modifies the nature, the aspect and, as it were, the rhythm of the whole: without this mutual penetration and this in a manner of speaking qualitative progress, there would be no addition possible. - It is therefore thanks to the quality of quantity that we form the idea of a quantity without quality. It thus becomes evident that, apart from any symbolic representation, time will never take on for our consciousness the aspect of a homogeneous medium, in which the terms of a succession are externalised in relation to one another. But we arrive naturally at this symbolic representation by the mere fact that, in a series of identical terms, each term takes on a double aspect for our consciousness: the one always identical with itself, since we think of the identity of the external object, the other specific, because the addition of this term brings about a new organisation of the whole. Hence the possibility of spreading out in space, in the form of numerical multiplicity, what I have called a qualitative multiplicity, and of regarding the one as the equivalent of the other. Now, nowhere is this double process accomplished so easily as in the perception of the external phenomenon, unknowable in itself, which takes for us the form of movement. Here we certainly have a series of terms identical with one another, since it is always the same moving body; but on the other hand the synthesis carried out by our consciousness between the present position and what our memory calls the earlier positions causes these images to permeate one another, to complete one another and, in a manner of speaking, to continue one another. It is therefore chiefly by way of movement that duration takes the form of a homogeneous medium, and that time is projected into space. But, failing movement, any repetition of a well-defined external phenomenon would have suggested the same mode of representation to consciousness. Thus, when we hear a series of hammer blows, the sounds form an indivisible melody in so far as they are pure sensations, and still give rise to what I have called a dynamic progress: but knowing that the same objective cause is at work, we cut this progress up into phases which we then regard as identical; and since this multiplicity of identical terms can no longer be conceived except by spreading out in space, we again arrive necessarily at the idea of a homogeneous time, the symbolic image of real duration. In a word, our self touches the external world at its surface; our successive sensations, although melting into one another, retain something of the reciprocal externality which objectively characterises their causes; and that is why our superficial psychological life unfolds in a homogeneous medium without this mode of representation costing us any great effort. But the symbolic character of this representation becomes more and more striking as we penetrate further into the depths of consciousness: the inner self, the self which feels and is impassioned, the self which deliberates and decides, is a force whose states and modifications permeate one another intimately, and undergo a profound alteration as soon as they are separated from one another in order to be unrolled in space. But as this deeper self forms one and the same person with the superficial self, the two necessarily seem to endure in the same way. And as the constant representation of an identical objective phenomenon which repeats itself cuts up our superficial psychic life into parts external to one another, the moments thus determined in their turn determine distinct segments in the dynamic and undivided progress of our more personal states of consciousness. Thus the reciprocal externality which their juxtaposition in homogeneous space secures for material objects reverberates, thus it spreads, right into the depths of consciousness: little by little our sensations detach themselves from one another like the external causes which gave rise to them, and the feelings or ideas like the sensations with which they are contemporaneous. - What clearly proves that our ordinary conception of duration depends on a gradual invasion of space into the domain of pure consciousness is that, in order to deprive the self of the faculty of perceiving a homogeneous time, it suffices to detach from it this more superficial layer of psychic facts which it uses as regulators. Dream places us precisely in these conditions; for sleep, by slowing down the play of the organic functions, modifies above all the surface of communication between the self and external things. We then no longer measure duration, but we feel it; from quantity it returns to the state of quality; the mathematical estimation of elapsed time no longer takes place; but it gives way to a confused instinct, capable, like all instincts, of committing gross blunders and sometimes also of proceeding with extraordinary sureness. Even in the waking state, daily experience ought to teach us to make the distinction between duration-quality, the duration which consciousness reaches immediately, which the animal probably perceives, and time materialised, so to speak, time become quantity by a development in space. At the moment I write these lines, the hour is striking on a neighbouring clock; but my inattentive ear does not notice it until several strokes have already made themselves heard; I have therefore not counted them. And yet an effort of retrospective attention is enough for me to add up the four strokes already sounded and add them to those I hear. If, turning back into myself, I then question myself carefully about what has just happened, I perceive that the first four sounds had struck my ear and even stirred my consciousness, but that the sensations produced by each of them, instead of being juxtaposed, had melted into one another in such a way as to endow the whole with an aspect of its own, in such a way as to make of it a kind of musical phrase. In order to estimate retrospectively the number of strokes sounded, I tried to reconstitute this phrase in thought; my imagination struck one stroke, then two, then three, and as long as it had not reached the exact number four, sensibility, when consulted, replied that the total effect differed qualitatively. It had therefore noted in its own way the succession of the four strokes struck, but quite otherwise than by an addition, and without bringing in the image of a juxtaposition of distinct terms. In short, the number of strokes struck was perceived as quality, and not as quantity; this is how duration presents itself to immediate consciousness, and it retains this form so long as it does not give way to a symbolic representation drawn from extension. - Let us therefore distinguish, in conclusion, two forms of multiplicity, two very different estimations of duration, two aspects of conscious life. Beneath homogeneous duration, the extensive symbol of true duration, an attentive psychology disentangles a duration whose heterogeneous moments permeate one another; beneath the numerical multiplicity of states of consciousness, a qualitative multiplicity; beneath the self with well-defined states, a self in which succession implies fusion and organisation. But we are most often content with the first, that is to say with the shadow of the self projected into homogeneous space. Consciousness, tormented by an insatiable desire to distinguish, substitutes the symbol for the reality, or perceives the reality only through the symbol. As the self thus refracted, and thereby subdivided, lends itself infinitely better to the requirements of social life in general and of language in particular, consciousness prefers it, and gradually loses sight of the fundamental self. To recover this fundamental self, as an unaltered consciousness would perceive it, a vigorous effort of analysis is necessary, by which the internal and living psychological facts will be isolated from their image, first refracted, then solidified in homogeneous space. In other words, our perceptions, sensations, emotions and ideas present themselves under a double aspect: the one clear, precise, but impersonal; the other confused, infinitely mobile, and inexpressible, because language cannot grasp it without fixing its mobility, nor adapt it to its own commonplace form without making it fall into the common domain. If we end by distinguishing two forms of multiplicity, two forms of duration, it is evident that each of the facts of consciousness, taken separately, must take on a different aspect according as it is considered within a distinct multiplicity or within a confused multiplicity, in the time-quality in which it occurs, or in the time-quantity into which it is projected. When I walk for the first time, for example, in a town where I am going to stay, the things around me produce on me at the same time an impression which is destined to last and an impression which will be ceaselessly modified. Every day I see the same houses, and as I know they are the same objects, I constantly designate them by the same name, and I also imagine that they always appear to me in the same way. Yet if, after a fairly long time, I turn back to the impression I experienced during the first years, I am astonished at the singular, inexplicable and above all inexpressible change that has taken place in it. It seems that these objects, continually perceived by me and ceaselessly painting themselves in my mind, have ended by borrowing from me something of my conscious existence; like me they have lived, and like me grown old. This is not pure illusion; for if today's impression were absolutely identical with yesterday's, what difference would there be between perceiving and recognising, between learning and remembering? Yet this difference escapes the attention of most people; one will hardly notice it except on condition of being warned of it, and of then questioning oneself scrupulously. The reason is that our external and, so to speak, social life has more practical importance for us than our inner and individual existence. We tend instinctively to solidify our impressions in order to express them in language. Hence it comes about that we confuse the feeling itself, which is in perpetual becoming, with its permanent external object, and above all with the word which expresses this object. Just as the fleeting duration of our self is fixed by its projection into homogeneous space, so our ceaselessly changing impressions, wrapping themselves round the external object which is their cause, take on its precise outlines and its immobility. Our simple sensations, considered in their natural state, would offer still less consistency. A certain flavour, a certain scent pleased me when I was a child, and are repugnant to me today. Yet I still give the same name to the sensation experienced, and I speak as if, the scent and the flavour having remained identical, my tastes alone had changed. I thus solidify this sensation too; and when its mobility becomes so evident that it becomes impossible for me to fail to recognise it, I extract this mobility in order to give it a name of its own and solidify it in its turn in the form of a taste. But in reality there are neither identical sensations nor multiple tastes; for sensations and tastes appear to me as things as soon as I isolate and name them, and in the human soul there is hardly anything but progresses. What must be said is that every sensation is modified by being repeated, and that if it does not seem to me to change from one day to the next, it is because I now perceive it through the object which is its cause, through the word which translates it. This influence of language on sensation is more profound than is generally thought. Not only does language make us believe in the invariability of our sensations, but it will sometimes deceive us as to the character of the sensation experienced. Thus, when I eat a dish reputed to be exquisite, the name it bears, pregnant with the approval given to it, interposes itself between my sensation and my consciousness; I may believe that the flavour pleases me, when a slight effort of attention would prove the contrary to me. In short, the word with sharply defined outlines, the brutal word, which stores up what is stable, common and consequently impersonal in the impressions of mankind, crushes or at the very least covers over the delicate and fleeting impressions of our individual consciousness. To fight on equal terms, these would have to express themselves in precise words; but these words, hardly formed, would turn against the sensation which gave birth to them, and, invented to bear witness that the sensation is unstable, they would impose on it their own stability. Nowhere is this crushing of immediate consciousness so striking as in the phenomena of feeling. A violent love, a deep melancholy invade our soul: they are a thousand diverse elements which melt into one another, which permeate one another, without precise outlines, without the slightest tendency to externalise themselves in relation to one another; their originality is at this price. Already they are distorted when we disentangle a numerical multiplicity in their confused mass: what will it be when we spread them out, isolated from one another, in this homogeneous medium which will now be called, as one pleases, time or space? A moment ago each of them borrowed an indefinable colouring from the medium in which it was placed: here it is now discoloured, and quite ready to receive a name. The feeling itself is a being which lives, which develops, which consequently changes ceaselessly; otherwise one could not understand how it should lead us little by little to a resolution: our resolution would be taken immediately. But it lives because the duration in which it develops is a duration whose moments permeate one another: by separating these moments from one another, by unrolling time in space, we have made this feeling lose its animation and its colour. Here we are, then, in the presence of the shadow of ourselves: we believe we have analysed our feeling, we have in reality substituted for it a juxtaposition of inert states, translatable into words, each of which constitutes the common element, the residue, consequently impersonal, of the impressions felt in a given case by society as a whole. And that is why we reason about these states and apply our simple logic to them: having set them up as genera by the mere fact of isolating them from one another, we have prepared them to serve in a future deduction. Now if some bold novelist, tearing aside the cleverly woven web of our conventional self, shows us beneath this apparent logic a fundamental absurdity, beneath this juxtaposition of simple states an infinite penetration of a thousand diverse impressions which have already ceased to be at the moment they are named, we praise him for having known us better than we knew ourselves. This is not so, however, and by the very fact that he unrolls our feeling in a homogeneous time and expresses its elements in words, he in his turn presents us with only a shadow of it: only he has arranged this shadow in such a way as to make us suspect the extraordinary and illogical nature of the object which casts it; he has invited us to reflection by putting into the external expression something of that contradiction, of that mutual penetration, which constitutes the very essence of the elements expressed. Encouraged by him, we have drawn aside for an instant the veil which we interposed between our consciousness and ourselves. He has brought us back into the presence of ourselves. We should experience a surprise of the same kind if, breaking the frames of language, we endeavoured to grasp our ideas themselves in their natural state, and such as our consciousness, delivered from the obsession of space, would perceive them. This dissociation of the constitutive elements of the idea, which ends in abstraction, is too convenient for us to do without it in ordinary life and even in philosophical discussion. But when we imagine that the dissociated elements are precisely those which entered into the texture of the concrete idea, when, substituting for the penetration of the real terms the juxtaposition of their symbols, we claim to reconstitute duration out of space, we inevitably fall into the errors of associationism. I shall not dwell on this last point, which will be the subject of a thorough examination in the following chapter. Let it suffice to say that the unreflecting ardour with which we take sides in certain questions proves well enough that our intellect has its instincts: and how are we to represent these instincts to ourselves, if not by an impetus common to all our ideas, that is to say by their mutual penetration? The opinions to which we hold most are those we could account for least easily, and the very reasons by which we justify them are rarely those which determined us to adopt them. In a certain sense, we adopted them without reason, for what makes them valuable in our eyes is that their shade answers to the common colouring of all our other ideas, that we saw in them, from the first, something of ourselves. Thus they do not take on in our mind the commonplace form they will assume as soon as they are drawn out of it to be expressed in words; and although in other minds they bear the same name, they are not at all the same thing. To tell the truth, each of them lives in the manner of a cell in an organism; everything which modifies the general state of the self modifies it too. But whereas the cell occupies a determinate point of the organism, an idea which is truly ours fills our whole self. It is far, moreover, from being the case that all our ideas are thus incorporated into the mass of our states of consciousness. Many float on the surface, like dead leaves on the water of a pond. By this I mean that our mind, when it thinks them, always finds them again in a kind of immobility, as if they were external to it. Among these are the ideas we receive ready-made, and which remain in us without ever being assimilated to our substance, or again the ideas we have neglected to cultivate, and which have withered in neglect. If, as we move away from the deep strata of the self, our states of consciousness tend more and more to take the form of a numerical multiplicity and to spread out in a homogeneous space, it is precisely because these states of consciousness take on a more and more inert nature, a more and more impersonal form. We must not be surprised, then, if only those of our ideas which belong to us least are adequately expressible in words: to these alone, as we shall see, does the associationist theory apply. External to one another, they maintain among themselves relations into which the intimate nature of each of them does not enter at all, relations which can be classified: it will therefore be said that they are associated by contiguity, or by some logical reason. But if, digging beneath the surface of contact between the self and external things, we penetrate into the depths of the organised and living intellect, we shall witness the superposition, or rather the intimate fusion, of many ideas which, once dissociated, seem to exclude one another in the form of logically contradictory terms. The most bizarre dreams, in which two images overlap and present to us at one and the same time two different persons, who would yet be only one, will give a faint idea of the interpenetration of our concepts in the waking state. The imagination of the dreamer, isolated from the external world, reproduces on mere images, and parodies in its own way, the work which goes on ceaselessly, on ideas, in the deeper regions of intellectual life. Thus is verified, thus will be clarified by a more thorough study of internal facts, the principle I stated at the outset: conscious life presents itself under a double aspect, according as it is perceived directly or by refraction through space. - Considered in themselves, the deep states of consciousness have no relation to quantity; they are pure quality; they intermingle in such a way that one cannot say whether they are one or several, nor even examine them from this point of view without at once distorting them. The duration they thus create is a duration whose moments do not constitute a numerical multiplicity: to characterise these moments by saying that they encroach on one another would still be to distinguish them. If each of us lived a purely individual life, if there were neither society nor language, would our consciousness grasp the series of internal states in this indistinct form? Not entirely, no doubt, because we should retain the idea of a homogeneous space in which objects are sharply distinguished from one another, and because it is too convenient to set out in a line in such a medium, in order to resolve them into simpler terms, the in a manner of speaking nebulous states which at first strike the gaze of consciousness. But also, let us mark this well, the intuition of a homogeneous space is already a step towards social life. The animal probably does not represent to itself, as we do, besides its sensations, an external world quite distinct from itself, which is the common property of all conscious beings. The tendency by virtue of which we picture clearly to ourselves this externality of things and this homogeneity of their medium is the same as that which leads us to live in common and to speak. But as the conditions of social life are more completely realised, so too the current which carries our states of consciousness from within outwards becomes more pronounced: little by little these states are transformed into objects or things; they detach themselves not only from one another, but also from us. We then perceive them only in the homogeneous medium in which we have congealed their image and through the self which lends them its commonplace colouring. Thus a second self is formed which covers over the first, a self whose existence has distinct moments, whose states detach themselves from one another and are expressed without difficulty in words. And let me not be reproached here with splitting the person in two, with introducing into it in another form the numerical multiplicity I had at first excluded from it. It is the same self which perceives distinct states, and which, then fixing its attention more closely, will see these states melt into one another like needles of snow in prolonged contact with the hand. And, to tell the truth, for the convenience of language it has every interest in not re-establishing confusion where order reigns, and in not disturbing this ingenious arrangement of in a manner of speaking impersonal states by which it has ceased to form "a kingdom within a kingdom". An inner life with well-distinguished moments and sharply characterised states will answer better to the requirements of social life. Indeed, a superficial psychology may be content to describe it without thereby falling into error, provided however that it restricts itself to the study of facts once produced, and neglects their mode of formation. - But if, passing from statics to dynamics, this psychology claims to reason about facts in the making as it has reasoned about accomplished facts, if it presents the concrete and living self to us as an association of terms which, distinct from one another, are juxtaposed in a homogeneous medium, it will see insurmountable difficulties rise up before it. And these difficulties will multiply the more it exerts itself to resolve them, for all its efforts will only bring out more and more clearly the absurdity of the fundamental hypothesis by which time has been unrolled in space, and succession placed at the very heart of simultaneity. - We shall see that the contradictions inherent in the problems of causality, of freedom, of personality in a word, have no other origin, and that, to dispose of them, it suffices to substitute the real self, the concrete self, for its symbolic representation.

o: Il n'est pas difficile de comprendre pourquoi la question de la liberté met aux prises ces deux systèmes opposés de la nature, mécanisme et dynamisme. Le dynamisme part de l'idée d'activité volontaire, fournie par la conscience, et arrive à la représentation de l'inertie en vidant peu à peu cette idée : il conçoit donc sans peine une force libre d'un côté, et de l'autre une matière gouvernée par des lois. Mais le mécanisme suit la marche inverse. Les matériaux dont il opère la synthèse, il les suppose régis par des lois nécessaires, et bien qu'il aboutisse à des combinaisons de plus en plus riches, de plus en plus malaisées à prévoir, de plus en plus contingentes cri apparence, il ne sort pas du cercle étroit de la nécessité, où il s'était enfermé d'abord. - En approfondissant ces deux conceptions de la nature, on verrait qu'elles impliquent deux hypothèses assez différentes sur les rapports de la loi avec le fait qu'elle régit. A mesure qu'il élève plus haut ses regards, le dynamiste croit apercevoir des faits qui se dérobent davantage à l'étreinte des lois : il érige donc le fait en réalité absolue, et la loi en expression plus ou moins symbolique de cette réalité. Au contraire, le mécanisme démêle au sein du fait particulier un certain nombre de lois dont celui-ci constituerait, en quelque sorte, le point d'intersection ; c'est la loi qui deviendrait, dans cette hypothèse, la réalité fondamentale. - Que si, maintenant, on cherchait pourquoi les uns attribuent au fait et les autres à la loi une réalité supérieure, on trouverait, croyons-nous, que le mécanisme et le dynamisme prennent le mot simplicité dans deux sens très différents. Est simple, pour le premier, tout principe dont les effets se prévoient et même se calculent : la notion d'inertie devient ainsi, par définition même, plus simple que celle de liberté, l'homogène plus simple que l'hétérogène, l'abstrait plus simple que le concret.
