It would be seen that most of our daily actions are performed in this way, and that, thanks to the solidification in our memory of certain sensations, certain feelings, certain ideas, impressions from without call forth from us movements which, conscious and even intelligent though they are, resemble reflex acts in many respects. It is to these actions, very numerous but for the most part insignificant, that the associationist theory applies. Taken together, they form the substratum of our free activity, and play towards this activity the same part as our organic functions in relation to the whole of our conscious life. I shall grant to determinism, moreover, that we often abdicate our freedom in graver circumstances, and that, through inertia or indolence, we allow this same local process to take its course when our whole personality ought, so to speak, to vibrate. When our most trusted friends agree in advising us to take some important step, the feelings which they express with so much insistence come to settle on the surface of our self, and to solidify there in the manner of the ideas of which I was speaking just now. Little by little they will form a thick crust which will cover our personal feelings; we shall believe we are acting freely, and it is only on thinking it over later that we shall recognise our mistake. But then, too, at the moment when the act is about to be performed, it is not rare for a revolt to take place. It is the self from below which rises to the surface. It is the outer crust which bursts, yielding to an irresistible thrust. There was therefore going on, in the depths of this self, and beneath these very reasonably juxtaposed arguments, a seething and by that very fact a growing tension of feelings and ideas, not unconscious, no doubt, but to which we did not wish to pay heed. If we think it over carefully, if we gather our recollections with care, we shall see that we ourselves formed these ideas, we ourselves lived these feelings, but that, through an inexplicable reluctance to will, we had thrust them back into the obscure depths of our being each time they emerged at the surface. And that is why we seek in vain to explain our sudden change of resolution by the apparent circumstances which preceded it. We wish to know by virtue of what reason we made up our minds, and we find that we made up our minds without reason, perhaps even against all reason. But that is precisely, in certain cases, the best of reasons. For the action performed then no longer expresses some superficial idea, almost external to us, distinct and easy to express: it answers to the whole of our feelings, of our thoughts and of our most intimate aspirations, to that particular conception of life which is the equivalent of all our past experience, in short, to our personal idea of happiness and of honour. So it has been a mistake, in order to prove that man is capable of choosing without a motive, to go looking for examples in the ordinary and even indifferent circumstances of life. It could easily be shown that these insignificant actions are bound up with some determining motive. It is in solemn circumstances, when what is at stake is the opinion of ourselves which we shall give to others and above all to ourselves, that we choose in spite of what it is agreed to call a motive; and this absence of any tangible reason is the more striking the more profoundly free we are. But the determinist, even when he refrains from setting up the grave emotions or deep states of the soul as forces, nonetheless distinguishes them from one another, and thus arrives at a mechanistic conception of the self. He will show us this self hesitating between two contrary feelings, going from the one to the other, and finally deciding for one of them. The self and the feelings which stir it are thus likened to well-defined things, which remain identical with themselves throughout the whole course of the operation. But if it is always the same self that deliberates, and if the two contrary feelings that move it do not change either, how, by virtue of that very principle of causality which determinism invokes, will the self ever come to a decision? The truth is that the self, by the mere fact of having experienced the first feeling, has already changed somewhat when the second comes on: at every moment of the deliberation the self is modified and consequently modifies also the two feelings which stir it. Thus is formed a dynamic series of states which permeate one another, reinforce one another, and will issue in a free act by a natural evolution. But the determinist, obeying a vague need of symbolic representation, will designate by words the opposed feelings which divide the self between them, as well as the self itself. By making them crystallise in the form of well-defined words, he takes away in advance every kind of living activity, first from the person, and then from the feelings by which it is moved. He will then see, on the one side, a self always identical with itself, and, on the other, contrary feelings, no less invariable, which contend for it; victory will necessarily go to the stronger. But this mechanism, to which one has condemned oneself in advance, has no other value than that of a symbolic representation: it cannot hold out against the testimony of an attentive consciousness, which presents inner dynamism to us as a fact. In short, we are free when our acts spring from our whole personality, when they express it, when they have with it that indefinable resemblance which one sometimes finds between the work and the artist. It will be urged in vain that we then yield to the all-powerful influence of our character. Our character is still ourselves; and because it has pleased us to split the person into two parts in order to consider in turn, by an effort of abstraction, the self which feels or thinks and the self which acts, it would be somewhat childish to conclude that one of the two selves bears upon the other. The same reproach will apply to those who ask whether we are free to modify our character. Certainly our character is modified imperceptibly every day, and our freedom would suffer from it if these new acquisitions came to be grafted on to our self and not to melt into it. But as soon as this fusion has taken place, it must be said that the change which has come about in our character is truly ours, that we have appropriated it. In a word, if it is agreed to call free every act which springs from the self, and from the self alone, the act which bears the mark of our person is truly free, for our self alone will claim its paternity. The thesis of freedom would thus be verified if one consented to look for this freedom only in a certain character of the decision taken, in the free act, in a word. But the determinist, well aware that this position escapes him, takes refuge in the past or in the future. Sometimes he transports himself in thought to an earlier period, and asserts the necessary determination, at that precise moment, of the future act; sometimes, supposing the action already performed, he claims that it could not have come about otherwise. The opponents of determinism do not hesitate to follow him on to this new ground, and to introduce into their definition of the free act, not without some danger perhaps, the prevision of what one might do and the recollection of some other course for which one might have decided. It is fitting, then, to take up this new point of view, and to seek, setting aside external influences and the prejudices of language, what pure consciousness teaches us about future or past action. We shall thus grasp from another side, and in so far as they bear explicitly upon a certain conception of duration, the fundamental error of determinism and the illusion of its opponents. "To be conscious of free will," says Stuart Mill, "means to be conscious, before having chosen, of having been able to choose otherwise1." That is indeed how the defenders of freedom understand it: and they assert that when we perform an action freely, some other action would have been equally possible. They invoke on this point the testimony of consciousness, which makes us grasp, besides the act itself, the power of deciding for the contrary course. Conversely, determinism claims that, certain antecedents being posited, only one resulting action was possible: "When we suppose," Stuart Mill continues, "that we would have acted otherwise than we did, we always suppose a difference in the antecedents. We pretend to have known something that we did not know, or not to have known something that we did know, etc.2" And, faithful to his principle, the English philosopher assigns to consciousness the role of informing us about what is, not about what might be. - I shall not dwell, for the moment, on this last point; I reserve the question of knowing in what sense the self perceives itself as a determining cause. But beside this question of a psychological order there is another, of a rather metaphysical nature, which the determinists and their opponents settle a priori in opposite senses. The argument of the former implies, in fact, that to given antecedents there corresponds only one possible act; the partisans of free will suppose, on the contrary, that the same series could issue in several different acts, equally possible. It is on this question of the equal possibility of two contrary actions or of two contrary volitions that I shall dwell first: perhaps we shall thus gather some indication of the nature of the operation by which the will chooses. I hesitate between two possible actions X and Y, and I go from the one to the other in turn. This means that I pass through a series of states, and that these states can be divided into two groups, according as I incline more towards X or towards the contrary course. Indeed, these opposed inclinations alone have a real existence, and X and Y are two symbols by which I represent, at their points of arrival so to speak, two different tendencies of my person at successive moments of duration. Let us then designate by X and Y these tendencies themselves: will our new notation present a more faithful image of the concrete reality? It must be noticed, as I said above, that the self grows, is enriched and changes, as it passes through the two contrary states; otherwise, how would it ever come to a decision? There are therefore not, strictly speaking, two contrary states, but rather a multitude of successive and different states within which I disentangle, by an effort of imagination, two opposed directions. Hence we shall come still nearer to reality by agreeing to designate by the invariable signs X and Y, not these tendencies or states themselves, since they change unceasingly, but the two different directions which our imagination assigns to them for the greater convenience of language. It will remain understood, moreover, that these are symbolic representations, that in reality there are not two tendencies, nor even two directions, but rather a self which lives and develops by the effect of its very hesitations, until the free action drops from it like an over-ripe fruit. But this conception of voluntary activity does not satisfy common sense, because common sense, being essentially mechanistic, loves clear-cut distinctions, those which are expressed by well-defined words or by different positions in space. It will therefore picture a self which, after having traversed a series MO of facts of consciousness, and having arrived at the point O, sees itself confronted with two directions OX and OY, equally open. These directions thus become things, veritable roads into which the highway of consciousness would lead, and which it would depend only on the self to enter indifferently. In short, for the continuous and living activity of this self, in which we had discerned, by abstraction only, two opposed directions, one substitutes these directions themselves, transformed into inert, indifferent things which await our choice. But then the activity of the self must certainly be put somewhere. It will be put at the point O; it will be said that the self, having arrived at O, and faced with two courses to take, hesitates, deliberates, and finally decides for one of them. As it was hard to picture the twofold direction of conscious activity in all the phases of its continuous development, these two tendencies have been made to crystallise apart, and apart also the activity of the self; one thus obtains an indifferently active self which hesitates between two inert and, as it were, solidified courses. Now, if it decides for OX, the line OY will nonetheless remain; if it chooses OY, the road OX will remain open, waiting, if need be, for the self to retrace its steps in order to make use of it. It is in this sense that one will say, speaking of a free act, that the contrary action was equally possible. And even if one does not construct a geometrical figure on paper, one thinks of it involuntarily, almost unconsciously, as soon as one distinguishes several successive phases in the free act, representation of the opposed motives, hesitation and choice, thus concealing the geometrical symbolism under a kind of verbal crystallisation. Now it is easy to see that this truly mechanistic conception of freedom ends, by a natural logic, in the most inflexible determinism. The living activity of the self, in which we discerned by abstraction two opposed tendencies, will in fact end by issuing either in X or in Y. Now, since it is agreed to localise the twofold activity of the self at the point O, there is no reason to detach this activity from the act in which it will issue, and which forms one body with it. And if experience shows that one decided for X, it is not an indifferent activity that must be placed at the point O, but rather an activity directed in advance in the direction OX, in spite of apparent hesitations. If, on the contrary, observation proves that one decided for Y, it is because the activity localised by us at the point O favoured this second direction, in spite of some oscillations in the direction of the first. To declare that the self, having arrived at the point O, chooses indifferently between X and Y is to stop halfway along the road of geometrical symbolism; it is to make crystallise at the point O only a part of that continuous activity in which we did indeed discern two different directions, but which, in addition, issued in X or in Y: why not take account of this last fact as of the other two? Why not assign it its place, too, in the symbolic figure which we have just constructed? But if the self, having arrived at the point O, is already determined in one direction, it is no use the other road remaining open: the self cannot take it. And the same crude symbolism on which it was claimed to found the contingency of the action performed ends, by a natural extension, in establishing its absolute necessity. In short, defenders and opponents of freedom agree in making the action preceded by a kind of mechanical oscillation between the two points X and Y. If I decide for X, the former will tell me: you hesitated, deliberated, therefore Y was possible. The others will reply: you chose X, therefore you had some reason for doing so, and when Y is declared equally possible, this reason is forgotten; one of the conditions of the problem is left aside. - If now I dig beneath these two opposed solutions, I shall discover a common postulate: both sides place themselves after the action X has been performed, and represent the process of my voluntary activity by a road MO which forks at the point O, the lines OX and OY symbolising the two directions which abstraction distinguishes within the continuous activity of which X is the end. But whereas the determinists take account of all that they know and note that the road MOX has been traversed, their opponents affect to be ignorant of one of the data with which they constructed the figure, and after having drawn the lines OX and OY, which ought to represent, taken together, the progress of the self's activity, they make the self return to the point O to oscillate there until further notice. For it must not be forgotten that this figure, a veritable splitting of our psychic activity into two within space, is purely symbolic, and, as such, can be constructed only if one places oneself in the hypothesis of a deliberation completed and a resolution taken. It is no use your drawing it in advance; for you will then be supposing yourself to have arrived at the end, and to be witnessing the final act in imagination. In short, this figure does not show me the action in the doing, but the action done. Do not ask me, then, whether the self, having traversed the road MO and having decided for X, could or could not have chosen Y: I should reply that the question is devoid of meaning, because there is no line MO, no point O, no road OX, no direction OY. To put such a question is to admit the possibility of adequately representing time by space, and a succession by a simultaneity. It is to attribute to the figure one has drawn the value of an image, and no longer merely of a symbol; it is to believe that one could follow on this figure the process of psychic activity, like the march of an army on a map. One has witnessed the deliberation of the self in all its phases, and up to the act performed. Then, recapitulating the terms of the series, one perceives the succession in the form of simultaneity, one projects time into space, and one reasons, consciously or unconsciously, upon this geometrical figure. But this figure represents a thing, and not a progress; it corresponds, in its inertia, to the recollection, in some sort congealed, of the whole deliberation and of the final decision that was taken: how could it furnish us with the slightest indication of the concrete movement, of the dynamic progress, by which the deliberation issues in the act? And yet, once the figure is constructed, one goes back in imagination into the past, and insists that our psychic activity followed precisely the road traced by the figure. One thus falls back into the illusion which I pointed out above: one explains a fact mechanically, and then substitutes this explanation for the fact itself. And so, from the very first steps, one runs up against inextricable difficulties: if the two courses were equally possible, how did one choose? if only one of them was possible, why did one believe oneself free? - And one does not see that this twofold question always comes back to this: is time space? If I run my eyes over a road traced on the map, nothing prevents me from turning back and looking to see whether it forks here and there. But time is not a line along which one passes again. Certainly, once it has elapsed, we have the right to represent its successive moments to ourselves as external to one another, and so to think of a line which crosses space; but it will remain understood that this line symbolises, not time elapsing, but time elapsed. This is what defenders and opponents of free will alike forget, the former when they affirm and the latter when they deny the possibility of acting otherwise than one has done. The former reason thus: "The road is not yet traced, therefore it can take any direction whatever." To which the reply will be: "You forget that one can speak of a road only once the action has been performed; but then it will have been traced." - The others say: "The road has been traced in this way; therefore its possible direction was not any direction whatever, but this very direction." To which the rejoinder will be: "Before the road was traced, there was no direction either possible or impossible, for the very simple reason that there could as yet be no question of a road." - Set aside this crude symbolism, the idea of which obsesses you without your knowing it; you will see that the argument of the determinists takes this childish form: "The act, once performed, is performed"; and that their opponents reply: "The act, before being performed, was not yet performed." In other words, the question of freedom comes out of this discussion untouched; and this is easily understood, since freedom must be sought in a certain shade or quality of the action itself, and not in a relation of this act to what it is not or to what it might have been. All the obscurity comes from the fact that both sides represent deliberation to themselves in the form of an oscillation in space, whereas it consists in a dynamic progress in which the self and the motives themselves are in a continual becoming, like veritable living beings. The self, infallible in its immediate observations, feels itself free and declares it; but as soon as it seeks to explain its freedom to itself, it no longer perceives itself except by a kind of refraction through space. Hence a symbolism of a mechanistic nature, equally unfit to prove the thesis of free will, to make it understood, and to refute it. But the determinist will not admit defeat, and, putting the question in a new form, he will say: "Let us leave aside actions already performed, and consider only acts to come. The question is whether, knowing from today all the future antecedents, some higher intelligence could predict with absolute certainty the decision which will come of them." - I readily consent to the problem being put in these terms: I shall thus be given the opportunity of formulating my idea with greater rigour. But I shall first draw a distinction between those who think that knowledge of the antecedents would allow a probable conclusion to be formulated, and those who speak of an infallible prevision. To say that a certain friend, in certain circumstances, would very probably act in a certain way is not so much to predict the future conduct of our friend as to pass judgement on his present character, that is to say, in the last resort, on his past. Though our feelings, our ideas, our character in a word, are constantly being modified, it is rare to observe a sudden change; it is rarer still that one cannot say of a person one knows that certain actions seem fairly consistent with his nature, and that certain others are absolutely repugnant to it. All philosophers will agree on this point, for to establish a relation of fitness or unfitness between a given conduct and the present character of a person one knows is not to bind the future to the present. But the determinist goes much further: he asserts that the contingency of our solution is due to the fact that we never know all the conditions of the problem; that the probability of our prevision would increase in proportion as we were furnished with a greater number of these conditions; and that, finally, complete and perfect knowledge of all the antecedents without any exception would make the prevision infallibly true. Such, then, is the hypothesis which has to be examined. To fix our ideas, let us imagine a person called upon to take an apparently free decision in grave circumstances; we shall call him Peter. The question is whether a philosopher Paul, living at the same period as Peter or, if you prefer, several centuries before, could, knowing all the conditions in which Peter acts, have predicted with certainty the choice which Peter made. There are several ways of representing to oneself the state of a person at a given moment. We try to do so when we read a novel, for example; but whatever care the author has taken to depict the feelings of his hero and even to reconstruct their history, the outcome, foreseen or unforeseen, will add something to the idea we had of the character: therefore we know this character only imperfectly. In truth, the deep states of our soul, those which are expressed in free acts, express and sum up the whole of our past history: if Paul knows all the conditions in which Peter acts, it is presumably because no detail of Peter's life escapes him, and because his imagination reconstructs and even relives this history. But there is a capital distinction to be made here. When I myself pass through a certain psychological state, I know precisely the intensity of this state and its importance in relation to the others; not that I measure or compare, but because the intensity of a deep feeling, for example, is nothing other than this feeling itself. On the contrary, if I seek to give you an account of this psychological state, I shall be able to make you understand its intensity only by a precise sign of a mathematical nature; I shall have to measure its importance, compare it with what precedes and with what follows, and finally determine the share which falls to it in the final act. And I shall declare it more or less intense, more or less important, according as the final act is to be explained by it or without it. For my consciousness, on the contrary, which perceived this inner state, there was no need of a comparison of this kind; the intensity appeared to it as an inexpressible quality of the state itself. In other words, the intensity of a psychic state is not given to consciousness as a special sign which would accompany this state and determine its power, after the manner of an algebraic exponent: I have shown above that it expresses rather its shade, its own colouring, and that, if it is a feeling, for example, its intensity consists in being felt. Hence two ways of assimilating the states of consciousness of others will have to be distinguished: the one dynamic, which would consist in experiencing them oneself; the other static, by which one would substitute for the very consciousness of these states their image, or rather their intellectual symbol, their idea. One would then imagine them, instead of reproducing them. Only, in this latter case, one will have to join to the image of the psychic states the indication of their intensity, since they no longer act upon the person in whom they take shape, and since this person no longer has occasion to experience their force by feeling them. But this indication itself will necessarily take on a quantitative character: one will note, for example, that a certain feeling has more force than another feeling, that more account must be taken of it, that it has played a greater part; and how would one know this, if one did not know in advance the subsequent history of the person one is concerned with, and the acts in which this multiplicity of states or inclinations issued? Hence, for Paul to represent to himself adequately the state of Peter at any moment of his history, one of two things will be necessary: either that, like a novelist who knows where he is leading his characters, Paul should already know Peter's final act, and thus be able to join to the image of the successive states through which Peter is going to pass the indication of their value in relation to the whole of his history; - or that he should resign himself to passing through these various states himself, no longer in imagination, but in reality. The first of these hypotheses must be set aside, since the question is precisely whether, the antecedents alone being given, Paul will be able to foresee the final act. We are thus obliged to modify profoundly the idea we had formed of Paul: he is not, as we had at first thought, a spectator whose gaze plunges into the future, but an actor, who plays Peter's part in advance. And note that you cannot spare him any detail of this part, for the most trivial events have their importance in a history, and, supposing they had none, you could judge them insignificant only in relation to the final act, which, by hypothesis, is not given. Nor have you the right to shorten, were it by a second, the various states of consciousness through which Paul is going to pass before Peter; for the effects of the same feeling, for example, are added together and reinforce one another at every moment of duration, and the sum of these effects could be experienced all at once only if one knew the importance of the feeling, taken as a whole, in relation to the final act, which remains precisely in the dark. But if Peter and Paul have experienced the same feelings in the same order, if their two souls have the same history, how will you distinguish the one from the other? Will it be by the body in which they dwell? They would then differ constantly in some respect, since at no moment of their history would they represent to themselves the same body. Will it be by the place they occupy in duration? They would then no longer be present at the same events; now, by hypothesis, they have the same past and the same present, having the same experience. - You must now make up your mind to it: Peter and Paul are one and the same person, whom you call Peter when he acts and Paul when you recapitulate his history. In proportion as you made more complete the sum of the conditions which, once known, would have allowed Peter's future action to be predicted, you were keeping closer to the existence of this person, you were tending more and more to relive it in its smallest details, and you thus arrived at the precise moment when, the action being performed, there could no longer be any question of foreseeing it, but simply of acting. Here again every attempt at reconstructing an act which springs from the will itself leads you to the pure and simple observation of the accomplished fact. It is therefore a question devoid of meaning, this one: could the act or could it not be foreseen, given the complete whole of its antecedents? For there are two ways of assimilating these antecedents, the one dynamic, the other static. In the first case, one will be led by imperceptible transitions to coincide with the person one is concerned with, to pass through the same series of states, and thus to come back to the very moment at which the act is performed; there can therefore no longer be any question of foreseeing it. In the second case, one presupposes the final act by the mere fact of setting down, beside the indication of the states, the quantitative estimate of their importance. Here again the one side is led to observe simply that the act is not yet performed at the moment when it is about to be performed, the other that once performed it is performed for good. The question of freedom comes out of this discussion untouched, as it did out of the preceding one. On going more deeply into this twofold argument, we shall find, at its very root, the two fundamental illusions of reflective consciousness. The first consists in seeing in intensity a mathematical property of psychological states, and not, as I said at the beginning of this essay, the special quality, the proper shade, of these various states. The second consists in replacing the concrete reality, the dynamic progress which consciousness perceives, by the material symbol of this progress when it has reached its end, that is to say, of the accomplished fact together with the sum of its antecedents. Certainly, once the final act is consummated, I can assign to all the antecedents their proper value, and represent to myself in the form of a conflict or a composition of forces the combined play of these various elements. But to ask whether, the antecedents being known as well as their value, one could predict the final act, is to commit a vicious circle; it is to forget that, with the value of the antecedents, one gives oneself the final action which is to be foreseen; it is to suppose wrongly that the symbolic image by which one represents the completed operation was drawn by this operation itself in the course of its progress, as on a recording apparatus. It would be seen, moreover, that these two illusions in their turn imply a third, and that the question whether the act could or could not be foreseen always comes back to this: is time space? You began by juxtaposing in an ideal space the states of consciousness which succeeded one another in Peter's soul, and you perceive the life of this person in the form of a trajectory MOXY drawn by a moving body M in space. You then erase in thought the part OXY of this curve, and you ask yourself whether, knowing MO, you could have determined in advance the curve OX which the moving body describes from the point O. That, at bottom, is the question you were putting when you brought in a philosopher Paul, Peter's predecessor, charged with representing to himself in imagination the conditions in which Peter will act. You were thus materialising these conditions; you were making of the time to come a road already traced on the plain, which one can contemplate from the top of the mountain without having travelled it, without ever having to travel it. But you were not long in perceiving that the knowledge of the part MO of the curve would be insufficient, unless, however, you were told the position of the points of this line, not only in relation to one another, but also in relation to the points of the whole line MOXY; which would amount to giving oneself in advance the very elements which are to be determined. You then modified your hypothesis; you understood that time does not ask to be seen, but lived; you concluded from this that if your knowledge of the line MO did not constitute a sufficient datum, it was because you were looking at it from outside, instead of merging with the point M, which describes not only MO but also the whole curve, and thus adopting its movement. You therefore brought Paul to coincide with Peter, and naturally it is the line MOXY that Paul traced in space, since, by hypothesis, Peter describes this line. But you thus no longer prove that Paul foresaw Peter's action; you merely observe that Peter acted as he did, since Paul has become Peter. It is true that you then come back, without noticing it, to your first hypothesis, because you constantly confuse the line MOXY in the tracing with the line MOXY traced, that is to say, time with space. After having identified Paul with Peter for the needs of the case, you make Paul take up his former post of observation again, and he then perceives the complete line MOXY, which is not surprising, since he has just completed it. What makes the confusion natural, and even inevitable, is that science appears to furnish undisputed examples of a prevision of the future. Do we not determine in advance the conjunctions of heavenly bodies, the eclipses of sun and moon, and the greater number of astronomical phenomena? Does not the human intellect then embrace, in the present moment, as large a portion of duration to come as one pleases? - I readily grant it; but a prevision of this kind bears not the least resemblance to that of a voluntary act. Indeed, as we are about to see, the reasons which make the prediction of an astronomical phenomenon possible are precisely the same as those which prevent us from determining in advance a fact springing from free activity. For the future of the material universe, although contemporaneous with the future of a conscious being, has no analogy with it. To make this capital difference palpable, let us suppose for a moment that an evil genius, more powerful still than the evil genius of Descartes, were to command all the movements of the universe to go twice as fast. Nothing would be changed in astronomical phenomena, or at any rate in the equations which allow us to foresee them, for in these equations the symbol t does not designate a duration, but a ratio between two durations, a certain number of units of time, or finally, in the last analysis, a certain number of simultaneities; these simultaneities, these coincidences, would still occur in equal number; only the intervals which separate them would have diminished, but these intervals do not enter into the calculations at all. Now these intervals are precisely lived duration, the duration which consciousness perceives: and so consciousness would very soon warn us of a shortening of the day if, between sunrise and sunset, we had endured less. It would not measure this shortening, no doubt, and perhaps it would not even perceive it at once under the aspect of a change of quantity; but it would note, in one form or another, a falling-off in the ordinary enrichment of the being, a modification in the progress which it is accustomed to accomplish between the rising of the sun and its setting. Now, when the astronomer predicts an eclipse of the moon, for example, he is only exercising in his own way the power which we attributed to our evil genius. He commands time to go ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times faster, and he has the right to do so, since in this way he changes only the nature of the conscious intervals, and these intervals, by hypothesis, do not enter into the calculations. That is why, into a psychological duration of a few seconds, he will be able to fit several years, even several centuries, of astronomical time: such is the operation he engages in when he draws in advance the trajectory of a heavenly body or represents it by an equation. In truth, he confines himself to establishing a series of relations of position between this body and other given bodies, a series of simultaneities and coincidences, a series of numerical relations: as for duration properly so called, it remains outside the calculation, and would be perceived only by a consciousness capable not only of witnessing these successive simultaneities, but of living their intervals. One can even conceive that this consciousness might live a life slow enough, sluggish enough, to embrace the whole trajectory of the heavenly body in a single apperception, as happens to ourselves when we see the successive positions of a shooting star traced out in the form of a line of fire. This consciousness would then really find itself in the same conditions in which the astronomer places himself in imagination; it would see in the present what the astronomer perceives in the future. In truth, if the astronomer foresees a future phenomenon, it is on condition of making it up to a certain point a present phenomenon, or at least of enormously reducing the interval which separates us from it. In short, the time of which one speaks in astronomy is a number, and the nature of the units of this number cannot be specified in the calculations: one may therefore suppose them as small as one pleases, provided the same hypothesis extends to the whole series of operations, and the successive relations of position in space are thus preserved. One will then witness, in imagination, the phenomenon one wishes to predict; one will know at what precise point of space and after how many units of time this phenomenon occurs; it will then suffice to restore to these units their psychic nature in order to push the event back into the future, and to say that one has foreseen it, whereas in reality one has seen it. But these units of time, which constitute lived duration, and which the astronomer can dispose of as he pleases because they offer no hold to science, are precisely what interests the psychologist, for psychology is concerned with the intervals themselves, and no longer with their extremities. Certainly pure consciousness does not perceive time in the form of a sum of units of duration; left to itself, it has no means, nor even any reason, for measuring time; but a feeling which lasted half as many days, for example, would no longer be the same feeling for it; this state of consciousness would lack a multitude of impressions which have come to enrich it and to modify its nature. It is true that when we impose a certain name on this feeling, when we treat it as a thing, we believe we can reduce its duration by half, for example, and by half also the duration of all the rest of our history; it would still be the same existence, it seems, on a reduced scale. But we then forget that states of consciousness are progresses, and not things; that if we designate each of them by a single word, it is for the convenience of language; that they live, and that, living, they change unceasingly; that, consequently, one cannot cut off any moment from them without impoverishing them of some impression and thus modifying their quality. I quite understand that one may perceive the orbit of a planet all at once, or in a very short time, because its successive positions, or the results of its movement, alone matter, and not the duration of the equal intervals which separate them. But when it is a question of a feeling, it has no precise result, except that of having been felt; and to estimate this result adequately one would have to have passed through all the phases of the feeling itself, and occupied the same duration. Even if this feeling has finally found expression in some step of a determinate nature, comparable to the position of a planet in space, the knowledge of this act will hardly help me to estimate the influence of the feeling on the whole of a history, and it is this influence which has to be known. All prevision is in reality a vision, and this vision takes place when one can reduce more and more an interval of future time while preserving the relations of its parts to one another, as happens with astronomical predictions. But what is it to reduce an interval of time, if not to empty or impoverish the states of consciousness which succeed one another in it? And does not the very possibility of seeing an astronomical period in miniature thus imply the impossibility of modifying a psychological series in the same way, since it is only by taking this psychological series as an invariable basis that one can make an astronomical period vary arbitrarily as regards the unit of duration? When, therefore, one asks whether a future action could be foreseen, one unconsciously identifies the time of which the exact sciences speak, and which reduces to a number, with real duration, whose apparent quantity is truly a quality, and which one could not shorten by an instant without modifying the nature of the facts which fill it. And what doubtless makes this identification easier is that in a multitude of cases we have the right to operate on real duration as on astronomical time. Thus, when we call the past to mind, that is to say, a series of accomplished facts, we always abridge it, without, however, altering the nature of the event which interests us. This is because we know it already; because, having arrived at the end of the progress which constitutes its very existence, the psychological fact becomes a thing, which can be represented all at once. We are therefore here in the same position as that in which the astronomer places himself when he embraces in a single apperception the orbit which a planet will take several years to traverse. It is indeed with the recollection of a past fact of consciousness, not with the anticipated knowledge of a fact of consciousness to come, that astronomical prevision must be compared. But when it is a question of determining a fact of consciousness to come, if it is at all deep, the antecedents must be regarded no longer in the static state, in the form of things, but in the dynamic state and as progresses, since their influence alone is in question: now their duration is this very influence. That is why there can be no question of abridging the duration to come in order to represent its fragments in advance; one can only live this duration as it unrolls. In short, in the region of deep psychological facts, there is no appreciable difference between foreseeing, seeing and acting. Hardly more than one course will be left open to the determinist. He will give up alleging the possibility of foreseeing from today a certain act or state of consciousness to come, but will assert that every act is determined by its psychic antecedents, or, in other words, that facts of consciousness obey laws like the phenomena of nature. This argument consists, at bottom, in not entering into the detail of concrete psychological facts, from an instinctive fear of finding oneself face to face with phenomena which defy all symbolic representation, and consequently all prevision. The proper nature of these phenomena is then left in the dark, but it is asserted that, in their capacity as phenomena, they remain subject to the law of causality. Now this law requires that every phenomenon be determined by its conditions, or, in other words, that the same causes produce the same effects. Either, then, the act must be indissolubly bound up with its psychic antecedents, or the principle of causality must suffer an incomprehensible exception. This last form of the determinist argument differs less than one might think from all those which have been examined previously. To say that the same inner causes produce the same effects is to suppose that the same cause can appear several times over on the stage of consciousness. Now my conception of duration tends to nothing less than to assert the radical heterogeneity of deep psychological facts, and the impossibility of two of them being altogether alike, since they constitute two different moments of a history. Whereas the external object does not bear the mark of time elapsed, and thus, in spite of the diversity of moments, the physicist may find himself again in the presence of identical elementary conditions, duration is something real for the consciousness which keeps its trace, and one cannot speak here of identical conditions, because the same moment does not occur twice. It will be urged in vain that, though there are no two deep states of the soul which are alike, analysis would disentangle within these different states stable elements capable of being compared with one another. This would be to forget that psychological elements, even the simplest, have their own personality and their own life, if they are at all deep; they are constantly becoming, and the same feeling, by the mere fact of being repeated, is a new feeling. Indeed, we have no reason to keep its old name for it, except that it corresponds to the same external cause or is expressed outwardly by similar signs: one would therefore be committing a real begging of the question in deducing from the alleged similarity of the two states that the same cause produces the same effect. In short, if the causal relation still exists in the world of inner facts, it can in no way resemble what we call causality in nature. For the physicist, the same cause always produces the same effect; for a psychologist who does not let himself be led astray by apparent analogies, a deep inner cause gives its effect once, and will never produce it again. And if it is now alleged that this effect was indissolubly bound up with this cause, such an assertion will mean one of two things: either that, the antecedents being given, the future action could have been foreseen; or that, the action once performed, every other action appears, in the given conditions, as impossible. Now we have seen that these two assertions were equally devoid of meaning, and that they too implied a faulty conception of duration. Nevertheless, it does not seem to me useless to dwell on this last form of the determinist argument, were it only to clear up, from my point of view, the meaning of the two words determination and causality. It is in vain that I urge that there can be no question either of foreseeing a future action in the manner of an astronomical phenomenon, or of asserting, once the action is performed, that every other action would have been impossible in the given conditions. It is in vain that I add that, even in this form, "the same causes produce the same effects", the principle of universal determination loses every kind of meaning in the inner world of facts of consciousness. The determinist will perhaps yield to my argument on each of these three points in particular, will recognise that in the psychological world no one of these three senses can be attributed to the word determination, will even, no doubt, fail to discover a fourth, and yet will not cease to repeat that the act is indissolubly bound up with its antecedents. We are therefore here in the presence of an illusion so deep, of a prejudice so tenacious, that we could not get the better of them without attacking them in their very principle, which is the principle of causality. By analysing the concept of cause, I shall show the equivocation it contains, and without thereby defining freedom, I shall perhaps go beyond the purely negative idea of it which I have formed up to now. We perceive physical phenomena, and these phenomena obey laws. This means: 1st, that phenomena a, b, c, d previously perceived are capable of occurring again in the same form; 2nd, that a certain phenomenon P, which had appeared following the conditions a, b, c, d, and these conditions only, will not fail to recur as soon as the same conditions are given. If the principle of causality told us nothing more, as the empiricists claim, we should readily grant to these philosophers that their principle comes from experience; but it would no longer prove anything against our freedom. For it would remain understood that determinate antecedents give rise to a determinate consequent wherever experience makes us observe this regularity; but the question is precisely whether it is to be found again in the domain of consciousness, and the whole problem of freedom lies there. I grant you for a moment that the principle of causality merely sums up the uniform and unconditional successions observed in the past: by what right, then, do you apply it to those deep facts of consciousness in which no regular successions have yet been disentangled, since we fail to foresee them? And how can you rest on this principle in order to establish the determinism of inner facts, when, according to you, the determinism of observed facts is the sole foundation of this principle itself? In truth, when the empiricists bring the principle of causality to bear against human freedom, they take the word cause in a new acceptation, which is, moreover, that of common sense. To observe the regular succession of two phenomena is, in fact, to recognise that, the first being given, one already perceives the other. But this wholly subjective connection between two representations does not suffice for common sense. It seems to common sense that, if the idea of the second phenomenon is already implied in that of the first, the second phenomenon itself must exist objectively, in one form or another, within the first phenomenon. And common sense was bound to arrive at this conclusion, because the precise distinction between an objective connection among phenomena and a subjective association among their ideas already presupposes a fairly high degree of philosophical culture. One will therefore pass imperceptibly from the first sense to the second, and one will represent the causal relation to oneself as a kind of preformation of the phenomenon to come in its present conditions. Now this preformation may be understood in two very different senses, and it is precisely here that the equivocation begins. Mathematics, in fact, furnishes us with the image of a preformation of this kind. The same movement by which a circumference is traced in a plane generates all the properties of this figure: in this sense, an indefinite number of theorems pre-exist within the definition, although they are destined to unroll in duration for the mathematician who will deduce them. It is true that we are here in the domain of pure quantity, and that, since geometrical properties can be put in the form of equalities, it is quite conceivable that a first equation, expressing the fundamental property of the figure, should be transformed into an indefinite multitude of new equations, all virtually contained in it. On the contrary, the physical phenomena which succeed one another and are perceived by our senses are distinguished by quality no less than by quantity, so that one would have some difficulty in declaring them at the outset equivalent to one another. But precisely because our senses perceive them, nothing prevents us from attributing their qualitative differences to the impression they make upon us, and from supposing, behind the heterogeneity of our sensations, a homogeneous physical universe. In short, matter will be stripped of the concrete qualities with which our senses clothe it, colour, heat, resistance, even weight, and one will finally find oneself in the presence of homogeneous extension, of space without bodies. There will then hardly remain any other course to take than to cut out figures in space, to make them move according to mathematically formulated laws, and to explain the apparent qualities of matter by the form, the position and the movement of these geometrical figures. Now position is given by a system of fixed magnitudes, and movement is expressed by a law, that is to say, by a constant relation between variable magnitudes; but form is an image, and however tenuous, however transparent one supposes it, it still constitutes, in so far as our imagination has, so to speak, the visual perception of it, a concrete and therefore irreducible quality of matter. Consequently this image will have to be swept away and replaced by the abstract formula of the movement which generates the figure. Picture to yourself, then, algebraic relations entangling themselves one in another, objectifying themselves by this very entanglement, and giving birth, by the mere effect of their complexity, to concrete, visible and tangible reality: you will only be drawing the consequences of the principle of causality, understood in the sense of an actual preformation of the future within the present. It does not seem that the scientists of our time have pushed abstraction so far, except perhaps Sir William Thomson. This ingenious and profound physicist supposes space to be filled with a homogeneous and incompressible fluid in which vortices move, thus generating the properties of matter: these vortices are the constituent elements of bodies; the atom thus becomes a movement, and physical phenomena are reduced to regular movements taking place within an incompressible fluid. Now, if one will only notice that this fluid is of a perfect homogeneity, that there exists between its parts neither an empty interval separating them nor any difference whatever by which they might be distinguished, one will see that every movement taking place within this fluid is in fact equivalent to absolute immobility, since before, during and after the movement nothing changes, nothing is changed in the whole. The movement spoken of here is therefore not a movement which takes place, but a movement which is thought; it is a relation between relations. It is admitted, perhaps without being clearly realised, that movement is a fact of consciousness, that in space there are only simultaneities, and we are furnished with the means of calculating these relations of simultaneity for any moment whatever of our duration. Nowhere has mechanism been pushed further than in this system, since the very form of the ultimate elements of matter is there reduced to a movement. But Cartesian physics could already be interpreted in an analogous sense; for if matter is reduced, as Descartes would have it, to homogeneous extension, the movements of the parts of this extension can be conceived through the abstract law which governs them or through an algebraic equation between variable magnitudes, but cannot be represented in the concrete form of images. And it could easily be proved that the more the progress of mechanical explanations allows this conception of causality to be developed, and consequently the atom to be relieved of the weight of its sensible properties, the more the concrete existence of the phenomena of nature tends thus to vanish into algebraic smoke. Understood in this way, the relation of causality is a necessary relation in the sense that it will approach indefinitely the relation of identity, as a curve approaches its asymptote. The principle of identity is the absolute law of our consciousness; it asserts that what is thought is thought at the moment when one thinks it; and what constitutes the absolute necessity of this principle is that it does not bind the future to the present, but only the present to the present: it expresses the unshakeable confidence which consciousness feels in itself so long as, faithful to its role, it confines itself to observing the actual apparent state of the soul. But the principle of causality, in so far as it would bind the future to the present, would never take the form of a necessary principle; for the successive moments of real time are not bound up with one another, and no logical effort will succeed in proving that what has been will be or will continue to be, that the same antecedents will always call forth identical consequents. Descartes had understood this so well that he attributed to a constantly renewed grace of Providence the regularity of the physical world and the continuation of the same effects: he constructed, in a manner of speaking, an instantaneous physics, applicable to a universe whose duration would be wholly contained in the present moment. And Spinoza held that the series of phenomena, which takes for us the form of a succession in time, was equivalent, in the absolute, to the divine unity: he thus supposed, on the one hand, that the relation of apparent causality between phenomena reduced to a relation of identity in the absolute, and, on the other, that the indefinite duration of things was wholly contained in a single moment, which is eternity. In short, whether one goes deeply into Cartesian physics, Spinozist metaphysics or the scientific theories of our time, one will find everywhere the same concern to establish a relation of logical necessity between cause and effect, and one will see that this concern is expressed in a tendency to transform relations of succession into relations of inherence, to annul the action of duration, and to replace apparent causality by a fundamental identity. Now, if the development of the notion of causality, understood in the sense of necessary connection, leads to the Spinozist or Cartesian conception of nature, conversely every relation of necessary determination established between successive phenomena must come from our perceiving in a confused form, behind these heterogeneous phenomena, a mathematical mechanism. I do not claim that common sense has an intuition of the kinetic theories of matter, still less perhaps of a mechanism after the manner of Spinoza; but it will be seen that the more necessarily the effect seems bound up with the cause, the more we tend to put it in the cause itself, as the mathematical consequence is in the principle, and thus to suppress the action of duration. That under the influence of the same external conditions I do not behave today as I behaved yesterday is not at all surprising, because I change, because I endure. But things, considered apart from our perception, do not seem to us to endure; and the more deeply we go into this idea, the more absurd it seems to us to suppose that the same cause should not produce today the same effect that it produced yesterday. We do indeed feel, it is true, that if things do not endure as we do, there must nevertheless be in them some incomprehensible reason which makes phenomena seem to succeed one another, and not to unfold all at once. And that is why the notion of causality, though approaching indefinitely that of identity, will never seem to us to coincide with it, unless we clearly perceive the idea of a mathematical mechanism, or unless a subtle metaphysics comes to remove some fairly legitimate scruples on this point. It is nonetheless evident that our belief in the necessary determination of phenomena by one another grows firmer in proportion as we hold duration to be a more subjective form of our consciousness. In other words, the more we tend to set up the causal relation as a relation of necessary determination, the more we thereby assert that things do not endure as we do. Which amounts to saying that the more the principle of causality is strengthened, the more the difference which separates a psychological series from a physical series is accentuated. From which it follows finally, however paradoxical this opinion may appear, that the supposition of a relation of mathematical inherence between external phenomena ought to bring with it, as a natural or at least plausible consequence, belief in human freedom. But this last consequence will not concern me for the moment; I am seeking here only to determine the first sense of the word causality, and I think I have shown that the preformation of the future in the present is easily conceived in mathematical form, thanks to a certain conception of duration which is, though it may not seem so, fairly familiar to common sense. But there is a preformation of another kind, more familiar still to our mind, because immediate consciousness furnishes us with its image. We pass, in fact, through successive states of consciousness, and, although the following one was not contained in the preceding one, we did at that time represent its idea to ourselves more or less confusedly. The realisation of this idea, moreover, did not appear as certain, but simply as possible. Between the idea and the action, however, there have come to place themselves barely perceptible intermediaries, the whole of which takes on for us that sui generis form which is called the feeling of effort. And from the idea to the effort, from the effort to the act, the progress has been so continuous that we could not say where the idea and the effort end, where the act begins. It is conceivable, then, that in a certain sense one may still say here that the future was preformed in the present; but it will have to be added that this preformation is very imperfect, since the future action of which one has the present idea is conceived as realisable but not as realised, and since, even when one sketches out the effort necessary to accomplish it, one is well aware that there is still time to stop. If, then, one decides to conceive the causal relation in this second form, one may assert a priori that there will no longer be between cause and effect a relation of necessary determination, for the effect will no longer be given in the cause. It will reside there only in the state of a pure possible, and as a confused representation which will perhaps not be followed by the corresponding action. But we shall not be surprised that this approximation suffices for common sense, if we consider the ease with which children and primitive peoples accept the idea of an inconstant nature, in which caprice plays a part no less important than necessity. And this representation of causality will be more accessible to the common intelligence, since it demands no effort of abstraction, and implies only a certain analogy between the external world and the inner world, between the succession of objective phenomena and that of facts of consciousness. In truth, this second conception of the relation of cause to effect is more natural than the first, in that it answers at once to the need of a representation. Did I not say, in fact, that if we look for the phenomenon B within the very phenomenon A which regularly precedes it, it is because the habit of associating the two images ends by giving us the idea of the second phenomenon as enveloped in that of the first? It is natural that we should push this objectification to the end, and make of the phenomenon A itself a psychic state in which the phenomenon B would be contained in the form of a confused representation. In doing so we merely suppose that the objective connection of the two phenomena is similar to the subjective association which suggested the idea of it to us. The qualities of things will thus become veritable states, fairly analogous to those of our self; one will attribute to the material universe a vague personality, diffused through space, which, without being precisely endowed with a conscious will, passes from one state to another by virtue of an inner thrust, by virtue of an effort. Such was the ancient hylozoism, a timid and even contradictory hypothesis, which left matter its extension while attributing to it veritable states of consciousness, and unrolled the qualities of matter along extension at the same time as it treated these qualities as inner, that is to say simple, states. It was reserved for Leibniz to remove this contradiction, and to show that if the succession of external qualities or phenomena is understood as the succession of our own ideas, these qualities must be made simple states or perceptions, and the matter which supports them an unextended monad, analogous to our soul. Thenceforth the successive states of matter can no more be perceived from without than our own psychological states are; the hypothesis of pre-established harmony will have to be introduced in order to explain how all these inner states are representative of one another. Thus with our second conception of the relation of causality we arrive at Leibniz, as with the first at Spinoza. And in both cases we are only pushing to the extreme, or formulating with greater precision, two timid and confused ideas of common sense. Now it is evident that the relation of causality, understood in this second way, does not entail the determination of the effect by the cause. History itself bears witness to this. We see that the ancient hylozoism, the first development of this conception of causality, explained the regular succession of causes and effects by a veritable deus ex machina: it was sometimes a necessity external to things and hovering over them, sometimes an inner Reason, guiding itself by rules fairly similar to those which direct our conduct. The perceptions of Leibniz's monad do not necessitate one another either; God must have regulated their order in advance. Leibniz's determinism does not, in fact, come from his conception of the monad, but from his constructing the universe out of monads alone. Having denied any mechanical influence of substances upon one another, he had nevertheless to explain how their states correspond. Hence a determinism which has its origin in the necessity of admitting a pre-established harmony, and not at all in the dynamic conception of the relation of causality. But let us leave history aside. Consciousness testifies that the abstract idea of force is that of an indeterminate effort, of an effort which has not yet issued in the act and in which this act as yet exists only in the state of an idea. In other words, the dynamic conception of the relation of causality attributes to things a duration quite analogous to our own, whatever the nature of this duration may be: to represent the relation of cause to effect in this way is to suppose that the future is no more bound up with the present in the external world than it is for our own consciousness. It follows from this twofold analysis that the principle of causality contains two contradictory conceptions of duration, two no less incompatible images of the preformation of the future within the present. Sometimes we represent all phenomena, physical or psychological, as enduring in the same way, and consequently as enduring in our way; the future will then exist in the present only in the form of an idea, and the passage from the present to the future will take on the aspect of an effort, which does not always succeed in realising the idea conceived. Sometimes, on the contrary, we make duration the proper form of states of consciousness; things then no longer endure as we do, and we admit for things a mathematical pre-existence of the future in the present. Moreover, each of these hypotheses, taken by itself, safeguards human freedom; for the first would end by putting contingency even into the phenomena of nature; and the second, by ascribing the necessary determination of physical phenomena to the fact that things do not endure as we do, invites us precisely to make of the self that endures a free force. That is why every clear conception of causality, one in which we are consistent with ourselves, leads to the idea of human freedom as to a natural consequence. Unfortunately the habit has been formed of taking the principle of causality in both senses at once, because the one flatters our imagination more, and the other favours mathematical reasoning. Sometimes we think chiefly of the regular succession of physical phenomena and of that kind of inner effort by which one becomes the other; sometimes we fix our mind on the absolute regularity of these phenomena, and from the idea of regularity we pass by imperceptible degrees to that of mathematical necessity, which excludes duration understood in the first manner. And we see no harm in tempering these two images by each other, and in letting the one or the other prevail, according as we are more or less concerned with the interests of science. But to apply the principle of causality, in this equivocal form, to the succession of facts of consciousness is to create for oneself, wantonly and without any plausible reason, inextricable difficulties. The idea of force, which in reality excludes that of necessary determination, has contracted, so to speak, the habit of amalgamating itself with that of necessity, as a very consequence of the use that is made of the principle of causality in nature. On the one hand, we know force only through the testimony of consciousness, and consciousness does not affirm, does not even understand, the absolute determination of acts to come: that, then, is all that experience teaches us, and if we kept to experience, we should say that we feel ourselves free, that we perceive force, rightly or wrongly, as a free spontaneity. But on the other hand, this idea of force, carried over into nature, having travelled side by side with the idea of necessity, comes back corrupted from the journey. It comes back from it imbued with the idea of necessity; and in the light of the part we have made it play in the external world, we perceive force as determining in a necessary manner the effects that are to issue from it. Here again, the illusion of consciousness arises from its considering the self, not directly, but by a kind of refraction through the forms that it has lent to external perception, and which the latter does not give back to it without having, as it were, left its colour upon them. A sort of compromise has been effected between the idea of force and that of necessary determination. The wholly mechanical determination of two external phenomena by each other now assumes in our eyes the same form as the dynamic relation of our force to the act that emanates from it; but in return this latter relation takes on the aspect of a mathematical derivation, human action issuing mechanically, and therefore necessarily, from the force that produces it. That this fusion of two different, almost opposed, ideas offers advantages to common sense is not in doubt, since it allows us to represent to ourselves in the same way, and to designate by one and the same word, on the one hand the relation that exists between two moments of our own existence, and on the other the relation that binds together the successive moments of the external world. We have seen that if our deepest states of consciousness exclude numerical multiplicity, we nevertheless break them up into parts external to one another; that if the elements of concrete duration permeate one another, duration expressing itself in extension presents moments as distinct as the bodies scattered in space. Is it surprising that between the moments of our existence, objectified so to speak, we should establish a relation analogous to the objective relation of causality, and that an exchange, again comparable to a phenomenon of endosmosis, should take place between the dynamic idea of free effort and the mathematical concept of necessary determination? But the dissociation of these two ideas is an accomplished fact in the natural sciences. The physicist may speak of forces, and even represent their mode of action to himself by analogy with an inner effort, but he will never bring this hypothesis into a scientific explanation. Even those who, with Faraday, replace extended atoms by dynamic points will treat the centres of force and the lines of force mathematically, without concerning themselves with force itself, considered as activity or effort. It is therefore understood here that the relation of external causality is purely mathematical, and bears no resemblance to the relation of psychic force to the act that emanates from it. The moment has come to add: the relation of inner causality is purely dynamic, and has no analogy with the relation of two external phenomena that condition each other. For the latter, being capable of recurring in a homogeneous space, will enter into the composition of a law, whereas deep psychic facts present themselves to consciousness once, and will never appear again. A careful analysis of the psychological phenomenon first led me to this conclusion: the study of the notions of causality and duration, considered in themselves, has only confirmed it. I can now formulate my conception of freedom. We call freedom the relation of the concrete self to the act that it performs. This relation is indefinable, precisely because we are free. For we analyse a thing, but not a progress; we break up extension, but not duration. Or else, if we persist in analysing all the same, we unconsciously transform the progress into a thing, and duration into extension. By the mere fact of claiming to break up concrete time, we unroll its moments in homogeneous space; in place of the fact in the making we put the fact accomplished, and since we began by, as it were, congealing the activity of the self, we see spontaneity resolve into inertia and freedom into necessity. - That is why every definition of freedom will prove determinism right. Shall we, in fact, define the free act by saying of this act, once accomplished, that it might not have been? But this assertion - like the contrary assertion - implies the idea of an absolute equivalence between concrete duration and its spatial symbol: and as soon as we admit this equivalence, we arrive, by the very development of the formula just stated, at the most inflexible determinism. Shall we define the free act as "that which could not be foreseen, even when all its conditions are known in advance"? But to conceive all the conditions as given is, in concrete duration, to place oneself at the very moment at which the act is being accomplished. Or else we admit that the matter of psychic duration can be represented symbolically in advance, which amounts, as I have said, to treating time as a homogeneous medium, and to admitting in a new form the absolute equivalence of duration and its symbol. By going more deeply into this second definition of freedom, we shall therefore once more arrive at determinism. Shall we, finally, define the free act by saying that it is not necessarily determined by its cause? But either these words lose all kind of meaning, or we mean by them that the same inner causes will not always provoke the same effects. We admit, then, that the psychic antecedents of a free act are capable of recurring, that freedom unfolds in a duration whose moments resemble one another, and that time is a homogeneous medium, like space. By that very fact we shall be brought back to the idea of an equivalence between duration and its spatial symbol; and by pressing the definition of freedom that we have laid down, we shall once again draw determinism out of it. In short, every demand for clarification concerning freedom comes down, without our suspecting it, to the following question: "Can time be adequately represented by space?" - To which I reply: yes, if it is a question of time flown; no, if you speak of time flowing. Now the free act takes place in time flowing, and not in time flown. Freedom is therefore a fact, and among the facts we observe there is none clearer. All the difficulties of the problem, and the problem itself, arise from the wish to find in duration the same attributes as in extension, to interpret a succession by a simultaneity, and to render the idea of freedom in a language into which it is evidently untranslatable.

o: Pour résumer ce qui précède, nous laisserons d'abord de côté la terminologie et même la doctrine de Kant, sur lesquelles nous reviendrons plus loin, et nous nous placerons au point de vue du sens commun. Nous dirons que la psychologie actuelle nous a paru surtout préoccupée d'établir que nous apercevons les choses à travers certaines formes, empruntées à notre constitution propre. Cette tendance s'est de plus en plus accentuée depuis Kant : tandis que le philosophe allemand séparait nettement le temps de l'espace, l'extensif de l'intensif, et, comme nous dirions aujourd'hui, la conscience de la perception extérieure, l'école empiristique, poussant l'analyse plus loin, essaie de reconstituer l'extensif avec l'intensif, l'espace avec la durée, et l'extériorité avec des états internes. - La physique vient d'ailleurs compléter l’œuvre de la psychologie sur ce point : elle montre que si l'on veut prévoir les phénomènes, on doit faire table rase de l'impression qu'ils produisent sur la conscience et traiter les sensations comme des signes de la réalité non comme la réalité même. Il nous a semblé qu'il y avait lieu de se poser le problème inverse, et de se demander si les états les plus apparents du moi lui-même, que nous croyons saisir directement, ne seraient pas, la plupart du temps, aperçus à travers certaines formes empruntées au monde extérieur, lequel nous rendrait ainsi ce que nous lui avons prêté. A priori, il paraît assez vraisemblable que les choses se passent ainsi. Car à supposer que les formes dont on parle, et auxquelles nous adaptons la matière, viennent entièrement de l'esprit, il semble difficile d'en faire une application constante aux objets sans que ceux-ci déteignent bientôt sur elles : en utilisant alors ces formes pour la connaissance de notre propre personne, nous risquons de prendre pour la coloration même du moi un reflet du cadre où nous le plaçons, c'est-à-dire, en définitive, du monde extérieur. Mais on peut aller plus loin, et affirmer que des formes applicables aux choses ne sauraient être tout à fait notre œuvre ; qu'elles doivent résulter d'un compromis entre la matière et l'esprit ; que si nous donnons à cette matière beaucoup, nous en recevons sans doute quelque chose; et qu'ainsi, lorsque nous essayons de nous ressaisir nous-mêmes après une excursion dans le monde extérieur, nous n'avons plus les mains libres. Or, de même que pour déterminer les rapports véritables des phénomènes physiques entre eux nous faisons abstraction de ce qui, dans notre manière de percevoir et de penser, leur répugne manifestement, ainsi, pour contempler le moi dans sa pureté originelle, la psychologie devrait éliminer ou corriger certaines formes qui portent la marque visible du monde extérieur. - Quelles sont ces formes ? Isolés les uns des autres, et considérés comme autant d'unités distinctes, les états psychologiques paraissent plus ou moins intenses. Envisagés ensuite dans leur multiplicité, ils se déroulent dans le temps, ils constituent la durée.
